You are a clinical information extraction system. Read ONE outpatient consultation transcript (lines like "[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): text") and return ONE JSON object with the clinical information it contains, in the trained clinical-extraction format. Return only the JSON.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.
- A medicine the patient takes is not an allergy. A stopped medicine is not current. Dose, frequency, route and indication belong only to the medicine they were said for.
- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.
- Use the right status for plan items (planned, completed, recommended, conditional). Do not add a follow-up that was not arranged.
- If speakers disagree or a detail is unclear (dose, date, allergy, name), keep both statements and describe the real doubt in clinical_uncertainties.
- Cite one or two segment ids per item in evidence_ids. clinical_evidence is []. All confidence fields are null.

Transcript (encounter 30223)
[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Mehta, I checked you before the doctor calls. Blood pressure is 138 over 86, pulse 78, temperature 36.8, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. Please sit, he will be in shortly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Arjun, come in, and your wife too, please. I am all ears. What has been going on with you?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing, doctor, truly. Same old headache only. She has made a full drama and dragged me here.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It is not the same, doctor. For years it was his migraine, but this past month he wakes up with the pain, and he has been vomiting with it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Arre, don't exaggerate na. Vomiting happened twice, that is all, not every day. Morning headache, maybe a little, I don't know, it goes after tea.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hmm, I want to hear it properly. Arjun, how long have these headaches actually been with you?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Since college, so twenty years, more or less. It is migraine. It comes, I take a tablet, I carry on with work. I am fine.
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The old ones, yes. But the new morning pattern, sorry, I said one month just now, it is closer to three weeks. Three weeks he is worse on waking.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three weeks is also too much. Maybe, um, ten days. It is not a big thing, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the timing is a bit unclear, somewhere between ten days and three weeks. When it comes in the morning, what does the pain actually feel like?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Throbbing, same as always, left side. Light bothers me a bit. I lie down for some time and it eases. Nothing new in it.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he is snoring like anything these days, the whole night, and in the daytime he is so tired he dozes off on the sofa. He will never admit it.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not snore. And I am not tired. I work the full day, I am perfectly okay. She worries for no reason.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I am holding both versions for a moment. Any vomiting today, any fever, or any weakness in an arm or a leg?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no weakness, and the vomiting was not today. Last time was Sunday, and once before that, so twice only.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about double vision, any fit, confusion, or pain in the neck?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No, none of that. Vision is fine. I am telling you, it is the usual migraine, nothing else.
[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did say the light was hurting, and once he felt a bit sick in the car. But no, he has not had any fit, that much is true.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what medicines you are actually taking for the headache.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, when the headache starts. Maybe twice a week. And Crocin, paracetamol, one gram, if it is mild. I don't need much.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a week? Arjun, you have been taking the sumatriptan almost every morning this month, I have seen the strips. And the Crocin also, two or three times in a day, not just sometimes.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Those strips are old ones, she is counting old strips. I take fifty mg by mouth, only when I need it. Not every day. Please, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other regular tablets, for pressure or sugar or anything?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing regular. I am not a tablet person at all.
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father takes metformin for his diabetes, five hundred mg, but that is my father-in-law, not Arjun. And my sister takes biotin for her hair, that one is also not his.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, we will keep those separate, they are not yours. Any allergy to a medicine or a food?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No allergies. Nothing.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Wait, when he was small his mother said penicillin gave him a rash. He has avoided it since then. He always forgets to mention.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): That is some old story from childhood. I don't even remember a rash. I have taken so many antibiotics. There is no allergy, forget it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will note that you two don't agree, and we will be careful with penicillin anyway. Do you smoke, or take alcohol?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Alcohol only at weddings, one peg, very rare. I work in accounts, a sitting job, not much exercise.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He quit smoking six years back, actually. He says he doesn't smoke, but he used to, about ten a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, let me look at you quickly. Follow my finger, pupils are equal and reacting to light. There is no stiffness in the neck.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now squeeze my fingers, and push up with both feet. Power is normal on both sides. Touch your nose for me, coordination is fine, and I am not seeing any weakness.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): See, everything is normal only. Can we finish? I have a client call at four, this is eating my afternoon.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Almost. The back of the eyes looks clear, no swelling of the disc that I can make out. Walk to the door and back, gait is steady.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, sorry to interrupt, his weight today is 92 kilos and height is 172 centimetres, if you want them. He said the cuff felt tight, so the blood pressure I told you was the repeat reading.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that helps. Arjun, with this newer morning pain and the vomiting, I was going to book an MRI of the brain for this week.
[SEG0039] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, please book it. I have been saying something is not right. Also he grinds his teeth at night, but that one is old.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Teeth grinding is just tension from the office, for years, not a disease. And I don't want any scan. Waste of money. The headache is the same migraine I have always had.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand you feel it has not changed. Morning headache with vomiting is still a pattern I don't like to wave away. Your examination, though, is reassuring.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Actually, let me change that plan. I will not book the MRI today. We might do the scan if the morning headaches and the vomiting do not settle in two weeks.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks, fine. It will settle, it always settles. I don't even think we need to come back.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I would still like to see you in two weeks, whether it has settled or not, so we can decide properly. The visit itself is fixed. The scan is only if things are not better.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And what about the snoring and the tiredness? Could it be some sleep problem? My brother has sleep apnea and he uses a machine at night.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Her brother is a different case, he is very obese and all. I am not tired, I do not snore, I don't have that. Please don't start a new topic.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am not saying it is sleep apnea. That is one possibility I cannot rule out, along with a change in your migraine, or, less likely, something structural, given the morning vomiting. The scan stays a maybe, only if this does not settle.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Migraine, that is all it is. You can write migraine. The other things are just theory, doctor.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the sumatriptan, please don't take it every day even if the strips are in the drawer. Keep fifty milligrams for a clear attack, not more than two days in a week. Paracetamol one gram, maximum three times a day, not beyond that.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Three times, okay okay. I already don't take that much. Sumatriptan twice a week is what I do. She just worries too much.
[SEG0051] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, the paracetamol, sometimes he takes two tablets of 650, not the one gram. I have seen both boxes at home, Crocin 650 and the one gram. I am not sure which he finishes more.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Mostly the one gram. The 650 box is her sister's, I think, for period pain or something. I don't take that one.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we leave the sister's tablets completely out of this. For you, Arjun, when you take paracetamol, stick to one gram. I had been thinking of starting propranolol as a preventive, but with the picture still not clear I will not start it today.
[SEG0054] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had migraine also, quite bad. She used to take some blue tablet, I never knew the name of it.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, mother's migraine, half the family has something. The tablet name, who remembers. It doesn't change my case.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): A family tendency does fit your long history. I am not ordering any blood tests today. If the vomiting becomes daily, or you get weakness, new confusion, or a sudden thunderclap pain, come straight to emergency, don't wait out the two weeks.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): I can give the two-week follow-up slip at the desk when you leave. Do you want a morning or an evening slot, doctor?
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning slot, two weeks from today. You give him the slip. Arjun, keep a small note of headache days and any vomit, and bring it along. If you are clearly better we may skip the scan, and if not, we might send you for the MRI at that visit.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Diary, scan, all extra work. I will come in two weeks only because she will force me. I am still telling you it is nothing.
[SEG0060] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will be there, I will make sure of it. Thank you, doctor. He slept only four hours last night, and of course he will not tell you that himself.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four hours is very little, we can pick up the sleep at the next visit. Go safely, both of you.

You are a clinical information extraction system. Read ONE outpatient consultation transcript (lines like "[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): text") and return ONE JSON object with the clinical information it contains, in the trained clinical-extraction format. Return only the JSON.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.
- A medicine the patient takes is not an allergy. A stopped medicine is not current. Dose, frequency, route and indication belong only to the medicine they were said for.
- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.
- Use the right status for plan items (planned, completed, recommended, conditional). Do not add a follow-up that was not arranged.
- If speakers disagree or a detail is unclear (dose, date, allergy, name), keep both statements and describe the real doubt in clinical_uncertainties.
- Cite one or two segment ids per item in evidence_ids. clinical_evidence is []. All confidence fields are null.

Transcript (encounter 02094)
[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, thanks for waiting, come in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): hello, doctor
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): what's the the main thing today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, it's no symptoms. I don't know what's causing it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll just record a few vital signs
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, this won't take long...
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature 36.4, blood pressure 127 over 70, respiratory rate 16. And pulse is 84 beats a minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll go over that shortly. When did this begin?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yesterday, it came on out of nowhere.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): how troublesome is it day to day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly severe.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does anything else come with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, when it starts I tend to get a new partner as well. With new partner, I'd give it it a four, out of ten.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any discharge or sores at all?

Transcript (encounter 00861)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, doctor, I've done my back. Lifting a patient at work, a big chap, he slipped, and I caught him, and something went in my lower back. It's been three days. I'm a nurse, I should know better, and my mum says it's because I never stretch.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ouch. A spasm in the lower back, three days ago. Is that right?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, a back spasm, right across the bottom. I couldn't get out of the car.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the pain go anywhere?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Down the left leg, as far as the knee. Not below.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it feel stiff?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Stiff, like a board, especially in the morning.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about coughing or sneezing?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I yelp when I cough. The cat sneezed and I nearly died.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now, some important questions. Any numbness between your legs, in the saddle area?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no numbness there.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble passing urine?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my bladder's fine.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels? Any loss of control?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No weakness, I can walk. Slowly.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 400 mg, three times a day. And paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no allergies.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in your medical background?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Asthma, migraine, and a bit of scoliosis since my teens.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): A caesarean, in 2016.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Back problems in the family?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Mum has bad back trouble. Dad has high blood pressure, no, that's irrelevant, sorry.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your work.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a nurse on a care ward. Lots of lifting.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoking?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Gin at the weekend, a couple.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exercise?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Zumba on Wednesdays, though not this week.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, let me check you. Pulse 76, blood pressure 124 over 78, temperature 36.7, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 14, weight 68 kilos.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Normal then? ~
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Normal. Now, I'll feel along your back. Tell me where it's worst.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): There. And there. ~
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's tenderness and tightness in the muscles on the left side of the lower back.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm. ~
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lift your left leg straight, lying down. Does that reproduce the leg pain?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, at about forty degrees. ~
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the straight leg raise is mildly positive on the left.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that bad? ~
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any problem with your breathing?
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, my asthma's quiet.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any problem with your water or tummy, apart from what we've said?
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, all normal.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me repeat what I think. A pulled muscle in the lower back, but I can't rule out a slipped disc pressing on a nerve, given the leg pain.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I need a scan? ~
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. I'd like to arrange physiotherapy for you, and an X-ray of the spine.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the leg pain isn't better in two weeks, I'd like to arrange an MRI of your lower back.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And if it gets worse? ~
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get numbness between your legs, or any trouble with your bladder or bowels, go straight to the emergency department.
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Is that the only red flag? ~
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): The main one. Keep moving, gentle walking, no bed rest.
[SEG0061] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thank you. ~
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's not better in two weeks, come back and see me.
[SEG0063] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What can I do for you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the knee, doctor. I'm worried sick about it, I really am.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the rain was pouring and the bus was jammed, I was ages getting across, and then—
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. Sorry. Um, going down the stairs it catches me, and at night it's wicked.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months... no, nearer five months. It came on after the new year.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I end up like my mother? She had the two knees done. I'm not able for an operation, I just—
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop there. Morning stiffness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, about ten minutes till I get going. Is that bad? Should I be worried if it's only—
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Locking? Giving way?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't lock, and it hasn't given way.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hips or back?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just the right knee. Nothing else.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Could it be a clot though? I was reading last night and I haven't slept... well, I do sleep, but then I'm googling like a mad thing.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a clot. Stairs and night pain is the joint. What are you putting on it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel from the chemist. I rub it on twice a day. One percent, I think... maybe. I never properly looked at the tube.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother takes metformin for his sugar, the diabetes, and he says tablets wrecked his stomach, so I got nervous, but—
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tablets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac, the tablets, from the chemist as well. Only sometimes, when the pain is bad. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Strength?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams... no, seventy-five. The box says seventy-five. One of them, maybe two or three times in the week.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach problems?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No stomach problems. None.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. A small bit of heartburn if I take the tablet late in the evening. I couldn't tell you when that started. I didn't think it counted.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that dangerous? Do I stop the tablets altogether? The gel is the same drug, isn't it, will that burn me too? I've been fretting all week.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel is grand. If the heartburn comes, leave the tablets off. If you take one, take it with food, not on an empty stomach.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Eleven stone... no, sorry, twelve stone four. I always mix it up. They weighed me in the surgery last month.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That weight is loading the knee. Cut the biscuits. Short walks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister is on biotin, big tablets, for her hair. Would that do the knee any good? She keeps telling me to try it. Is it safe with the diclofenac? How many would I even take?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. That's your sister's. Biotin will not fix the knee. Don't start it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair enough. God, the weather though. I was telling my granddaughter, she's seven, she had camogie on Saturday and the rain never stopped. They were out on the pitch the whole hour. She thought it was brilliant, of course.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): They were soaked, and she lost one sock in the dressing room, just one sock. The cars around the school were bumper to bumper. We laughed the whole way home on the bus.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The knee.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. So what will you do? Physio? Someone said an injection. I'm terrified of needles, but if it works I'll do it. Does it work? How sore is it? Can you walk the same day?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Physio is one option. A steroid injection into the knee is another. I am not booking either today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Which is better though? If I try the physio first, can I still have the injection if it's no good? And how long are people waiting? The lists are a fright, aren't they?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either can wait. We decide next time, if the pain is still there.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it arthritis? Please say it straight. I've had myself in a wheelchair by Christmas, which is ridiculous, I know, but at three in the morning it doesn't feel ridiculous.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most likely osteoarthritis of the right knee. I can't confirm that without an x-ray, and I am not ordering one today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No x-ray? Is that safe? What if it's something else, a tumour or that? I know I sound mad.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing suggests a tumour. Osteoarthritis fits. Come back in six weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. And if it gets worse before that, the stairs are a killer, what do I do? Ring you? Go back to the chemist?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ring the surgery if you cannot walk on it or it swells right up. Otherwise the gel twice a day, the tablets only now and again with food, and keep moving.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the heartburn go if I ease off the tablets? And should I be on something for the stomach? I don't want an ulcer. My head is racing.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off and it should settle. No stomach tablet from me today. Six weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'll try to stay off Google. Thanks a million.

[SEG0077] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. If you're breathing harder at rest, come in sooner.

[SEG0080] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the patch and walk you down. Also your truck keys were up front.
[SEG0081] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks. Told you it's not even that bad.

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. What's been going on with them?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, I stopped the cholesterol tablet. I read something online and then I couldn't sleep, and I just stopped.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which one was it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. The 20 — no, wait, it was 40 milligrams. I'm sure of that. I took it at night.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you stop?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. Sometime after that article. I really don't know.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, we won't make up a month. What did you read that scared you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That statins wreck your muscles and your memory, and if you stop you'll have a heart attack. Is any of that true? Did I set myself up for a heart attack?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to tell you that you did. Those articles mix a real thing, muscle aches in some people, with a lot of scare language. Stopping a statin does not by itself cause a heart attack.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Why is that stuff everywhere if it's wrong? I don't get how I'm supposed to know what to trust.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's everywhere because scary headlines travel. The useful bit is the muscle-ache risk, and we can talk about that without the rest of it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): But could it still happen? What are the chances? Should I be in the ER? I've been worried sick. I check my pulse in the grocery store.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crushing chest pain, yes, that is the ER. Checking your pulse at the store is the worry talking, not a heart attack. We'll make a plan, and I'm not going to scold you.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry. My sister says I google too much. We were over there and her dog ate a whole stick of butter, which, um, doesn't matter.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Are you still taking the blood pressure pill?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The lisinopril. But not every day. I take it every other day.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): The prescription is 20 milligrams by mouth once a day, right?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty, yes. I do every other morning. I got scared it would hurt my kidneys if I took it daily. Is that a real thing? My neighbor's kidneys failed and she was on blood pressure medicine.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can affect the kidneys in some people, which is exactly why we do bloodwork, but skipping on your own isn't the safer version. I'm glad you said it out loud.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I take one today? I didn't, because yesterday was my day. And what if my pressure is already fine and I'm overdoing it?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check before we answer that. 146 over 88. Pulse 74, regular. Lungs are clear, and there's no swelling around the ankles.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 146 bad? Like stroke bad? My dad had a stroke when he was 71, and I turn 64 in June, so I've been doing the math.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): 146 over 88 is high for you, not an emergency. Thinking out loud, it could be the every-other-day lisinopril, it could be you rushing in here anxious, it could be salt. My working impression is it's mainly the missed doses, but I won't lock that in off one reading.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't even add salt. Well, actually, except on corn. Does that count? And is corn bad?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Corn is fine. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No shortness of breath. No dizziness either, which is weird, I thought high pressure would make me dizzy.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any aching in the legs, or swelling you can see?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Swelling, no. My thighs ache, though. Not terrible, like I walked too far. How long, I can't tell you. Maybe since Thanksgiving, or was it Christmas. I don't know.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the ache is while you've been off the statin. I'm not going to blame a pill you aren't taking. Could be you're deconditioned, could be thyroid, could be nothing serious. I will not put a name on it today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it myopathy? I saw that word. Do I need a muscle biopsy? Please tell me no.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No biopsy. I am not calling it myopathy. Let's see what the tests say before we name it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): There's one more thing and it's probably dumb. My husband has diabetes and he takes metformin, a thousand milligrams twice a day. I get tired after pasta and I keep looking at his bottle. Would one of his pills help me?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't take his metformin. That medicine is his, not yours, and being tired after pasta does not mean you have diabetes.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't taken any, I just look. Also, way back, the pharmacy mentioned a baby aspirin, but I was never given it and I never took a single one. Was I supposed to?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave aspirin out. You were never started on it, so it isn't part of what you take.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): If I restart the statin tonight, will my thighs get worse? What dose would you even use? I'm really afraid of the 40.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I was going to do is restart atorvastatin at 20 milligrams by mouth at night, half the old dose, starting tonight, and recheck you in a month.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Tonight, even with the thigh ache? I don't even remember if my cholesterol was high last time. And what if my liver can't take it? My mother had liver trouble, cirrhosis or maybe just fatty liver, nobody explained it to me.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on. The ache, no recent cholesterol number in front of me, and a family liver history I didn't have a minute ago. Scratch the restart. I am not starting the statin today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So I stay off it? Is a month dangerous? What are you actually testing? I have like ten questions.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to throw in a thyroid test for the aches, and I'm dropping that. The plan is a fasting lipid panel and a comprehensive metabolic panel, liver and kidneys, this week. We revisit the statin decision in a month, not before.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting means nothing after midnight, right? Can I drink water? And what if the thigh ache moves and I think it's my chest and I panic?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is fine. No food for about eight hours. Real chest pressure, shortness of breath, or pain going to the arm or jaw, that is the ER. The thigh ache alone, you can call the office.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And the lisinopril, every day or every other day until the labs? I need you to just say it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every day. 20 milligrams by mouth each morning, including tomorrow, even though you took one yesterday. If you miss a morning, don't double up, just take the next one.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I get dizzy when I go back to daily? Do I stop again? I don't want to fall in the kitchen.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're lightheaded enough that you might fall, skip that dose and call me. Don't slide back to every other day on your own.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the blood test show if I already ruined something by stopping? I keep thinking the damage is done.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lipid panel shows where the cholesterol is now. It cannot time-stamp damage, and I won't pretend it can. That's why the decision waits until I see you in a month.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I book that on the way out? And do you want my husband's pill list, or just mine?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just yours. Book a follow-up with me in one month, and get the labs done this week, fasting. The front desk can set both of those up.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. One month. I'll try not to google tonight. Thanks for not yelling at me.

[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, um, great, thank you for your help.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the loose stools, did they start that same night or afterwards?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I think the next morning. Or maybe two days later. I really don't know, doctor. Dates are just gone.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the timing open then. How many times have you been to the loo?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. It was the chicken curry and the prawns, basically. Yoh, that prawn thing was rich.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did anyone else from the wedding get sick?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. My cousin, his wife, and I think two bridesmaids. Same thing, puking and the runs. So the whole table, almost.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, and the DJ played until late, the robot on the way home was out, we sat in the bakkie forever. Not important, I know.

[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still nauseous?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, ja. Not like the first day. I can sit here without feeling I'm going to bring up.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. A bit warm in the night, sometimes, not really. I don't know, doctor. I never checked.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): A little when I stand up fast. And I'm thirsty all the time, mouth like cotton.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Since the vomiting stopped, are you keeping water down?

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And somebody told you not to?

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I understand the reason, but please stop the loperamide from now. If there's an infection we want it out, not held in. Any medicines you take every day?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, for the blood pressure. Five milligrams... no, sorry, it's ten milligrams. Every morning. Been on it for years.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): So high blood pressure, on ten milligrams each morning, as you've just said. Did you manage today's dose?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. This morning, by mouth, with a sip of water. That one I'm sure of.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies? Medicines, food?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on back. The desk put down heart racing, but tell me what's actually going on.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, it flutters, or it races, I don't know, doctor. It's hard to describe.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When it races, is that a couple of extra beats, or fast for a whole stretch?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Fast for a stretch. And I get out of breath with it, like I can't fill my lungs.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the breathing start first, or the heart?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Heart first, then the breath. Usually. Well, actually, sometimes they hit together. I don't know.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been happening?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A couple months? I kept thinking it'd just stop.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): My partner says it was already going on back in the winter, but I can't put a date on it. I really don't know.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, no solid start date, we'll leave that open. Is it every single day?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Mostly at night, in bed. And before exams, or before meetings at work. Which sounds silly.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. School, work, or both?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. I'm twenty-three, doing a master's, and I work part-time at a marketing firm downtown. Client meetings are the bad ones.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): At night, do you wake up gasping, or are you still awake when it starts?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Still awake. Just lying there. Heart going, can't catch my breath, and then I kind of... yeah.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these spells?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain at all.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passed out? Gotten lightheaded?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fainting, and I'm not lightheaded with these. I don't know, doctor, it just feels like I can't get air.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, no fainting and no lightheaded spells with it. How long does an episode last?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Five minutes, sometimes twenty. I never time it, so that's a guess.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee, soda, energy drinks — what's a normal day?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): A lot of coffee. Four, well actually five cups. And two Monsters if there's a deadline. My partner swears that's the whole thing.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): They might be onto something, but I'm not pinning it there yet. Do you smoke or vape?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. Not cigarettes. The disposable nicotine ones. A pod every couple of days, more when I'm cramming. Is that bad?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Enough nicotine to push the heart rate up, yes. Any alcohol?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer on the weekend sometimes. That's it. Oh, and your parking garage almost made me late, I circled forever.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): That garage gets everyone. People will call this anxiety — do you feel stressed or panicky when the racing starts?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. I don't think it's that. Exams are just exams. I don't know why everyone jumps to anxiety.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're telling me it isn't stress, so that's what I'll write. Thinking out loud, though, the timing with meetings still nags at me. Any medicine you've used for the racing?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Propranolol. They started it last fall, ten milligrams once a day, by mouth, for the heart racing.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you still taking that?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I stopped it in March. It made me tired, and I don't know, I didn't feel like it was doing anything.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair. Anything else that got prescribed and never actually started?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Buspirone, for nerves. I never filled it. Never took one pill. Which, I'm not anxious, so.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then buspirone stays off the list. Anything at all in your system now — vitamins, somebody else's pill?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No vitamins. I took one of my roommate's Adderall before a final, months ago, just once. Not my prescription, and I didn't do it again.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-time use of someone else's Adderall doesn't go on your medication list. Drug allergies, or allergies to anything else?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe penicillin, or that might be my brother, I always mix us up. I can't remember a rash or what happened.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we'll call penicillin uncertain, not a confirmed allergy. Any diagnosed problems — asthma, thyroid disease, a heart condition?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing like that. No asthma. Nobody ever said I had a thyroid problem. Never had surgery, either.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family history — rhythm problems, heart disease, high blood pressure?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know about rhythm stuff. My dad has high blood pressure. That's all I've heard.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while we talk. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur, and the rate's about ninety-six sitting here. Blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy-four, oxygen ninety-eight percent. Lungs are clear, no wheeze.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-six, like, bad? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit quick for resting, not a danger number on its own. Working this through — heavy caffeine, nicotine, spells at night and before exams or meetings, no chest pain. My impression is this may be sinus tachycardia stirred up by the coffee and the vaping.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I also can't rule out an arrhythmia, or a thyroid issue. That's a working impression, not a final label, and it does not sound like a heart attack.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. So my heart's not, um, failing or something.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think so. You're young and the exam is reassuring. I do want an ECG before you leave today, and thyroid bloodwork, a TSH and a free T4.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? I've got a seminar at four. Um, I can stay a little.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): ECG here before you go, and the lab order is in — today or first thing tomorrow is fine. If the palpitations haven't settled in a few weeks, we might do a Holter monitor, but I'm not ordering that now. If the shortness of breath doesn't ease up, we might get a chest x-ray, only in that case.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): For now, drop the energy drinks and cut the coffee way back. When an episode starts, try slow breathing, in for four counts and out for six. I'll see you back in two weeks to go over the results. If you faint or get chest pain, come in sooner than that.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, we were ages finding a space. Um, it's the burning again when I wee.
[SEG0002] person_2 (NURSE): Pop yourself down. Observations are done — blood pressure one hundred and twenty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six. Coat can stay on the chair.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Is seventy-six fast? I always go like this in clinics. Is that blood pressure a bad number?
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both are fine. How many times has this happened?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): This is the third time this year, I think. It stings the whole time I'm passing water, and just after.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You said third in the car. There was February as well, after that cold weekend.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Did I? Well, actually, maybe the fourth then. I lose count. Sorry. Is four times, like, kidney dangerous?
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not from the count alone. When did this bout start?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Um. Sunday, I reckon. Or it might've been Saturday night, I'm not sure. So about three days. Does the exact day change the test?
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. Going more often?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Every half hour, nearly. And that desperate feeling, like I won't make the loo. It was grim on the bus.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the wee?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I looked. There isn't any. Would blood mean hospital? I can't do hospital today.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. Fever, or shivering?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. No shivering. I do feel washed out and tired, though. Is tired a bad sign?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain in either loin?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my back's alright. It's a low ache at the front, just above the pubic bone. Not terrible. More annoying.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vaginal discharge or itching?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No, nothing like that.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not what you—
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Danielle, please don't. It's embarrassing. Can we leave it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes or no. Discharge or itching?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Um. Well, actually, there is a bit of itching. And maybe a tiny bit of white discharge since yesterday. Hardly anything. I didn't want to say it in front of my sister.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that thrush as well? Can thrush make the burning worse? Her wedding's next month and I've got fittings, I cannot be dealing with this on top of the shoes.
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The wedding can wait. Just answer him.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might be. Have you taken any tablets for this?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I took leftover trimethoprim. Danielle's, from the cabinet. I know I shouldn't have. 200 milligrams, morning and night.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They were from my chest infection in May. I did tell her not to.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many days?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Two days. I stopped on Tuesday, they'd run out. So not a proper course. Is that going to ruin the urine test? Will it still show a bug?
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can. Nitrofurantoin was prescribed in March. Still taking it?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I stopped it in March. It made me queasy, so I only managed two days and then I stopped. I never went back for a swap. Should I have?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pivmecillinam, from January. Did you take any of that?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I never started those. Full box, still in the kitchen drawer. I wasn't sure about them, so I left them. Are they a problem sitting there?
[SEG0035] person_2 (NURSE): Sorry to interrupt. The summary says sertraline 100 milligrams once a day. Are you taking that?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's not right. I take 50 milligrams, one tablet at night. It's always been 50. Why would it say 100?
[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): After Christmas you told Mum they'd put it up to 100. I'm sure of it.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I didn't. It's 50, I promise. Please don't change it today — it's for my anxiety, and I've had anxiety for years.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not changing it. Your anxiety treatment stays as it is. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None at all. No drug allergies. I was fine on the trimethoprim, if that's useful. They can just appear, though, can't they?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the couch. I'll check your abdomen.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen's soft. Mild tenderness just above the pubic bone. No loin tenderness.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Is mild bad? It isn't going up to the kidneys, is it? I've got to fetch the dog at four, and Danielle's got work, so if this is hospital I need to ring someone now.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not the kidneys. Most likely another bout of cystitis. With the itch I can't rule out thrush.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's not definite. Could it be an STI? Ben's working away all week. Do I have to tell him today? He's hopeless on the phone and I'll just spiral.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not definite until the sample's back. You don't need to call him today.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. What do I have to give? Will it hurt? I went before we came in, there might be nothing there. How many days for the result?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): A midstream urine for culture. It doesn't hurt. Couple of days. The nurse has the pots.
[SEG0049] person_2 (NURSE): I'll sort a labelled pot at the desk when you're done.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): If nothing grows, do I still get tablets? I don't want another antibiotic if I can help it. Nitrofurantoin made me sick. Mum keeps saying cranberry juice — does that actually do anything?
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): No antibiotic today. If the culture is negative, we might do a vaginal swab. Plenty of water. Cranberry will not clear it.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): A swab? Does that hurt? And how much water, because I work a desk job at the council and I can't live in the toilets. Should I phone in sick tomorrow?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can go to work. If you're no better in three days, come back. Sooner if you spike a fever or get loin pain.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): And if it blows up tonight, is that A&E or am I being dramatic? Also, does Danielle need testing because I pinched her tablets? Sorry, that's a daft one.
[SEG0055] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm perfectly fine. Finished my own course back in May. I'll wait outside.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ring 111 if you worsen tonight. A&E only if you're very unwell. She does not need a test.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry about the questions, I know there were loads. I'll do the sample now.
[SEG0058] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Parking meter won't wait forever. You wanted milk as well.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pot's at the desk. We're done.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, take your time. Let's start with what the report said. Do you have it with you?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Right here. It says, uh, fatty liver. Mild. And I've been kind of freaking out since.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand. Fat in the liver is quite common, and mild is the reassuring word there. Your family doctor sent you to talk through your medicines, right?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. She said the liver can be affected by, you know, tablets. So I brought the list.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good thinking. We'll go through each. First, how have you been feeling? Any symptoms?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much. Some mild discomfort on my right side, under the ribs. Sometimes. It's, um, more of a nagging than a pain.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): A nagging discomfort under the right ribs. How often?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of times a week? After big meals, I guess. I haven't really...
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's okay. You haven't noticed it anywhere else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just there.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed your eyes or skin looking yellow?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no yellow. My wife would have said something, she notices everything.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now the medicines. What's the first one on your list?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformin. 500 mg, twice a day, with meals. For my diabetes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin, 500 mg twice a day, for the diabetes. Which type of diabetes?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Type 2. Diagnosed about six years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Next?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. 20 mg, at bedtime. It's for, uh, cholesterol. I've had high cholesterol for a long time.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin, 20 mg at bedtime, for your cholesterol. Any muscle aches with that?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Hmm, maybe my calves sometimes, but I don't know if that's the...
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll keep an eye on that. What else?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, 10 mg. Once a day, in the morning. For blood pressure.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lisinopril, 10 mg once a day for blood pressure. Is that all?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, and the baby aspirin. 81 mg. My cardiologist, um, a few years ago... Anyway, I take it every morning too.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Aspirin, 81 mg every morning. So four medicines in total. Anything over the counter? Supplements?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else. I'm kind of scared to take anything extra now, because of the liver.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's sensible. Just check with us or the pharmacist before you add anything new.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I will.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything in the family I should know about? Liver trouble, or other illness?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes too. He had it for a long time.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, thank you. Let me have a quick feel of your tummy.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your abdomen is soft, and I can't feel anything unusual under the ribs on the right.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief. I was afraid you'd find a lump or something.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Let me also read your numbers. Blood pressure is 134 over 82, and weight is 94 kilograms.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): The weight's gone up a little. I know. I'm, um...
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): It happens. Let me say back what I'm hearing. Mild fatty liver on the scan, a nagging right-sided discomfort now and then, and four regular medicines.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that's it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those four medicines are all well-established, and none is a common cause of fatty liver. I'd like to order liver blood tests to see how your liver is working.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Like, regular blood work?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, a simple blood draw. You can do it at the lab on your way out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): And what should I do about the fat? Is there a pill for it?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not really. Gradual weight loss, regular movement, and cutting back on sugary drinks help the most. Even a small loss makes a difference.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I can try that. I just... I'm not sure where to start.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Start small. Swap one sugary drink a day for water, and add a ten-minute walk after dinner.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Water and a walk. I can do that.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. I'd like to see you again in three months, so we can look at the blood results and how things are going.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Three months. Okay. Thank you. I feel a lot calmer now.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): You did well to come in, and bring the list. See you then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come on in, I'm the one who checked him in. Weight's thirty-one pounds, temp ninety-eight point four, pulse one eighteen. He fussed the whole time out front.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks. Sorry we blew in late, the rain had the 405 just crawling.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I know, I sat forever at that off-ramp. Garage give you any trouble?
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Third level, then the elevator that smells like a wet dog. We almost did the stairs with the stroller.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): That elevator's been rank all week, maintenance keeps saying tomorrow. Doctor's finishing a note, she'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fine. He's wiped. Oh, random, but that dinosaur shirt is from my nephew's birthday last month, bounce place on Lincoln, total circus, cake in everybody's hair.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Ha, those places are chaos. Alright, I'll let her know you're here.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm Dr. Shah. What brings him in?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Leo's ear. He's three. Been crying at night and grabbing the right one, started after this cold.
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Ear hurt. No.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right side only?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, the right. He won't let me near it.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the night crying been going on?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two nights. Um, the cold's been, what, almost a week. Runny nose, and a little cough.
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Mommy.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. I felt him, he wasn't hot, and I didn't even bother with the thermometer.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting? Anything draining from the ear?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No throwing up. No gunk coming out.
[SEG0020] person_4 (PATIENT): Stop.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well, actually, hold on. My mom had him yesterday afternoon and she said he felt hot, like really warm. She never took a temperature though. I still don't think it was a fever.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Drinking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, juice and milk. He's just cranky.
[SEG0024] person_4 (PATIENT): Juice!
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Daycare?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Little Oaks, three mornings. They called me yesterday 'cause he was crying, so I picked him up. Not sick-sick, just miserable.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And this is dumb, but his dad texted me in the car to ask if Leo could catch his sugar thing. He's been living on his metformin. I told him no, that's not how it works, right?
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, that's your husband's medicine, not Leo's. What has Leo actually taken?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The bubblegum Tylenol. Kids' one. I gave maybe five mils? I think that's the line on the cup. Last night and again this morning for the ear.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else lately?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We did one dose of that purple kids' cough syrup, I can't remember the name, the bottle's just purple, and I stopped it. He was bouncing off the walls. And back in January urgent care sent cefdinir and we never picked it up, never gave a drop.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Medicine allergies?
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Um. Amoxicillin, long ago. He got a rash, maybe. I'm not sure it was from that.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): When, and what kind of rash?
[SEG0035] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can't pin the date. He was still a baby, under one, could've been longer ago than that. Little red spots? Or it was just a drool rash. My sister was the one who freaked out, I barely remember.
[SEG0036] person_4 (PATIENT): No no!
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any surgeries? Ear infections before this?
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No surgeries. First time his ear's done this.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I need to look. Hold his head.
[SEG0040] person_4 (PATIENT): Stop! Ow!
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right eardrum is pink, I can still see the landmarks, no hole, no pus. Left ear looks normal. Throat's a bit red. Neck isn't swollen. Lungs are clear.
[SEG0042] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So is it infected?
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might be an early ear infection, or it might just be fluid and pressure after the cold. I can't say which for certain today.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): We're going to watch it. Keep using the Tylenol for pain, you can switch to ibuprofen if you want, the berry children's one is fine. No antibiotic starting today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We have that berry Motrin at home. I haven't opened it this week.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Because of that maybe-amoxicillin rash I'm not using amoxicillin. I'll send cefdinir suspension to your pharmacy, one hundred twenty-five milligrams per five mils, eight mils by mouth once a day for five days. Don't fill it unless he's still miserable tomorrow night or he gets a real fever.
[SEG0047] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. That's the one we never used before, yeah.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Home.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): If he's not turning the corner in two days, or sooner if he spikes a fever or the ear starts draining, come back. Otherwise you don't need another visit.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What if he just cries tonight again?
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain medicine, fluids, and if you're worried he's worse, call us. Don't start the cefdinir just for one more fussy night.
[SEG0052] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Alright. He's usually a terror in the car, so, fun drive home in this rain.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Drive safe. We're done.
[SEG0054] person_4 (PATIENT): Bye. Ear.
[SEG0055] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks. Come on, Leo.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nora, Aoife, in you come out of that rain. Grand soft day if you like drowning.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm wringing wet, doctor. The brolly turned inside out at the roundabout. Are you well yourself?
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a bother. Have a seat there. What's brought the two of you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the legs. They're swelled up like puddings, the two of them, and I get puffed.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has to stop halfway up the stairs at home. I filled the pill box this morning and I still don't trust it, so I came with her.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Before all that, did you see little Cian on the hurling on Sunday? My grandson, eight years of age, and he's already shouting at the referee.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I had it on in the background for a bit.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Two points he got, and one of them from out on the wing with his left, and he's right-handed. His father went hoarse. They had tea and ham sandwiches in the clubhouse after, and the rain was hopping off the roof.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mam, leave the match.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm nearly done. The referee was Tommy Hegarty's young lad from our own parish. Tommy used to cut our grass when his back was right. The jersey was down to Cian's knees and his boots were caked in muck, and they still made him man of the match, if you wouldn't mind.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): And the weather, doctor, it's been pure miserable. I had the good coat on me and it's destroyed. Mrs Dunne next door says her dog won't even go out in it.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a great day out for him all the same. We'll park the hurling there. Tell me about these legs.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The two ankles, and it creeps up towards the shins by evening. I'd say two weeks. Ah no, I'm a liar, it's a good month now.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): A month. Both sides, worse by evening. Does anything ease it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): If I put the feet up on the stool after the news, they go down a small bit. In the morning they're not as bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The shoes don't go on by teatime. She's in the slippers all evening.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the puffing, is that new with the swelling?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs mostly. I have to stop and hold the rail. On the flat I'm grand enough.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She used to take the stairs in one go. Not for the last month.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are you sleeping? How many pillows?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Two pillows now. I was always a one-pillow woman. If I slip down I feel a bit stuffed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest with that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest. Not a twinge.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough? Phlegm? Wheeze?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. I'm clear that way.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when you stand up, any dizziness?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh now, if I hop up off the chair I go woozy for a second. That's the last while, maybe a fortnight. Then it passes, like.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've seen her grab the table. She hasn't fallen, thank God.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or pain when you pass water?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and the waterworks are grand. I go a bit more because of the water tablet, that's all.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. You have the heart failure a few years, and the blood pressure. Still the case?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. The heart failure, and the pressure. I'm under Dr Brennan for the heart, but I haven't seen him since the winter.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations along the way?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The gallbladder, years ago, keyhole. Nothing since. My father went with a heart attack at seventy, but sure that was his own doing, he lived on rashers.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll note that. Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked in my life. Drink, hardly at all, a small sherry at Christmas if there's trifle.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She lives with me. I do the dinners and the tablets. She's not on her own.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Let's go through the tablets, because the letter in front of me and what people actually swallow are often two different stories. The letter says furosemide twenty milligrams, one every morning. The water tablet.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not what we've got, doctor. The box from the chemist says forty milligrams, and I put one in the morning slot. I don't know where twenty came from.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I just take what she sets out. I couldn't tell you the milligrams. It's the little yellow water one.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the letter has twenty and the box has forty, and we can't call it either way till I see the box. We'll come back to what I'll write. What else is in the pill box?
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril, for the blood pressure. Two and a half milligrams. No, sorry, I'm looking at the old strength in my head, they put her up, it's five milligrams, one in the morning.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams once in the morning. Anything else of the ramipril?
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is the bit I'm mortified about. There was an old bottle of the two and a half still in the press, and I thought it was a separate tablet, so I was putting one of those in at night as well. Only for a few days. I binned it this morning when I read the label properly.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't know I was getting two. I thought the night one was for sleeping or something. Sure I can't read the tiny writing.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you may have had an extra ramipril at night for a few days, and we're not certain how many nights. We'll treat the proper dose as five milligrams once each morning. Is there another tablet you can't name?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): There's a little white one, tiny yoke, after the breakfast. Every day. I haven't a clue what it is.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The label is washed out. I can't read a word of it. I just keep putting the little white one in the box because it was in the cupboard with the others, and I've no idea what it's for.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't guess. Bring me that box next time and we'll identify it. Anything that was stopped?

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): The aches went off after he stopped it, thank God. When was that, Aoife? After Christmas? I couldn't put a date on it.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think February, but I haven't the discharge letter, so I wouldn't swear to the month.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped, and the date is unclear. Any allergies I should know before I prescribe?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a one. I can take whatever you throw at me. No allergies.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mam, the penicillin. You came out in a rash all over in the hospital years ago, and they told you never to take penicillin again.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the heat, Aoife, the ward was roasting. I'm not allergic to penicillin. I don't care what they wrote.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm only saying what they told us. I wasn't going to let it go unsaid.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record it as disputed, not as a definite allergy, and I won't be using penicillin today anyway. Let me have a look at you. Shoes off, thanks.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's pitting oedema on both sides, up to about the middle of the shin. Your lungs are clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is ninety. Hang on, let me count that again. No, it's eighty-eight. And the blood pressure today is one thirty-six over seventy-eight.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? My neighbour says once you're over a hundred you're in trouble, but she says a lot of things. She told me to eat beetroot.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): One thirty-six over seventy-eight is acceptable for you today. Forget the beetroot for a minute. Let me say back what I've heard, and correct me.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling of both legs for a month, worse by evening and a bit better with the feet up, breathless on the stairs the same length of time, two pillows, no chest pain and no cough. [SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the lot. And Cian got man of the match, but you said park that.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet is furosemide, the letter says twenty milligrams and the box says forty, so that dose is not agreed. [SEG0066] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's fair. What are you going to do?
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): My impression is provisional, that fluid is building up again from the heart failure, and the dizziness might be the tablets or just standing up too fast, I can't separate those yet. [SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dizziness was there before I added the night one. It was only four days, and the old bottle is in the bin since this morning. She needs the blood pressure tablet, Dr Brennan was very firm about it.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. I won't stop the ramipril. Stay on five milligrams once every morning, and nothing of it at night.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): For the fluid, I was going to put the furosemide up to eighty milligrams.
[SEG0071] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They tried a bigger dose before and she went very wobbly, and Dr Brennan said the kidneys were a bit touchy. I'd be afraid of eighty.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want to be falling around the kitchen, doctor.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then scratch the eighty, that's me changing the plan. I'll write furosemide forty milligrams, one each morning, so there's one clear dose from here, and I won't push it higher until I see the kidneys.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll also send you for a blood test, kidney function and potassium, this week. I nearly said a chest x-ray, but the lungs are clear so we won't do that.
[SEG0075] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can bring her down to the blood place Thursday.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thursday is fine. Bring the little white tablet in its box when you come back, and throw nothing else out before I see it.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get worse?
[SEG0078] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets much worse, or you get chest pain, or you faint, don't wait for me, go to the emergency department. Keep the feet up in the evenings as you've been doing. Come back here in two weeks and we'll look at the bloods and that white tablet.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Grand. Aoife will have me organised. Tell Cian I was talking about his points, he'll be delighted.
[SEG0080] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will. Mind yourselves on the way out, the path is slippy.

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, Sam, the booking note says you've swallowed a bit of Lego. Is that right?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... yeah. I swallowed a bit of Lego. A little one. A flat grey piece.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me what happened, from the start.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): I was... um... holding it in my mouth. While I was building a spaceship. And then I sort of... gulped.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, that happens more than you'd think. When was this?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Yesterday. After tea. Or... no, it was before tea, actually.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yesterday, before tea. Did it go down easily, or did it get stuck anywhere?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It just went down. Straight away. It was a bit... um, weird.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble breathing once it had gone down?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No. It was fine.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any being sick or vomiting afterwards?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No... um, no. I wasn't sick.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And how is your tummy feeling now?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): It's... a bit achy. Not horrible. Just a tummy ache.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you call it mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Mild. I think. Um... yeah, mild.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did the ache start?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): This morning.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you point to where it is for me?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Here. Um. Round my belly button, like.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anything make it better or worse? Think about eating, or moving around.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... it's a bit worse when I run around. And lying down helps.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sensible. Now let's check your regular medicines. Do you take anything every day?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. A puffer, I think. And... something for my... um...
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take your time. What's the puffer for?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): For my asthma. The blue one. Salbutamol.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. How much of it, and how often do you use it?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... 100 micrograms. When I need it. Mum says it's written on the side.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's right, I can see that on your record. What else is there?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): A cream, for my eczema. Hydrocortisone. Once a day, on my elbows.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the last one?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... Movicol. The sachets. For my constipation. Mum makes me have it in orange juice. One sachet a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): That one's useful today. Keeping it going helps things move along.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it help the Lego come out?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It'll certainly not hurt. Hop up on the couch, and I'll have a feel of your tummy.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it going to be cold? Last time the doctor's hands were freezing.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've warmed them up, promise. Tell me if anything hurts when I press.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft, which is what I wanted to feel. You can sit up again.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): So what's going to happen to the Lego?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here's what I think. It's small, smooth plastic, so most likely it will pass through on its own.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): When?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually within a few days. It comes out with your poo, and you won't feel a thing.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I have to look in the toilet for it? That's gross.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): A quick look each day, please, with mum or dad helping. Just so we know it has gone.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Um. Okay. I'll make my brother do it.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, nice try. Now, here's what you can do while you wait. Eat normally, with lots of fruit and veg.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): And chips?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sometimes. Drink plenty of water too, and keep taking your Movicol every day.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Can I still build stuff?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, but not in your mouth. Lego goes in the box and nowhere else.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Okay. Um, I won't.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the ache gets bad, or you're sick, or you feel hot and unwell, tell mum and come straight in.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. I'll tell her. She'll probably tell me anyway.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three days, to check how things are going.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, can it be after school?
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll ask reception to find you an afternoon slot. Off you go, Sam, and well done for being so brave.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. Bye.
