[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab a few vitals before Dr. Alvarez comes in. Go ahead and have a seat.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Um, these cuffs always squeeze way too hard.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): They do. Let your arm go loose for me. Blood pressure is 138 over 86.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? I don't know, doctor— sorry. You're the nurse.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): All good. It's a little up there for a clinic reading, nothing I'm paging anyone about. Pulse is 78. Temperature's 36.8.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel kind of warm, but I don't think I'm actually sick.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Oxygen is 98 percent. You're set. She'll be in shortly. The decent magazine's already gone, fair warning.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey, sorry about the wait. I'm Dr. Alvarez. What's been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, headaches. I've had them forever, but they're different now. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Different how? Say it however it comes out.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): They used to show up in the afternoon, kind of behind my eyes. Now I wake up with them. Worse in the morning, before I even get to the coffee.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the morning part been happening?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe a month? Or six weeks? I'm terrible with dates.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): We don't need the exact day. The older headaches, how far back do those go?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. Since my thirties. I'm 47, so fifteen years? Something like that. My sister gets them too, but that's— never mind, not why I came.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can leave your sister aside. With these morning ones, any nausea, any vomiting?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I threw up twice this week. Not every morning. Just sometimes, and then I feel completely wrung out.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the light bother you, or noise?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Light, yeah, same as always. I end up pulling the blinds. Noise not really.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking when they hit?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan, the 50 milligram tablets. And Tylenol. Acetaminophen. I go through a lot of it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many days a week on the sumatriptan?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days lately. Five, six days a week. The box says not to, I know, I know.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the Tylenol, how much at a time?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Extra strength, 500 milligrams, two of them, maybe three times a day. Sometimes more if it's a bad one. I don't know, doctor, I lose count by dinner.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else in the mix, prescriptions or otherwise?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Vitamin D, those little gel capsules. And I was on propranolol for the headaches, but I stopped. Last year, I think. It made me so tired I just quit.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Whoever booked you mentioned snoring, and that you've been tired. Your husband, I think.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, he fusses. I snore, sure, everybody does. And I'm tired because my head hurts, not— I don't know. It's nothing.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): So from what he hears, you do snore?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, he says I do. I never hear it. And yeah, I'm wiped out in the afternoons, but that's the headaches. He's blowing it up.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll put it down and we won't go hunting for a sleep problem today. Any weakness, numbness, trouble getting words out, or double vision?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or a stiff neck?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Neck's not stiff. It's the head, that's all.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any hit to the head lately? A fall?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I tripped over the dog last month, but I didn't hit my head. Dog's fine. He's a menace on the stairs.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad he's okay. Quick look, then. Follow my finger... good, your eyes move fully. Pupils are equal.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Am I supposed to look at the finger or at you? Sorry.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Finger's perfect. Squeeze both my hands... strength is even on the two sides. Walk over to the door for me... balance looks fine.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Did I pass? I felt clumsy, but these shoes are slippery.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): You did fine. Neuro exam is normal. No focal signs that I can find.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you think it is? I don't know, doctor, my brain goes straight to the scary stuff.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): What fits best is medication overuse stacked on the migraines you've had for years. The new morning pattern, with the vomiting, means I can't totally rule out something else underneath.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Like a tumor? Don't say tumor. Or say it, I don't know.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying tumor. The exam doesn't point that way. If this new pattern doesn't settle after we ease off the pain pills, we might do a head CT. I'm not ordering one today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So we just wait and see?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's see how two weeks go. If the morning headaches and the vomiting haven't eased by then, come back and we'll set up the scan.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): And if they calm down I just stay home?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Exactly, only if it's not better. In the meantime, keep sumatriptan to no more than two days in a week. Same with the Tylenol, try not to take it every single day.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know if I can do that when it's really pounding.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): If one is truly awful, one 50 milligram sumatriptan is okay. Just not most days. Water, and a steadier bedtime, matter more than they sound. If you ever get a sudden worst headache of your life, weakness, confusion, or vomiting that will not stop, go to the ER.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll try. My husband is going to say I told you so, about the pills.
[SEG0054] person_1 (NURSE): I can hold a Thursday afternoon two weeks out, if you want it locked in before you leave.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks, hold off on booking. If things haven't settled in two weeks, she can call and we'll see her, and talk about that CT.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): He also wanted me to ask about a sleep study. I don't know, doctor. I think he's overdoing it.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave sleep alone for now. No sleep study from me today. Anything else you wanted to cover?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. The garage ate my parking ticket, but that's not medical. I think that's everything.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll take it a step at a time. Take care.

[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): So what can I do for you?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Around three days... no wait, it's more like two days.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, mornings. That makes it worse. It's mild, honestly. I'd say on and off.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does anything else come with it?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Let me think, it usually comes with tiredness.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): And the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I was getting to that!
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine, one at a time. I'll ask about everything.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The tiredness? That's been for about a month.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had a chronic cough with lots of phlegm before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, something like this happened last winter, and it went away on its own.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, a few quick ones: chest pain or weight loss?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain, no weight loss. I was getting out of breath at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever or coughing up blood?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): None of those, no.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything different when you pass water?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That's normal as far as I know.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are there any illnesses in your family?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother has an underactive thyroid. My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have any procedures done?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Just my womb taken out, fifteen years ago.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I have diabetes.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, heart disease. I've had eczema, yes. Anxiety, for about a year.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I think I reacted to some antibiotic once, years ago. I don't remember which one, or what happened exactly.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to drink heavily but I stopped four years ago.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, how about smoking?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I've never smoked in my life.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, tell me about your eating.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So, it's something called glic... gliclazide, 80 milligrams, maybe, twice a day for my sugar.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you have the packet or the prescription with you?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Not with me. I'll bring it next time. Aspirin, 75 milligrams, once a day. Hydrocortisone cream, when needed.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm, okay.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a round yellow one.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): For the anxiety, I believe. My wife sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. I'd been on glimepiride, not any more though, I stopped.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's start with the basic checks.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: height 153 centimetres, respiratory rate 14. And weight 94 kilos, BP is 109 over 73, temp 36.8 degrees, heart rate 73, SpO2 99 percent on room air.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you in a second, make yourself comfortable.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me feel here.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): There are coarse crackles at both bases and the fingers are slightly clubbed.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can relax now. So, based on the history and the examination, I'd lean towards a flare of bronchiectasis. I'd also keep a chest infection in mind.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think a chest X-ray makes sense here, for bronchiectasis flare. A sputum culture is what I'd like next, for purulent sputum. Let's use clarithromycin, 500 milligrams, twice a day, fourteen days. That's for bronchiectasis flare. It's a commonly used medicine and most people tolerate it well. Keep up your airway clearance exercises twice a day. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll remember that.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's review you in two weeks. Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor, goodbye.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Dlamini, obs are done. Blood pressure is one eighteen over 76, pulse 96, temperature 37.2, sats 98 percent on air, respiratory rate sixteen. She managed a few sips of water while we waited.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Sister. Come through, Mrs Dlamini. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, Doctor, hectic weekend. My cousin Lindiwe got married in Paarl on Saturday, the dress was something else, and the lamb was lekker, but since Sunday morning my tummy's been running non-stop.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): We sat on the N1 forever afterwards, some robot was out by the tunnel, but anyway. It's this diarrhoea. That's the actual thing.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): So it started Sunday morning, after the wedding meal?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja. Sunday morning, early. Yesterday I was on the loo, um, I lost count, maybe eight or nine times, something like that. Could've been more, I stopped counting after the rusk.
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Bongi, I stay with her during the week. She was back and forth to the toilet all yesterday, and she vomited too, three times on Sunday and once yesterday morning. Nothing up since then.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): I blame the potato salad, hey. My sister Nomsa has the same bug, and two cousins, and Nomsa phoned to say she's turning the corner already. The DJ played till late, shame, my feet are still cross, but that's not why I'm here.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few of you off the same plate, then. Any blood in the stool, or black stool?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No, no blood. Just watery brown stuff. Horrible, sorry.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish at all, chills, that sort of thing?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I haven't felt hot. Just washed out. Tired, you know, a bit.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cramps with the diarrhoea?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, low down in the tummy. They come and go, not terrible. If I sit still it eases a bit.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when you stand up, any dizziness?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. I got up quick by the kettle and the room did a tiny spin, but I'm not sure that counts. Probably nothing.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't hang anything on that. Are you getting fluids in?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Little sips of rooibos. Sometimes they stay down, sometimes not really, I feel iffy. I haven't eaten proper since Sunday, just that one dry rusk.
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, she took Imodium yesterday, against what they told her. Two capsules, two milligrams each, from the chemist. The sister at the day clinic said don't use that for a food bug, but she swallowed them anyway, and she's had none today because I took the box away.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, I just wanted it to stop. Didn't even help, hey. I won't take another one. The box is still in my bag if you want it, next to my lipstick and the Paarl parking ticket.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Leave the Imodium off completely. With this sort of illness loperamide can trap the germ inside, so it isn't the right move, even though the running is miserable.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She does take her blood pressure tablet every morning for her high blood pressure. Amlodipine, five milligrams. She had it today, she doesn't miss it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, carry on with the amlodipine as usual. That's a separate issue, and the pressure Sister got is fine.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Your mouth is a bit dry. Tummy's soft, mildly tender low down, no guarding, and the bowel sounds are busy. The skin on the back of your hand tents just slightly, so this is mild dehydration, not severe.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this is most likely a short gastro from the wedding food, seeing as the others fell ill too. I'm going to send a stool sample off today, and I'd start ciprofloxacin, 500 milligrams twice a day for three days, just to cover a bacterial food poisoning.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She's not mad about antibiotics. And Nomsa is already improving with no medicine at all, just tea.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, please not the cipro if you can help it. Years ago it gave me the shakes, when my knee was playing up, whole other saga with the physio in Bellville, never mind. I'd rather avoid it.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that changes it. Scratch the ciprofloxacin, and we won't send the stool today either. No blood, you're not feverish, it's only been a couple of days, and the others are settling. If it's not better in three days, or if you see blood, or you can't keep sips down, then we send a stool sample.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): What will actually help is fluid: small sips often, a Rehidrat sachet in a glass of clean water after a loose stool. Skip cooldrink, fruit juice, and the flat Coke idea, they pull water into the bowel. When you feel up to food, stick to dry toast, rice, or banana.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Rehidrat, ja, the chemist will have it. My neighbour still swears by flat Coke, I won't listen to her. And can you believe the wedding photos aren't even out, with what that photographer charged.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, leave the flat Coke. If it's not better in three days, come back and see me.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): And if I go downhill tonight, do I still wait?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, don't wait it out. Come back here, or go to casualty, if you can't keep even sips down, you stop passing urine, or you feel faint.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): The pulse of 96 fits with being a little dry. Blood pressure stayed steady while she was sitting. I'll stick the obs slip in the file.
[SEG0035] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep the sips going at home, and the Imodium stays in the cupboard. High up.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): She's strict, Doctor, worse than my mother, and my mother was a school principal in George. Anyway. Will I be right for church on Sunday? There's a bazaar.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe, if the tummy settles, but don't promise the bazaar. No antibiotic from me, and no stool test today. We only send a sample if it's not settling in three days or if there's blood. Fluids, and keep the amlodipine going.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): So the Rehidrat after each run, little sips, no juice. Ja, I can do that. I'm done with that potato salad.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the plan. Anything else worrying you before you go?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Only that I might have left the wedding gift in the car boot, the vase. Ag, Bongi will remember. I'm fine otherwise, just this tummy.
[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The vase is at home, don't stress. Doctor, if the stool is still watery on Friday I bring her back, ja?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. Friday is about three days. If it's not better by then, come back, and we'll send the stool. Sooner if she worsens.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Sorted. Thanks, Doctor, and thanks Sister. Next wedding I'm eating before I leave the house.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Go gently. See you if you need us.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Brendan? In you come. I put you on the machine on the way past, blood pressure was 138 over 82 and the pulse was 76. Doctor Walsh has your GP's letter about the cough.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, thanks. It's not an emergency or anything, I just can't shake this cough, and the wife said I was to stop putting it off.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit yourself down, Brendan. I'll hear it from you rather than the letter. How long have you had the cough?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, solid. It came on the back of a dose of the flu. I was rotten for about a week, fever and aches and the whole production, and then that faded and the cough just... stayed.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the fever and the aches themselves have settled?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Settled, yeah. I was back in work after ten days. I'm a stores supervisor in the hardware place in Naas, so there's a fair bit of lifting, and I was able for that once the flu lifted. It's purely the cough now.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): When is the cough at its worst?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Night-time, no question. I'll be just dropping off and up it comes, a dry tickle, and I'm awake for ages. The wife has moved into the spare room, which tells you... anyway. Mornings there's a small amount of white phlegm, and then it's dry the rest of the day.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in that phlegm?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have looked, more than once, and there's nothing red in it at all. And it's not a pain in the chest the way a heart pain would be, more a soreness across the front from the hacking itself.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or proper night sweats, the drenching kind?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog has me out the door at half six, rain or shine, down the canal and back, so the mornings are busy. Sorry, I went off on myself there. What was it you asked?
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever, or night sweats.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever since the flu went. I get a bit clammy when the cough wakes me, but the sheets aren't wet. It's not that drenching kind of sweat.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you breathless with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The canal walk is grand and the yard is grand. I'm not gasping or anything like that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight or your appetite fallen off?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No weight loss. The appetite is as good as ever, the wife still does the full dinner and I clear the plate. I haven't been near a scales, but I don't think I've lost any.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been abroad lately, or around anyone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Abroad, no. I haven't left the country in years, the last holiday was Kerry and that was before Covid. TB, no, I don't know a soul with that. My brother was in Spain in May, but that's his holiday, not mine, I wasn't with him.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on, including anything from the chemist?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril five milligrams, one in the morning, for the blood pressure, and I'm on that five years. The GP gave me clarithromycin, five hundred milligrams twice a day for five days, and I finished that about two weeks ago, it did nothing for the cough. At night I take ten mils of Benylin dry cough from the chemist, just to get over.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about before I...
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I came out in a rash all over when I was seventeen, and they told me not to take it again, so the GP wouldn't give me the usual antibiotic, that's why it was the clarithromycin. I've steered clear of penicillin ever since.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or did you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. My father smoked forty a day and I couldn't stick the smell of it in the house, so I never started. I take a pint of a Saturday and that's the height of it, I'm not a drinker.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen to your chest. Deep breath in... and out. And again for me.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): The lungs are clear, I don't hear any crackles. There's a little wheeze right at the end of the breath, on both sides. Your throat looks ordinary, and there are no glands up in the neck.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the wheeze a bad sign? I have noticed a bit of a whistle at night when I'm lying down, I was going to mention that and then I forgot, the way you do.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks on from a flu, worse at night, a bit of phlegm in the morning, and that wheeze. My head runs through a post-viral cough, a twitchy airway, even reflux, and TB does cross my mind when a cough drags on like this. I'm not naming any of those as the cause. I want to see a chest x-ray before I commit to a thing.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The x-ray, do I keep the jumper on or... oh, actually, the trousers. I said I hadn't lost weight, but I've gone in a notch on the belt and the waist is loose, I only copped it getting dressed this week. So I have lost a bit, I was wrong earlier.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): That detail matters, and we'll hold it alongside the film. I'm still not putting a name on this.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): And listen, I said no TB, and that's true as far as contact goes, I haven't been near anyone with it. My sister Niamh rang last week going on about our cousin Declan down in Limerick, he was in the hospital with a bad chest and she has it in her head that it was TB. I haven't laid eyes on Declan since a wedding in twenty nineteen, so I wouldn't call that contact.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a cousin with a chest illness your sister thinks was tuberculosis, and no contact yourself. I'm still not calling this TB, or calling it anything else. The picture has to come first.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll order a chest x-ray, today if they can fit you in. Keep taking the ramipril as you are, and the Benylin at night is fine if it helps you sleep. I won't be starting any new tablet until we've seen the film.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's something bad on the x-ray, what then? The wife will ask me the minute I get in the door, she has herself half convinced it's desperate, and I keep telling her it's probably nothing.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we deal with whatever the picture shows, not with a guess from me today. If you cough up blood, or you become properly breathless, or a fever comes back, don't wait on the appointment, go to the emergency department or the on-call GP. I'll see you back here in two weeks with the result.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, grand. I'll tell the wife, she'll be glad someone is actually looking at it instead of us arguing over it at the kitchen table.
[SEG0039] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Radiology can take him at half two, so I'll book the chest x-ray and the two-week review on the way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down, Mrs Kearney. How are you keeping?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, not the best, doctor. I'm after having the runs, and I was getting sick as well.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry to hear that. Tell me a bit about it, in your own time.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, we were down for my niece's wedding. The dress was gorgeous, I'll say that, but the hotel dinner and all, and then this started on me.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Nuala, her carer. I was with her the whole weekend. The reception was Saturday, lovely band, hotel out in Galway.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. When did the diarrhoea actually start, would you say?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know, doctor. Two days, I'd say? Or maybe it was Sunday. I'm all mixed up.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was Saturday night, a few hours after the meal. That's three days now, not two. She's losing track of it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right so. And the vomiting, is that still going on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's stopped. I haven't got sick since yesterday evening.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She did, doctor. She vomited this morning in the bathroom. I had to clean it up.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think that was this morning. I don't know, maybe I'm wrong, but I don't remember it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. How many times have you been to the toilet with the diarrhoea?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A good few. Six, or eight? I lose count once I'm going all the time.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nearer ten, I'd say, since yesterday morning. Watery, every time.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it, or anything black?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Just water, nearly.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the tummy itself, is there pain?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Cramps, low down. They come on fierce before I have to run, and they ease a small bit after.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you managing to drink at all?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit of water. I'm thirsty the whole time. I don't know if it's enough, doctor.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she's hardly passed urine. A small drop this morning, very dark, and nothing much since yesterday.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone else from the wedding taken bad?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister, and two of the cousins. Texting this morning, the same thing, runs and getting sick. They all sat at our table.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I had the fish, though, not the chicken. I don't know if that even matters.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): It might not be the one plate, so, if the whole table is down with it. Any fever, or shivers?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. I feel a bit cold now and again, but I haven't a clue, really.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I took her temperature this morning before we came out. It was 36.8, normal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking these days?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, the little white one, every morning. And I've been taking the Imodium for the runs.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Imodium is loperamide. How many of those have you had?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know, doctor. Maybe two after each time I go? Or, well, actually, was it one. The box said two to start. I'm not sure I did it right.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been taking them since Sunday, and the chemist told her not to, if it was a bug off the food. She took them anyway.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd stop the Imodium now. If this is a tummy bug, better to let it out than cork it up.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. I thought I was doing the right thing. Sorry, doctor.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're grand, no harm done yet. Do you know the name of the little white tablet?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It's just the blood pressure one. I've been on it for years.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril, five milligrams, one every morning. She doesn't miss that one.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely, stay on the ramipril. Any water tablet, or anything for the sugar?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just that, and the Imodium I was telling you about.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick look at you now, if that's alright. Pulse, pressure, and your tummy.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 98, blood pressure 112 over 68, and the temperature here is 37.1.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tongue is dry, and the skin on the back of your hand is a little slow coming back. Tummy is soft, tender low down, no guarding.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that serious, doctor? I don't know what any of that means.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's mild dehydration, that's all. Not severe. My first thought was to send a stool sample off today and maybe give you a tablet for the infection.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Would a sample not be the sensible thing, with so many of them sick?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was leaning that way, but actually, no. Others are ill the same way, there's no blood, and it's only a few days. I won't send a sample today.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled in three or four days, then we might send a stool off. No antibiotic either, I changed my mind on that. It should be a short food bug or a virus.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do I do, just wait? I don't know if I can face food.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sip Dioralyte, little and often, even a teaspoon every few minutes. Flat 7-Up if the Dioralyte turns your stomach. Plain food when you fancy it, nothing greasy, and leave the Imodium in the press.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know if I'll keep the Dioralyte down, doctor.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tiny sips all the same. If you can't keep any fluid down, or you go dizzy, or you see blood, or the urine dries up completely, come straight back or go on to the emergency department.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will you want to see her again this week?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not booking a routine visit. If you're not clearly better in three or four days, come back and we'll see about that stool test then.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I hope I'm not being a bother over nothing.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a bit of it. Mind yourself, and Nuala will keep an eye. You'll likely turn the corner shortly.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit down. What's the problem?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the diarrhoea, doctor, and I was vomiting as well, it all started after my cousin Rachel's wedding on Saturday. I know I'm going on, but the meal was a buffet at the Regent Hotel in Cheltenham, and I had the prawns to start and then the chicken, which was a bit lukewarm if I'm honest.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the diarrhoea start?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday evening, around ten, maybe half past. I was absolutely fine on the Saturday, danced, got the last train. Well, actually Sunday after lunch I felt queasy, and by that night it had started properly. So we're on Wednesday now, that's three days, yes.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many times today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try to keep a tally. Um, four before I left the house, then one in the station toilet, and I think one more since, so five or six today. Yesterday I gave up counting after six or seven, might have been eight. Watery, yellow, nothing formed.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I looked, because my mum always said look, and there's been no blood and no black stuff, just water really.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday night, twice, quite sudden, and then once more Monday morning before work. Nothing since about Monday lunchtime. The sick feeling is still there a bit, but I haven't actually been sick again.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood in the vomit?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no blood. It was just the dinner, then a bit bile-ish the last time.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keeping drinks down?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Since Monday afternoon, yes, little sips of water. I got those lemon rehydration sachets, Dioralyte, and I managed two of them yesterday. I did bring a mouthful of water back on Monday, but not since.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passing urine?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Less than usual. This morning it was quite dark, just a small amount, which isn't like me first thing. No stinging or anything.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dizzy?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): A little light-headed if I stand up too fast. This morning I sat on the edge of the bed for a minute. Not spinning, and I haven't fainted. I'm just washed out, tired in that floppy way.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone else from the wedding ill?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, my sister Helen texted, she's got the same, and cousin Mark, and Mark's wife. All three had the prawns. My brother-in-law had the beef and he's fine, he even went to the gym yesterday, which is a bit showing off. So I do think it's the food.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever? Pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever that I've noticed. I haven't got a thermometer, so I can't swear to a number, but I don't feel hot or shivery. The pain is crampy, low down, comes in a wave just before I have to go, then eases. Not agony.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Been abroad?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, this was Cheltenham, not abroad. I nearly went to Spain in March and the flights got cancelled, but that's months ago and I was well, completely separate.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Regular medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, the water tablet every morning for my blood pressure, I've been on it for years. And I shouldn't have, but the chemist on Monday said don't take anything to stop it if it's food poisoning, and I took Imodium anyway, those little green and grey capsules. Two yesterday evening so I could get the train, and two again this morning. They barely touched it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Strength of the water tablet?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Two and a half milligrams, um, bendro-something, bendroflumethiazide, yes that's it, once a day. I took it at seven this morning with a sip of water, same as always. Last year at the surgery they did a kidney blood test and said it was borderline, no actual figure, just borderline. I was meant to repeat it and I don't think I ever went back.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all. Penicillin's fine, I had a course for a tooth abscess a couple of years ago, no rash or anything.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mouth's dry. Pulse 98, blood pressure 112 over 74, temperature 36.7. Tummy's soft, tender low down, no guarding. Skin turgor is all right.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 98 worrying? I walked up from the car park and I always get anxious in waiting rooms, my heart races at the dentist as well.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mild dehydration, that's all. Stop the Imodium, it can drag a bug like this out.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, I won't take another. The box says one or two after each loose stool, and I'm sure it was just those four capsules in total. Do I carry on with the water tablet? I nearly skipped it, I'd read they don't mix with diarrhoea.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the bendroflumethiazide unless you stop keeping fluids down. Sip water or rehydration sachets through the day. No fizzy drinks and no dairy for now.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Lemon Dioralyte then, I've a box of six at home. My sister swears blackcurrant is better, which I think is nonsense. I only managed half a piece of toast this morning, no appetite to speak of.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either flavour is fine. If the diarrhoea is still like this in two days, or there's blood, or you can't keep fluids down, we'll send a stool sample. Not today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I brought an empty sample pot from the chemist, it's in my bag, I missed my chance this morning. So I just keep it?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't eased in two days, come back, or sooner if you're dizzy, passing blood, or not keeping fluids down.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So Friday-ish. Can I take paracetamol for the cramps? I've got the 500 milligram tablets, I took two last night and it settled a bit, but I wasn't sure alongside the Imodium.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Paracetamol is fine, two 500 mg tablets up to four times a day. Most likely a short-lived food-related gastroenteritis. Nothing else on examination beyond that dryness.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Helen's worse than me and she won't come in, she's stubborn. Should I tell her the same, and do I ring the hotel? There were about sixty of us and I still feel I should have said the chicken was lukewarm.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell her fluids, no loperamide, and to be seen if she worsens. The hotel's your call. You know when to come back.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Denise, come through. Sharon, grab the chair by the window. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough, and I'll try to keep it short, though I never do. Dry and tickly, back of the throat, worse when I lie down, and a sip of water helps for a minute. I reckon it's the tail of a cold, nothing more.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been at it six weeks, worse at night, up half the night. I hear her from the front room.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six is too long. I thought three weeks when I rang, but it was after Lorne, so four weeks. And I'm not up half the night. I wake once, have a sip, and I'm off again.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dry cough, four weeks on your reckoning, six on Sharon's, worse lying down, you blame a cold. Is there any phlegm?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all, dry as a bone. The aloe tissues are still in the packet, four dollars I won't get back.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever? Shivers, feeling hot?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Chemist thermometer yesterday said 36.4, normal for me. Runny nose and sore throat from the cold are finished, but I couldn't tell you the date that cold began.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gone completely, those two?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Completely. Barley sugar for the throat, not real medicine, and the nose just dried up on its own.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's puffed on the back stairs. She stops halfway.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not puffed. Coles yesterday, two bags, no trouble. It's coughing, not breathlessness, Sharon just worries.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You stopped halfway on Tuesday. I was behind you with the washing.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped to cough, not to get my breath. The milk was heavy, that's a different story.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze, or chest pain with the cough?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No wheeze, no chest pain. A sip of water eases the tickle for a minute, then it comes back.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about heartburn, or a sour taste?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really, no. One curry on Saturday caught me, and that was the curry. I don't get reflux.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the blood pressure. How long have you had that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was sixty-two. I'm seventy-one, so nine years, and it's still there. That's the other thing I wanted to mention, not just the cough.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you actually taking for it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): They put me on enalapril, no, ramipril, I mix those two up every time. Two and a half milligrams, no, ignore that, the bottle says five milligrams, once a day.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The cough is the cold, Sharon, not the tablet. I take the ramipril every morning, I don't miss that one, and I take it with the water tablet.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the water tablet, in your words.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the indapamide, two point five milligrams, mornings, for the pressure. Little white one. I've called it the water tablet for years, and the chemist on High Street knows exactly what I mean.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She missed the water tablet twice last week. They were still sitting in the dosette on Thursday and Sunday.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Those were spare Panadol, the little white ones look the same if the light's poor. I take the indapamide every single morning. I line them up on the saucer so I can see them.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): So ramipril five milligrams daily, new five weeks ago, and indapamide two point five, which you say you never skip. Anything else you take?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol, the odd one, if the knee niggles, not every day. And that's me. My brother Kevin is on lisinopril, not me. He coughed for months and they changed him, and Sharon brings it up every time we have tea.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Kevin's lisinopril stays off your list, it's his. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I can pretty much take what's put in front of me.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sulphur tablets. She came out in a rash years ago, when the old GP tried them for a water infection.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't reckon that was an allergy. I had a gastro at the same time, and I've had Bactrim since with no drama. I wouldn't put allergy on my form.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Kevin's got it, and Dad had it too. Mum didn't, she had the sugar, but that's not me and I won't wander off into Mum's story.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, not a single cigarette. A glass of sav blanc with dinner a few nights a week, and that's the limit. My sister Sharon lives in the front room, so I'm not rattling around the house alone.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The wine I'll vouch for. It's the stairs, and whether she should still be doing that morning walk down to the river.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check the pressure while we talk. 152 over 90, and the pulse is 74. Did you take a home reading?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): This morning I thought it said one-sixty over ninety-five, but I had the digits wrong. It was 146 over 84. I wrote it on the pad. The pulse was 70-something, I didn't bother keeping it.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Chest is clear, no wheeze, no crackles. Throat's not inflamed. Ankles aren't puffy.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): There you go, breathing's fine. My neighbour had a cough for a month after a cold, which proves nothing, I know, but it feels the same.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to call this an ACE-inhibitor cough. It might be the ramipril, it might be the tail of that virus, and reflux can give a dry cough even without heartburn. I can't separate those today, so there's no firm diagnosis, and the clear chest doesn't settle it either. We'll just note the length as somewhere between four and six weeks.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're not saying it is the tablet.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not concluding that. I am going to stop the ramipril, and tomorrow morning you start candesartan, eight milligrams, once a day, in its place. Keep taking the indapamide exactly as you are.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Do we bin the ramipril, then?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't bin it, and don't take any more of it. Bring the box next visit so the chemist record matches. If your lips or tongue swell, if you become properly breathless, or if you cough up blood, go to emergency, don't wait for me.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips or tongue, properly breathless, blood, emergency. And the candesartan is instead of the ramipril, not on top of it. I'll say it twice so I don't muddle the dosette.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Instead, not on top. I'm not ordering a chest x-ray today. If the cough hasn't eased when I see you next, then I'll arrange one.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): When is next? Thursday mornings suit me. Arvos don't, Sharon's at the pool and I won't get a lift.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): In three weeks. We'll recheck the pressure and see what the cough is doing. Still no firm label on it until we've watched it off the ramipril.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll book at the desk. And the morning walk, is that off?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): The walk can stay. No need to stop it on account of this.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Three weeks, candesartan eight instead of ramipril five, water tablet stays, walk stays. And the glass of wine is still allowed, or have you quietly cancelled that?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): The wine, as you described it, is fine. Keep a note of the cough and the morning readings on that pad.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll write them under the 146. And I'll tell the chemist, when I pick up the candesartan, not to pack the ramipril again. I do talk their ear off, they know me.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good plan. Sharon can grab that three-week appointment on the way out, and we'll take it from there.

[SEG0019] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Doctor Pillay at the hospital clinic, about two months back. Simvastatin. He stopped it because her legs were cramping.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja those cramps were horrible at night. They're better now. If you change my tablets will they come back?

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I take it with my rooibos, before breakfast. Is twenty even enough? My neighbour takes more than that.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Neighbours aren't a script, hey. You mentioned a little white one and a pink one for the pressure?
[SEG0025] person_2 (CAREGIVER): The little white one is perindopril, four milligrams, mornings. The pink one is Coversyl, also for the high blood. I wrote them as two things on my paper.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, I'm opening the medication list. Coversyl is perindopril. Same medicine, different jacket. So it's been double-counted.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Eish. So I've been swallowing two? I knew it. Is that why the ankle went fat?
[SEG0028] person_2 (CAREGIVER): No, Mama. I only pack the white one. The pink bottle is an old one from Clicks. I just wrote it down twice by mistake.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): You sure? I saw a pink one at supper on Tuesday. I don't imagine things.
[SEG0030] person_2 (CAREGIVER): That was my vitamin, shame, not yours. Yours is only the little white one.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, repeat that? Whose vitamin? This cursor keeps jumping.
[SEG0032] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Mine. Hers is perindopril four milligrams once every morning. The little white tablet, not the pink.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, then we won't count it twice. On your file I've got high blood and sugar. There's something for the sugar as well?
[SEG0034] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Metformin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day with meals. She's been on it five years... no, since twenty nineteen, so six years.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last month's lab is here. The HbA1c was seven point two percent. Not ugly. Blood pressure, the sister wrote one fifty two over ninety four... no, that's the old visit. Today is one thirty eight over eighty four, pulse seventy six.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Is one thirty eight safe? What if I fall? The passage is dark when load shedding hits, and I'm seventy eight, you know.

[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I can take anything. Is that still normal at my age?

[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): See, I told her it's the right. Is the water tablet failing? Should I sleep with my legs up? I already use a cushion.

[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Forty? But it was just brought down. Won't I live in the loo? Some days the clinic transport comes at seven.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): You'll pass more water for a few days, mostly morning if you take it when you wake, not at night. If you get cramps or you feel faint, phone us.
[SEG0046] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Must I throw the twenty milligram tablets away, or can she use two of them to make forty?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two of the twenties is fine until the new script is ready. I'll send forty milligram tablets to the chemist, one each morning. The medical aid should cover it.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): And the little white one stays? Do I need the cholesterol tablet back? My sister had a stroke and now I can't stop thinking about it.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perindopril stays, four milligrams once a day, only the white tablet. I'm not restarting the simvastatin today. Cholesterol can wait, it's not the ankle.
[SEG0050] person_2 (CAREGIVER): When must we come back? Should I bring that old pink bottle so you can see it?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can bring the bottles if you like, but you don't have to. Come back in two weeks so I can check the swelling and the pressure. If the swelling is worse before that, or she gets breathless, don't wait, come in.

[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any trouble swallowing, or feeling like food is catching?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, swallowing's fine. Everything goes down okay.

[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, my joints are good.

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, so there's the levothyroxine, 50 micrograms in the morning. And the omeprazole, 20 mg before breakfast.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And for the itching?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): The hydroxyzine, 25 mg at bedtime, for the itch. It makes me groggy, but it helps.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. It's the whiplash, from the car crash in the summer. I'm better but not right, if you know what I mean.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me how it is now.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My neck's stiff, especially in the mornings, and I get a pain across my shoulders by the afternoon. Worse after driving.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is it since the accident? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Four months. It was better at two months, then it plateaued. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the pain going down your arms, any numbness or tingling?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing in my arms. No tingling.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you using for the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Naproxen, 250 mg, twice a day, maybe? And paracetamol, 1 gram, but I only take that when it's bad, so not every day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. So 250 mg twice a day, as you recall it, and the paracetamol only when it's bad. Remind me of your history.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, a stomach ulcer, years ago, and my back's not great. Slipped disc.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any operations?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): An operation on my lower back, a discectomy, in 2014.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you working?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I'm a delivery driver. Hours in the van.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your neck. Sit on the couch. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tender over the muscles on both sides of the neck, tight and knotted in the upper shoulder muscles, and the movement is limited when you look over your shoulder.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that normal for four months on? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's common. Whiplash can take months to settle, and the muscles tighten and guard. I'd say this is a persisting whiplash strain.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it ever clear? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people recover, usually by six months, but you need to keep the neck moving. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been scared to. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand. Gentle exercises and physiotherapy help most. I'd like to arrange a referral for physio.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): When? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few weeks. Meanwhile, I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the neck, to be thorough, given the time that's passed.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Also, naproxen and your old stomach ulcer don't mix well, so please always take it with food.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been taking it on an empty stomach, I'll stop. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take it only with food, and if you get stomach pain, or black stools, stop it and ring us. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thank you. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Use a warm pack, and break up your driving with stops to stretch.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the pain spreads into your arm, or you get weakness or numbness in your hands, come back that day.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Howzit, come through and sit. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, I'm fine, honestly. My wife made the booking. I got stuck at the robot on Main Road forever because of load shedding, so I'm a bit rattled, but me, I'm alright.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. What is she actually worried about?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): She says I don't sleep, I just lie there staring, and in the day I'm like a ghost on the couch. I told her it's nothing, but she wouldn't drop it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, let's start with the nights. What happens once you're in bed?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I drop off okay, hey, around ten. Then I'm awake at three, sometimes half past two, and that's me finished. I just listen to the dogs and the fridge humming.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And by morning, do you feel as if you've slept?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm wrecked. Coffee doesn't touch it. I used to do the early shift no problem, now the kettle feels like a project.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this waking been going on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish. Months. I can't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. I mix those years up, sorry.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was something going on around then, at home or at work?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, maybe. My dad went, and I lost the job at the depot. Which one came first I couldn't tell you. The dates are just mush in my head.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry about your dad. Tell me about the job.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Depot supervisor, logistics, the big warehouse by the highway. Twenty two years. A new manager arrived, all spreadsheets, and they said the post was redundant. Redundant, after twenty two years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a heavy blow. How's your energy through the day?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I manage the school run if I push, then I'm on the couch till my wife gets home. She's a nurse, did I mention, so some weeks she's on nights and the house is dead quiet.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your mood itself? Have you been feeling down, or low in yourself?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm fine. Mood's alright. I'm not depressed, if that's where this is going. I'm just tired.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the things you usually enjoy? Rugby, a braai, seeing people?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Rugby's still rugby, I put it on. The rest is fine. I'm not avoiding anybody.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Speaking of braais, the neighbour had a massive one, boerewors and chops, and their new dog stole a sausage clean off the plate. I didn't hang about, though. Funny dog.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): You didn't hang about. Is that just the once, or have you been pulling back from people?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah. Ja. I suppose I have. I don't pitch anymore. Can't be bothered to talk. Even the rugby, it's on and I'm not watching. I wasn't straight with you just now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you correcting that. Is there sadness with it, or a heaviness?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): There is. I feel heavy. Some mornings I sit in the bakkie after drop-off and I just cry, which is mad, I'm forty six and I'm crying at a robot. I didn't want to come in and say I'm depressed, but it's been like that.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I need to ask this gently, and it's something I ask everyone, not because I assume the worst. Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I've never thought that. I've got the two boys, it's not in my head at all.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad that's clear. How's your appetite been?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Eating's normal. She cooks, I finish the plate. I haven't lost any weight.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any headaches, or feeling sick in your stomach, along with this?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. My stomach's fine. The coffee at your front desk is another story, mind, I wouldn't give that to an enemy.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Concentration, paperwork, driving?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Driving's okay once I'm moving. Forms, though, I lose the plot. The unemployment papers, I stare and nothing goes in. That's new for me.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you drinking more in the evenings to get through?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two beers, most nights, once the kids are down. Not brandy like my uncle used to. I don't smoke, never have. The beers don't even make me sleepy.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's in the house with you?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife Naledi, and the boys, eight and eleven. We rent in Glenwood. She's been carrying the money since the job went, and that makes me feel useless, but ja.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you tried any tablets for the sleep or the mood?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The GP at the day hospital put me on citalopram, twenty milligrams, one in the morning. I stopped it in March. My jaw went tight and I felt like I was buzzing, so I left it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March. Was there anything else on that script?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Zopiclone, seven point five milligrams. I only took it once. I was a zombie the whole next day, so I binned the box.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They also wrote amitriptyline, a small dose, supposed to help sleep. I never fetched it from the chemist. Never took one. It's not even in the house.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the citalopram you stopped, the zopiclone you took once, the amitriptyline you never started. Any allergies to medicines, or foods, or anything else?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No penicillin thing, no foods. My sister comes out in a rash with bees, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations, diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid problems?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. No sugar, no pressure. I'm boring on paper. My dad had a heart attack, that's what took him, I don't know if you need that.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note it, yes, your dad's heart attack sits in the family history. For you I'm not hearing a chronic list.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me take your pressure while we sit. One thirty two over eighty four, and your pulse is seventy six, regular. You look tidy enough, but your face has been flat, and you welled up talking about the bakkie.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sorry. The school wants money for a tour and I nearly said yes before I remembered I'm not earning. Eish, that one hit me in the parking lot.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): The money worry is sitting right in the middle of this, I think. Let me think out loud so it's not a black box. Early waking, no energy, you've lost interest, you're tearful, and it sits somewhere in the last winter or two, after the job and your dad. My working impression is a depressive episode, not a label I'm carving in stone today.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grief might be tangled through it. I can't cleanly say it's only the redundancy or only your dad, so I'm keeping both possibilities open.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing my mind. I thought you'd tell me to have a braai and get over it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. And I'm not starting a tablet today. You already stopped the citalopram, and I don't want to hand you another one before we've watched the next couple of weeks.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're still this low when I see you again, we might start sertraline at a small dose, but only if you want it and only if nothing has lifted. Not today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather skip tablets if I can. That buzzing scared me off. If you say we look again in two weeks, I can live with that.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the tiredness, I'm not sending bloods today either. If it hasn't eased by that visit, we might check your thyroid and a full blood count, so a physical cause isn't hiding in there.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I do want you to try, starting tonight, is dull and it works more often than people think. Same time out of bed every morning, twenty minutes outside in the light, and shift those beers earlier or skip them.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if any thought of hurting yourself shows up, even a small one, you don't wait for our appointment. Casualty, or phone the rooms, the same day. Naledi can bring you.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll do that. It's not there, I promise. She would drag me, you know her. Last week she nearly phoned you herself, then the dog ate her slipper, whole other saga.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks. Ask at reception to book it on your way out. If you slide before then, don't sit at home with it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, ja. Should I bring her? She talks straighter than I do when I start with I'm fine.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring her if she's free, it helps. We'll only decide on the bloods and on sertraline then, and only if we still need to.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Shame, thanks. I feel a bit lighter having said the crying bit out loud. Don't tell the boys about the robot, hey.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's between us. Book the two weeks at the desk, be decent to yourself this week, and I'll see you then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning, doctor. Lovely to meet you.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, it's been about three months now. And pain at night when I lie on it, too.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How troublesome is it day to day?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Severe, really. I've also had an ache down the upper arm, for nearly five years. As for ache down the upper arm, I'd say a couple of times a week.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had difficulty combing your hair before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing about six months ago. It went away.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing like fever?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Not at all, no fever.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any neck pain, swelling or chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any of them.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about smoking?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I've never touched a cigarette.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything you do to stay fit?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your eating.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you on your own at home?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with my elderly mother.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm on metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day. Simvastatin. I take it 20 milligrams, at night for my cholesterol.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Clopidogrel, 75 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, high blood pressure. I've had high cholesterol for two years now. I didn't want to make a fuss, you know.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And besides that?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got gout. I've had heart disease, yes.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, high blood pressure and gout are known to us, good to have that clear. Anything surgical in your history?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Just a triple bypass, eight years ago.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me get the readings out of the way.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bear with me while this finishes...
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: pulse 64, blood pressure 119 over 74, temperature is 36.7 degrees, saturation 97 percent.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the area, I'll be gentle.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, raise your arm for me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is pain when you lift the arm out to the side between about sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees, and the grip strength is normal.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, no problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, good, you can sit up again. Putting it all together, I think we're dealing with a rotator cuff tendon problem at this stage.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, what are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's a rotator cuff tendon problem, and we'll know more once the an ultrasound of the shoulder is back. [SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): That's it, yes.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll request an ultrasound of the shoulder, it'll help with shoulder pain. I'll request a shoulder X-ray, it'll help with shoulder pain. For this, naproxen, 250 milligrams, twice a day with food, for one week. That should help with shoulder pain.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I carry on if I feel better?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the shoulder moving gently within comfort and avoid heavy overhead lifting. Please take the tablets with food so they don't upset your stomach.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Let's get you seen by physiotherapy, I'll arrange the letter.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure, where do I go?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in four weeks. Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.

[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Last night I was boiling, proper teeth-chattering, then I took Panadol and by this morning the temperature felt normal. I'm not hot sitting here.

[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The discharge sheet says cephalexin, seven days. She's been saying five all week.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dose?

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nurofen?

[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Correct. No allergies.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, so, I know I said on the phone it was just the tiredness, but honestly it's more than that now. I just feel flat all the time, and the baby's fine, she's gorgeous, that's what makes it so confusing.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for coming in and for saying it so plainly. So you feel flat most of the time, even though the baby is doing well. Let's take it one piece at a time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, I'm all over the place. I haven't slept properly since, well, since she was born really, and she's five months now. Oh, and I forgot to say, my health visitor is the one who nudged me to come.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): No need to apologise. The health visitor nudged you, and you're feeling flat. How long has it been going on, would you say?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The low mood, the low mood has been there about four months. It was worse in the first two months, then a bit better, then worse again when I started thinking about going back to work.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So about four months of low mood, in waves, with the worst patch at the beginning and another when work came into view. Is there a time of day it's heaviest?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Mornings, mostly. Although hang on, the evenings are bad as well when she won't settle. My husband says I'm being hard on myself, but he's lovely, he does the nappies.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mornings, and evenings when she's unsettled. I'm going to ask a few straight questions, because I ask everybody who has been low. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no, nothing like that. I'd never.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me. And any thoughts of harming the baby?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): God, no. I'm terrified of anything happening to her, if anything I check on her too much. I got up four times last night just to see her chest moving.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very common, and I'm glad you said it out loud. What about panic attacks, those sudden waves of fear with a racing heart?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No panic attacks. I get a bit wound up in the supermarket, but nothing like that.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Now let me check what you're taking at the moment so I have it right. Last time we had you on sertraline, is that still going?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, sertraline, 100 mg, one every morning with my tea. And the thyroid tablet, the levothyroxine, 75 micrograms, one a day before breakfast. Oh, and the iron, ferrous fumarate, one at night, the pharmacist suggested it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): So sertraline 100 milligrams every morning, levothyroxine 75 micrograms once a day, and iron at night. Is that the underactive thyroid you've had for a while?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, the underactive thyroid, I was nineteen when they found it. And the anaemia, that was in the pregnancy, that's why the iron. I also get migraines now and then, but they've been quiet.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Underactive thyroid, anaemia, and migraines that have been quiet. Good. Has anyone in your family struggled with their mood?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): My mum had depression, after I was born actually, nobody called it that back then. She told me last month, which was a surprise. Sorry, that's a tangent.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all, that's useful. Your mum had depression, and it's something you've just learnt. Let me take your blood pressure and pulse while we talk, if you'd rest your arm on the desk.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 112 over 70 and your pulse is 84 beats per minute. Both perfectly comfortable numbers.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): That's good, I thought my heart would be racing, it feels like it is sometimes. Is it the thyroid, do you think? My sister-in-law said it could be the thyroid.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your sister-in-law has a fair point. I can't rule out that your thyroid has drifted off again and is adding to the flatness and tiredness, so we shouldn't put it all down to mood.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): So it might not be all in my head. That would be a relief, honestly.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): It was never all in your head. Low mood after a baby is common and treatable, and the thyroid is worth checking either way. I'd like to repeat your thyroid blood test, and I'll arrange it for you to have today.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Brilliant. And the tablets, do I carry on with those?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, we'll keep your tablets exactly as they are for now. The sertraline stays at 100 and we'll see what the blood test says before we change anything.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. And the sleep? I'm lucky if I get two hours in a row. I'd like to sleep at some point before she goes to university.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleep matters hugely here. Could your husband do one night feed so you get a four-hour block? Even a few nights of that can lift things. Does that sound possible?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): He did offer. I said no because he's got work, but I could say yes on the weekend at least.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say yes on the weekend, then, and let the housework go. Please also ring us the same day if your mood drops sharply or those thoughts of harming yourself ever appear.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I will, I promise. I just want to feel like me again.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): You will, and we're going to work on it together. I'd like to see you again in four weeks, once the results are back, and we'll go through them.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks, okay. I'll book at the desk on the way out.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. So, to say it back: blood test today, tablets unchanged, a weekend night off, and back with me in four weeks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You didn't waffle, you told me exactly what I needed to know. Go and enjoy that gorgeous girl.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Bye.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye, see you in four weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I'm not sure what I've come about, to be honest. The hospital said to come back and see you after I was in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, you were in for a chest infection three weeks ago. How have you been since you came home? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand, grand. Only I've no appetite. None at all. I push the food around the plate.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Since the hospital? Or before it? Honestly, I couldn't say. I've been off my food a while.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My trousers are loose, so I must have. A couple of stone, maybe? I don't weigh myself.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you feel sick, or does food stick, or does it hurt to eat? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none of that. I'm just not hungry. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mirtazapine, 15 mg, maybe? At bedtime, the little white one. And omeprazole, 20 mg in the morning.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the mirtazapine 15 mg, do you think? You said maybe.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): It could be 30. The chemist knows. I only take what they give me.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll check with the record. What's it for? ~
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): For my mood, after my wife died. Two years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm very sorry. Any operations?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Gallbladder, in the nineties.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me weigh you, and check your numbers. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on then. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, blood pressure 118 over 72, temperature 36.6, oxygen 96 percent, and you weigh 64 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that a lot? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your record says 74 kilos a year ago, so you've lost about ten kilos, which is significant. Any cough or breathlessness left from the chest infection?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): A little cough in the morning. No breathlessness.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd say the main thing is poor appetite after your recent illness, in the setting of low mood, so I'd call it reduced appetite following illness.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you think it's my mood? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's likely part of it, but with that much weight loss, I don't want to assume. I'd like to arrange blood tests, to look for anaemia, thyroid, and other causes.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
