[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mr Venkataraman, the booking says you want a review and that something to do with an old reaction is worrying you.
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, yes, doctor. Please call me Venkat, everyone does. That reaction business I will come to, but first let me tell you about this chest.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Go ahead. What is the chest doing?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): When I climb the stairs to my daughter's flat, third floor only, I get a tightness here in the middle. Then I stop, wait, and it goes.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): So tightness in the middle of the chest when you climb. How long has this been happening?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): For about one month only. Before that I was climbing like a goat. My grandson says I am slowing down.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long does it last when you stop?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Two minutes, maybe three. I have to hold the railing and pretend I am admiring the view.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. Does it spread anywhere, the arm or the jaw?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Not that I noticed. Same spot every time.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been short of breath with it?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no. Breath is fine. Only the tightness, and my heart doesn't flutter or anything like that.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now, tell me about the reaction. What's worrying you?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): See, my cousin in Chennai had a terrible thing with a tablet. He nearly died, doctor. So now I am worried about every tablet.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry to hear that. But I'm asking about you. Do you have a reaction of your own?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Years ago, I took some antibiotic for my throat and I reacted to it. My wife was there, she remembers more than me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): What kind of reaction? A rash, swelling, breathing trouble?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): That is the problem, I cannot recall. I only remember the doctor said, never take that antibiotic again. Hospital people made a note.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the name?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. It was something ending in 'cillin' or maybe 'mycin'. I told my wife to remember but she says ask Venkat.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. So we know it's an antibiotic, and you had some kind of reaction, but not which one or what happened.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Exactly. Is it a problem? Because you will be giving me tablets also, no?
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not prescribing anything today. But I want it on your record as an allergy to an antibiotic, so nobody gives you the wrong one.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. Good. That is why I came. My wife was telling me, do it before the next emergency.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sensible wife. Can you find the old hospital papers? Or ask your wife whether she kept the discharge letter?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): She keeps everything. Forty-five years of marriage and she has every bill. I will search the almirah.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please bring whatever you find. Also, if the old GP's surgery still exists, we can ask them for the note.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): That one is closed now. The doctor retired, and his son went to Dubai.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then the papers at home are our best chance. What did you do for work, Venkat?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I am a retired bank manager. Thirty-five years in the State Bank. Many files, I know the value of a record.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then you'll appreciate this. A clear record is worth more than ten guesses.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me repeat that back to be sure. Tightness on the stairs for a month, settling in minutes, and an antibiotic reaction years ago, details unknown.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Correct. You should work for the bank, doctor. Tell me one thing. This chest tightness. Is it dangerous?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't say yet, and I don't want to guess. That is exactly why I'd like to see you again once the papers are found.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. When should I come?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's say in four weeks. That gives you time to search the almirah and ask around.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks is fine. Should my wife come along? She remembers more than me.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please do bring her. Two memories are better than one.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. Four weeks is fine. Should I climb those stairs in the meantime?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take the lift if there is one, and rest when the tightness comes. If it lasts longer than ten minutes, call an ambulance.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten minutes. I will tell my daughter also. She will be so anxious.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell her yes. And Venkat, thank you for being so organised about this.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): It's my pleasure. Thank you, doctor. I will bring the papers and some of my wife's homemade sweets.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): The papers will do nicely. Goodbye, and mind the stairs.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. The spirometry is done, I'll read it out when you're ready, doctor.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The cough, mostly. Mornings are desperate, I'm hacking before the kettle's even boiled. And I'm breathless on the hill up from the shop. Mad rain all week, the collie next door won't step out in it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is the cough going?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Years, sure, always a morning thing. It's worse since the chest infection though, that was three weeks... no, five weeks ago. I was in bits.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The screen jumped. Five weeks?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Five weeks, yeah. Fever and green phlegm, the lot. They gave me amoxicillin and I finished the course. Fever's gone, and the green stuff cleared.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with the breathlessness?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No pain. And no blood, before you ask. Just the puffing and the cough.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the flat, or only on the hill?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Flat I'm grand enough. The hill to the house, I'm stopping halfway to get my breath. Yer man with the collie thinks I'm only nosing at his gate.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the phlegm still there in the mornings?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of white stuff, yeah. Not green anymore.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): A small bit at night, if I'm lying flat. Not every night.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the smoking. How many are you on?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): About ten a day... ah, maybe twenty, if I'm straight with you. Since I was sixteen. Forty-odd years of it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twenty a day, a long time. Did you ever try stopping?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): The patches, last year. Itched the skin something awful, so I gave them up after a couple of weeks. Dear old things too, from the chemist.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you using inhalers?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The blue one, salbutamol, when I need it. Some days that's four or five times. And the brown one, beclomethasone I think, two puffs... no, one puff, twice a day. I'm shocking for forgetting it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say the brown one again, I didn't catch the name.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Beclometasone. One puff twice a day, the days I remember. Maybe three or four days in the week, if that.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So not every day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No. It lives in the drawer more than in my pocket, I'll admit.
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): Will I give you the spirometry now?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Go on, yeah.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): FEV1 was one point eight litres, sixty-two percent predicted. FVC three point one litres, eighty-one percent. Ratio nought point five eight.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): One point eight, sixty-two percent. Hang on, I'm typing it in. What about the observations?
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Saturation ninety-five percent on room air. Pulse eighty-eight. Blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-four. Breathing eighteen a minute. Temperature thirty-six point seven.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll have a listen to the chest if you sit forward.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Work away. Mind the shirt, it's the good one. The wife ironed it before she went to her sister's in Cork, so I'm on beans on toast all week.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breath sounds are reduced at both bases, and I've a few wheezes on the right. No crackles.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Is that desperate news, doctor?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It fits with the smoking and the tight airways. I'd call it a working diagnosis of COPD. The infection looks settled.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): COPD. My brother had that. Ended up on the oxygen. He smoked more than me, mind.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. The amoxicillin was grand, no bother at all.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): The beclometasone we've got down here is two hundred micrograms. Is that the inhaler at home?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the one. Little brown thing, two hundred.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want that every day, one puff twice a day, not just when you remember. Keep the salbutamol for the breathlessness, two puffs when you need it.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I'll try. The blue one I do use. The brown one slips the mind.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): We might do a chest X-ray if the cough does not settle. And let's see you in two weeks, see how the regular inhaler is going.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks is grand. Do I need to be fasting? Last time I was in for bloods they left me sitting an age, and I'd had no breakfast.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fasting. It's just the cough and the breathing we'll be looking at. I'd like to refer you on to the stop-smoking service, if you'll go.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah I suppose I should. Twenty a day isn't clever and I know it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the cessation clinic from out here, doctor, if you want.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book it, please. And the review here in two weeks.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the two of them in.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Is the cessation one in this building or the other one? I get lost over there, the signs are useless.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): It's here, Thursday mornings as a rule. I'll give you the slip on the way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets worse before then, or you're feverish again, don't wait the two weeks. Come back sooner, or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): I will, yeah. The wife would have my head if I left it. She's home Sunday.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. We'll leave it there so.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. That computer's as slow as myself on the hill.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about it. Mind yourself, Mr Brennan.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Afternoon, is this seat fine?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly vomiting. There's a couple of other things, but that's the main one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did this begin? I'll explain everything as we go along.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been going on for four weeks.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much does it limit you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A five out of ten, I suppose.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had severe thirst and passing lots of urine?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, about the same, two months. There was being very confused, yes, but that went away.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on any regular medication?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing at the moment.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medical conditions, anything you've been treated for?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no conditions.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had any surgical procedures?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Just my septum straightened, in my thirties.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, kiwi. I've no idea what the reaction was, only that I'm not supposed to have it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I gave up cigarettes last spring. I used to drink heavily but I stopped four years ago. Not much, I mostly stay in these days. Yes, I work in a bakery, early starts. Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check a few things. Any chest pain, fall or fever?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope, nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any problems with your joints or muscles?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else aches.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your breathing, any trouble there?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing there.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get the readings out of the way.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature 36.5, blood pressure 102 over 57, saturation 98 percent, heart rate 103.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): They help me see the whole picture, more shortly.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I examine you now?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure thing.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nearly finished here.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are dehydrated and drowsy with a slow, odd rhythm on the monitor.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again. Putting it all together, it points towards a high calcium emergency.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Is this permanent?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like a high calcium emergency, but I'd like to confirm. Urgent blood tests is what I'd like next, for confusion and polyuria.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I need to prepare?
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to put you on sodium chloride 0.9%, 1 litre, over one hour, single dose. It's for dehydration.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): How soon will it work?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): You need hospital fluids and treatment now. Come back or go to emergency straight away if the symptoms get worse.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll remember that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back straight away. That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Mild, really.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing about six months ago. It went away.

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, um, no, my breathing's been fine.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me and what I found, this is probably possible carbon monoxide exposure at home. That's my thinking for now, and it may change as we learn more. Another possibility is a viral illness.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, so I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with possible carbon monoxide exposure at home do well once it's treated properly. I'd like to arrange a carboxyhaemoglobin blood test for possible carbon monoxide exposure.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that done today?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't use the boiler tonight and get it checked by an engineer, and keep a window open. The gas emergency service would be the right next step, I'll refer you. If you feel more dizzy or drowsy, that's the point to come in urgently. Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not the arm, not the jaw. It stays in the chest.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any sweating or nausea along with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating. No nausea.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And palpitations, heart racing or skipping?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Heart doesn't do that.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No giddiness. Feet are fine. I just want to finish and go.

[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): On and off is putting it kindly. He skips many days, some weeks only three or four tablets. I keep telling him.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it when I remember. Don't scold me here.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet, cholesterol or sugar?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin they gave for cholesterol. Twenty milligrams — no, it was ten. I stopped it, it didn't suit me.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped fully, or you still take it sometimes?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Fully stopped, around a year back. Isosorbide was also written on an old slip — that I never took, not even once.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): True, doctor. That isosorbide bottle is still sealed in the cupboard.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had the high BP?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve years... no, fifteen years. Since a long time.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any diabetes?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Last year the sugar test was normal.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check the pressure. Hmm, one sixty-six over one hundred — the cuff was crooked, ignore that. Repeat is one fifty-eight over ninety-four. Pulse is eighty-four, regular.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Ankles are not swollen.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think aloud. Sixty-four, BP for many years, this tightness on stairs and fast walking — my working impression is angina. Provisional only, not confirmed.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to book an echocardiogram this week, together with the ECG.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not sitting for some long test. I am exhausted, I want to go home.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He will simply refuse and walk out, doctor. Kindly keep it smaller today.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I am changing that. No echocardiogram. We will do a resting ECG, and blood tests — fasting sugar, a lipid profile, and kidney function.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): ECG and blood, fine. Do it and finish.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Continue amlodipine ten milligrams every morning, don't skip that one. Aspirin seventy-five, please take it daily, not on and off.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the tightness comes at rest, or you start sweating with it, go to emergency straight away. Don't wait at home.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Emergency, yes, I heard. Anything else?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week with the reports. We will talk once we see them.
[SEG0050] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will bring him only. He forgets dates otherwise.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Kindly see reception on the way out — they will arrange the ECG and the blood tests before you leave.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good afternoon, I'm Dr. Shah. Come, sit down. Your husband can wait outside for a bit, and we'll call him if you like.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, let him wait. I... I don't know, doctor, I'm very scared.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright, take your time. What has been happening?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm pregnant, I think eight or ten weeks, and there is spotting, and cramps also, like my periods.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was your last proper period?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The spotting is brown, doctor, not bright red. In the morning it looks a little pink sometimes.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll note the colour, but I still need the period date. Can you place the last one?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It was around Diwali, or after Diwali. I'm not sure which.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): No problem. Was there any bleeding after that period, before this spotting started?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing in between. Then this spotting came, and I don't know from when. Since Diwali or after, something like that. I keep mixing it up.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where do you feel the cramps?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Low down, both sides. Like period pain. Not the whole stomach.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many pads have you used since this morning?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother keeps phoning. She says lie down, drink coconut water, don't go anywhere. I don't know, doctor, I'm just frightened something is wrong with the baby.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mothers do that. Still, the pads — since morning, how many, and were they soaked?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, only one pad, and it's not soaked, just spots. No clots... well, actually, I thought there was a small clot yesterday, but no, it was only thick brown, not a clot.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any giddiness, any fainting, any pain in the shoulder?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No giddiness. I didn't faint. Shoulder is fine.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or burning when you pass urine?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Urine is normal, no burning.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nausea is there, mostly in the mornings. I haven't vomited. I don't know if it's the pregnancy or just the worry.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And sleep?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Very bad. I was awake half the night, not really from the pain, from thinking too much.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Folic acid, five milligrams, once a day, since the test was positive. And thyroxine, for my thyroid.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength of thyroxine, and how do you take it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning, on an empty stomach. The dose, I don't know, doctor. Maybe seventy-five micrograms. They changed it once. I get confused.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else, even for pain? Anything you have stopped?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to take mefenamic acid for period pain, two hundred and fifty milligrams. I stopped it when the test came positive. Not a single tablet after that.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergy, to a medicine or a food?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any illness we should know about, apart from the thyroid?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Thyroid only. It started last winter, or the one before, I can't remember. It's still there. I take the tablet daily, I think, most days. Sometimes I forget on Sundays. I don't know.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the thyroid problem is ongoing, and a few Sunday doses may be getting missed. Any operation in the past?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No operation.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink alcohol?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. No alcohol. I'm a primary teacher, on leave now. We live with my in-laws, so the house is never quiet.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me just check. Blood pressure is one hundred and eight over sixty-eight. Pulse is ninety-two. Temperature is thirty-seven point one.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft. There is mild tenderness across the lower abdomen. No guarding, and no rigidity.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): It hurts a little when you press, yes. Only a little.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shall we call your husband in, so he hears the plan as well?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, call him. He is sitting just outside, he was complaining about the parking earlier.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, the parking is a nightmare out there. She has been very unwell. The pain is bad, she was crying with it since yesterday, she could not even lie straight.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Arjun, it's not like that. The pain is like periods, I can manage. I was crying because I am scared, not because the pain is so bad.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the spotting, doctor, it has been two weeks. She told me two weeks.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say two weeks for sure. Maybe three weeks, or two, I don't know, doctor. It was around Diwali, or after. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So he says two weeks, you say two or three weeks, and the actual day is still around Diwali or after. I won't lock a date.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her thyroxine is a hundred micrograms. I saw that on the strip last month.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the old strip. I think the new one is seventy-five. I don't know, doctor, I didn't bring the box.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't guess the dose. Bring the strip with you next time. Apart from some Sundays, are you still taking it every morning?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, mornings, except some Sundays. I don't know how many I missed.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't be sure today what this is. It may be a threatened miscarriage, or it may only be spotting in early pregnancy. We need the tests before saying more.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Today we'll do a scan, a transvaginal ultrasound if you're agreeable, and blood tests — haemoglobin, blood group, and a serum beta-hCG.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): A scan today? Will it harm the baby? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): It won't harm the baby. It shows us if the pregnancy is inside the uterus and if there is a heartbeat. Please have the blood tests and the scan today, before you leave.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. For the cramps, can I take something?
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Start paracetamol, five hundred milligrams by mouth, three times a day, for the cramps, for the next few days. Don't take mefenamic acid or ibuprofen. Keep taking the folic acid, five milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want to see you back in this clinic in three days, with the reports. If you soak a pad within one hour, or you feel giddy, or the pain becomes severe, come back straight away, don't wait.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days, and if it gets heavy or I feel giddy, come immediately. I understand. I'm still very worried.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course you are. One step at a time. Reception will send you for the bloods and the scan now, and I'll see you in three days, sooner if those signs show up.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): morning, doctor. I've settled them in, ready when you are
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect, thanks. Hello there, so what's the trouble?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hello, doctor, I came in with them, if that's okay.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): right, please do extra information is always welcome
[SEG0005] person_4 (PATIENT): Well, I've been having fainting on exertion.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did it come on recently?
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): probably three days yeah
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): and the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): I was getting to that! Oh, and being very breathless that's been about the same, three days
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): have you had fainting on exertion before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, something like this happened a couple of years ago, and it went away on its own.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, I've got the readings for you. Heart rate 88, SpO2 90 percent on room air, temp 37.1 degrees, pressure 138 over 72.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): thanks
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll need to examine you for this, it won't take long.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): raise your arm for me
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is a loud second heart sound and a raised jugular pulse.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): that's the examination finished any cough, leg pain or fever?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): no, no cough, no leg pain, no fever i did have swollen ankles at one point, but that went away on its own
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): any rashes or skin problems otherwise?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): No rashes.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your mobility otherwise okay?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): no, nothing there
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's run through your medicines.
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): For my heart, I believe. My wife sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. Hydrocortisone cream, when needed. Escitalopram. I take it 10 milligrams, once a day. Erm, I take iron tablets, once a day. I'd been on metoprolol, not any more though, I stopped.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): My daughter has type 1 diabetes. My father had bowel cancer.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): What conditions have you been treated for in the past?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): I have heart failure yes, eczema
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Anxiety, for about a year. I've had low haemoglobin, yes.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): No, nothing as far as I know.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): do you do any exercise?
[SEG0037] person_4 (PATIENT): I swim twice a week.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you live by yourself?
[SEG0039] person_4 (PATIENT): No, I share a house with my brother.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): So where does that leave us? It's hard to say. Possible pulmonary hypertension is one possibility and a heart valve problem another, and I'd rather not commit yet.
[SEG0041] person_4 (PATIENT): Do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like possible pulmonary hypertension, but I'd like to confirm. I'll request an ECG, it'll help with syncope. We should do an echocardiogram for exertional syncope. That will help us see what's going on underneath and decide the next step. I think blood tests makes sense here, for breathlessness. No exertion for now, I am arranging urgent specialist tests.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm going to send a referral to the pulmonary hypertension service
[SEG0044] person_4 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if the symptoms get worse. That's when to be seen urgently. See me again in one week.
[SEG0046] person_4 (PATIENT): Good, I'll return then.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): that's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Mm, thank you, that's helpful.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, take a seat. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, not much, really. Heart just does this little flutter thing. I nearly didn't bother coming.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): A flutter. When do you actually notice it?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly at night, lying there. And before an exam, or those Monday meetings at work. Sitting up settles it in a couple of minutes. It's nothing.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not nothing. You've been sitting up at like two in the morning, heart going flat out. I can feel it through the mattress.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): You're exaggerating. It's a bit quick, that's all. I can still talk through it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on for?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Last winter, or the one before? I honestly can't pin it. Maybe around when uni went back, I don't know.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): With the racing, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Breathing's fine. I'm not getting puffed.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, or have you blacked out?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Never fainted. I'm not collapsing in the street or anything.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do get puffed, though. Stairs at the flat, you stop halfway. And at night you say you can't get a proper breath till it slows down.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That's just me being unfit. Well, actually, yeah, when it really takes off I do get breathless. Mostly at night. It's mild, though. Not dramatic.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. So the breathlessness comes with the fast heart, and it's worse at night. What are you drinking through the day, coffee, energy drinks?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit of coffee. And yeah, an energy drink if I've got a late shift and then study. Keeps me going. Not heaps.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's four or five long blacks, easy, and those big Monster cans, most days. And the vape's always in your hand.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The vape's barely anything. A disposable lasts me, I dunno, four days?
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nicotine plus that much caffeine can both push the heart along. How are you sitting with the exams, stress-wise?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. People make a big deal out of exams. I'm fine.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You were pacing the kitchen before that client meeting, saying your chest was hammering. You looked wrecked. Sorry, the car's on a short stay, but still.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the extra coffee, not stress. I don't do stress.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines? Anything from the chemist?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. I don't take tablets.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, thinking out loud. Young heart racing at night, worse before exams and meetings, all that coffee and a vape, a lot of this may be stimulant-related. But I can't exclude a rhythm problem, or the thyroid running a bit quick, just on the story.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen. Heart sounds are normal and the rhythm's regular just now, pulse eighty-eight. Chest is clear, no wheeze. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-six.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): See? All good. Probably don't need the fuss.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The exam can be normal between episodes, so it doesn't clear it. I'd like an ECG today, and bloods for thyroid function.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): An ECG? That's for old people, isn't it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): It just records the electrical pattern. If there's an extra beat or a fast circuit, we want to see it. And the thyroid test is one tube of blood, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll do the bloods. I've been on at him for weeks to get this checked.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): When an episode starts, try a slow breathing pattern. In for four, hold for four, out for four, sitting up the way you already do. It won't fix a rhythm problem, but it can take the edge off.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing exercises. Right. If you reckon.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And ease off the energy drinks. Cut the coffee back, and the vape if you can manage it. Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the results.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll book the fortnight and I'll hide the Monsters. He'll complain.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright. Fortnight. No promises on the vape, though.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Even dropping one or two coffees is a start. Any questions before you head out?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, I'm good. Still reckon it's nothing, but whatever.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, thanks, I'll see you then.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They want me signed off fit for the floor. I don't know, doctor, if ye even do those.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We do. Which knee?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The right one. On the inside.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that been at you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My wife filled the bit at the desk and put down three months, but she fusses.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what would you say yourself?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not three months. Two weeks, maybe three, the inside of that right knee. And I'm not limping, whatever she told your one outside.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, or does it lock, or give way?

[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Painkillers?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, the odd time. Two tablets. I don't know, doctor, whether they do a thing.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you take every day?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin, for the cholesterol. Twenty milligrams at night. I think. The box is at home, so I don't know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twenty, you said?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I think it's twenty. Could be wrong. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dose as twenty for now. Nurse put a pressure up... one hundred and seventy-eight over one hundred and two.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah here. Sure that's the white coat. I go sky high the minute I sit in that chair.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a second reading, the screen hopped. Let me read it properly. One hundred and sixty-four over ninety-six.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that still bad?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's up, yeah. Any chest pain, headache, or shortness of breath with it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I'm grand in myself.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only your wife has written breathless on the stairs on the form.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the knee catching, not the breathing. I'm not breathless. I don't know why she wrote that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family with pressure or strokes? I'm only asking while this loads.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a stroke, years back. Smoked the whole time. I'm only mentioning it, it's not why I'm here.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Look, with those numbers I'm going to start ramipril, two point five milligrams at night, and see you in a month.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to? I was put on a pressure tablet before and I coughed the house down. I can't mind the name of it. They stopped it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): An ACE inhibitor, was it? Ramipril, perindopril, one of those?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Years ago. Desperate cough, so that was the end of it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, then I'm changing that. No ramipril. No new tablet today at all.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, I'd rather that.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll lend you a monitor from the surgery. Morning and evening, seven days, sitting quietly, write every reading down.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to buy one? I don't know, doctor, the chemist ones are dear.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, ours. Collect it at the desk on the way out and bring it back with the sheet.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): And will you still sign the work form?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I've had a look there. No swelling on the knee, and it bends fully. I'll sign you for light duties only, no heavy lifting this next fortnight.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Light duties. The supervisor won't be delighted. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the true line. This may well be white coat hypertension, so I'm not calling it high blood pressure for definite until the home numbers are in.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So if they're high, then tablets?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If they're high when you come back, then we talk about a tablet. Not before. Come back in a fortnight with the book.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get a pain in the chest or a bad headache before that?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in sooner, or the emergency department if it's bad. Stay on the atorvastatin as you are. The pressure tablet is parked.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I've put Dr Naidoo's script on the desk. It says amoxicillin five hundred milligrams three times a day, started Monday, for sinusitis.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not what I've got. The bottle says two hundred and fifty milligrams, and I take that three times a day. I checked before we left, so I don't know where five hundred comes from.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box in our cupboard says five hundred, love. I saw it last night. Maybe there are two strengths floating around.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): The dose on the script and the dose you're describing don't match, so I won't guess a number. We'll come back to it. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): This rash. It itches like mad and I can't think. It might be something I ate, or the new cream, or the antibiotic, and I'm really frightened it's going to get worse.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll take those apart. When did the rash and the itch actually start?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, Thursday night, or Friday morning, I honestly can't say which. A few days, that's as close as I can get.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it going to spread to my face? Will it leave scars? Should I have gone to casualty instead?
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Reasonable things to worry about. I don't want to reassure you until I've looked. Where is it sitting worst?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): On my arms and my tummy, and across the chest. Red bumps that itch, some of them joining up. Well, actually a few on my neck as well. Not on the face.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the lips or tongue? Any chest tightness or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, and my breathing is normal. I'm sure about that part.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever, or feeling properly drained?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt hot yesterday afternoon, but I didn't check it, and I don't feel hot today. I am tired, and I'm sleeping badly from the itch. Is the tiredness a bad sign?
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Obs before she came in: temperature thirty six point eight, pulse eighty two, blood pressure one thirty two over eighty four, sats ninety eight percent.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok, I won't argue with the cuff. Can those numbers still be normal if this is an allergy? That's what I'm scared of.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): They can. Normal blood pressure and oxygen just mean you're stable in the chair. They don't name the rash. Talk me through the antibiotic, the cream, and what you ate.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Monday the GP started amoxicillin tablets for sinusitis, three times a day, whatever the strength is. Tuesday I opened a new Epimax cream from the chemist, twice a day on my arms and legs, for dry skin. Wednesday there were prawns at my brother's braai. All three happened, and I can't tell you which one did this.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is the same thing she had with penicillin as a child. Her mother told me she came out in blotches and they called it an allergy. Nobody seems to have written it down.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not true. I am not allergic to penicillin. I took it years ago and I was fine. She's mixing me up with my brother, so please don't record an allergy I don't have.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to collapse those two accounts into one. I'll record that your husband remembers a childhood penicillin rash and that you deny it. It matters, because amoxicillin is a penicillin. Thinking it through, this could be the drug, the cream, or the prawns, and I can't separate them yet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the antibiotic then? Do I stop it today? What happens to the sinus if I stop? And do I throw the cream out?
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not choosing one. A drug eruption, contact dermatitis from the Epimax, and a food reaction are all still open. Nothing is confirmed. Prawns usually give hives that shift around, and a fixed bumpy rash sits a bit less well with that, so food is lower on the list, not off it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mine doesn't move, it just stays and itches. So food is unlikely? Sorry, I know I keep asking.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Less likely, not impossible. Let me look.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): There's a widespread red papular rash on both arms, the abdomen and the upper chest, plus a few lesions on the neck. No swelling of the lips. No wheeze while you talk. The skin over the rash is warm, not clammy.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Warm, so is it infected? Do I need a different antibiotic? That feels mad if an antibiotic started it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Warmth over a rash is not cellulitis. I don't see pus, and there's no spreading hot edge. I wouldn't add another antibiotic today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): How long does a rash like this take to fade if I stop everything? And is Epimax even known for this? The pharmacist said it was gentle, so I thought it was safe.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Epimax is bland for most people, which is why it's used on dry skin, but a new product can still irritate or occasionally sensitise. A drug rash often appears a few days after the first tablet, so Monday to Thursday fits, and Tuesday for the cream fits as well. The timing doesn't pick a winner. That's where I am.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what is the actual plan? I can't leave with three maybes and no instruction.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop the amoxicillin from today, and stop the Epimax as well, until this is clearer. If the sinus aches, paracetamol is fine, not a new antibiotic. For the itch I'll prescribe cetirizine ten milligrams by mouth, once a day, at night.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams at night. Will it knock me out? Can I drive to work in the morning? What if the itch doesn't budge?
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): It makes some people drowsy, so take it at night and see how you feel before you drive. A cool cloth will do more than scratching. If it barely helps we can talk again, but start with that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): And the prawns, do I avoid all seafood for life? There's another braai this weekend and my brother will dish up.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Avoid prawns and other shellfish for now, not forever. Ordinary food is fine. We'll revisit it when I see you again.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can you test her for penicillin today, so this argument is over?
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not today. We might arrange patch testing if the rash has not settled in two weeks. I'm not booking it now. Bloods or a scan wouldn't answer this, so those aren't on the cards.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Does patch testing hurt? Is it on the back? If I skip it, could we miss something dangerous?
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Small discs taped to the back, left on for a couple of days, more itchy than painful. We only consider it if you're not better. The danger signs are lip or tongue swelling, wheezing, or blisters with you feeling very unwell. If any of those happen, go to casualty and don't wait for the appointment.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Swelling, wheeze, blisters, casualty. I'm putting that in my phone. Do I come back even if it fades?
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Let's see you in two weeks either way. If it hasn't settled by then, that's when we might do the patch test. Reception will book the visit.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): What if the sinus blows up before two weeks? And can I work? I just sit at a desk.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Work is fine. If the sinus pain or a fever comes back hard, or the rash spreads quickly, phone sooner. Otherwise two weeks stands. I'm not putting a firm diagnosis on this today.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll watch her at home. The dog will be glad we're back, she's been whining at the gate. We must fetch the cetirizine from the chemist, hey?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Sorry for all the questions. Rashes make me panicky.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ask as many as you need. Stop the amoxicillin and the cream, start the cetirizine tonight, and I'll see you in two weeks.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a fair summary. I simply had not counted the earlier nights.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Burning after meals, a heartburn pill that helps a little, this may be gastritis or acid reflux. I was going to suggest an over-the-counter antacid and skip blood tests. Before I settle on that, do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Socially covers a wide range. What does a usual evening look like?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I did not mean to be evasive a moment ago.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Yeah. It's the bottle with dinner, not a splash in a glass. He corks it and it's gone.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying it straight. I'm not going to lecture you. A bottle most nights does change the plan I just sketched, because wine can inflame the stomach and it can stress the liver.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Please tell me what you would advise.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you first. Your abdomen is soft. There is mild tenderness in the upper middle, the epigastrium. No guarding and no rebound, and I can hear bowel sounds.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that spot is tender under your hand.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He flinched. I saw it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I had also been considering an ultrasound this afternoon. Soft belly, no fever, I'm setting that aside. My impression is gastritis or acid reflux, possibly stirred up by the wine. Not confirmed, just the best fit so far.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound did sound rather involved for a stomach ache.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Instead I'll order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel with the enzymes and bilirubin, because of the wine and this upper abdominal pain. For the pain I was going to start omeprazole at forty milligrams. Thinking it through, twenty milligrams is the better starting dose.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be by mouth? And shall I keep taking the purple pill beside it?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): By mouth, twenty milligrams every morning before breakfast, for the stomach pain. Leave the purple pill off while you are on the omeprazole, so we are not stacking two acid medicines.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well. I will set the purple one aside.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can bring the wine down from a bottle toward a glass, or skip some nights, that will help both the stomach and the liver. No scolding in that, just how the organs work.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try. The evenings are quiet, and the wine has become a habit I am not proud of. There is a biography on the nightstand I keep meaning to finish instead.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I can put the bottle in the cupboard instead of on the counter. That helps a little, sometimes.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over those blood results and see if the omeprazole is doing its job. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or your skin turns yellow, do not wait for that appointment. Go to the emergency room.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have explained it clearly, and I am grateful.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't had high fever or blisters, no.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): That's normal as far as I know.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your heart given you any trouble?

[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no conditions.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My son has asthma.

[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, you know, nothing at the moment.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can I check a few measurements before we carry on?

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I think I understand everything. Thanks.

[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): Blood pressure 152 over 88, pulse 74, temperature 36.6, oxygen 97 percent, weight 71 kilos.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello Mr Winters. It's the itching, isn't it? Tell me about it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): All over. Mostly my back, my legs, my arms. Worse at night. I scratch until I bleed.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Two months. Since my kidneys got worse, I think.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there a rash?

[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any jaundice, or dark urine?

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Remind me of your history.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke or drink?

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Codeine. Makes me vomit.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Let me look at your skin. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's dry, scaly skin, and scratch marks on his back and arms, but no rash, and no signs of infection.
[SEG0021] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, his last bloods came back this morning. Creatinine's up a bit, and phosphate is high. ~

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. First, moisturise twice a day with a plain thick cream, keep your showers short and lukewarm, and avoid scented soaps.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd also like to start you on a tablet to lower your phosphate, calcium acetate, 500 mg, three times a day, with meals.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Will that help the itch? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Often, yes, because a high phosphate drives it. ~
[SEG0029] person_3 (NURSE): I'll go through the diet sheet with you, Mr Winters. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Alan. I'd also like to arrange more blood tests, for your parathyroid hormone, calcium and liver tests, and a review with the kidney team.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your nails short, and wear cotton at night.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in four weeks.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Thank you. ~

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Maybe ten minutes. I count the seconds, which probably makes it worse.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very understandable. And what about being hot all the time, which you described before? How's that?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Gone, honestly. It settled after the second week. I stopped sleeping with the window wide open.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a useful sign. Any chest pain when your heart races?

[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes are fine, thank goodness.

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): And besides the thyroid, any other medical problems I should know about?

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see a fine tremor in both hands. Eyes open now.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please never apologize for those. They're exactly what I want to hear.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I feel a bit calmer now.

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Around about four days... no wait, it's more like two days.

[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a mild temperature?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have. As for mild temperature, mostly mild. I'd say a few times a day.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about difficulty getting out of bed, have you noticed that?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had stiff aching shoulders and hips before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about visual changes, weight loss, jaw pain on chewing or headache?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I'd have said so.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything unusual with passing urine?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all fine.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sure.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, for about a year.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so low haemoglobin and high blood pressure are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, I don't think I have any, no.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes iron tablets, once a day for my blood count.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I was on telmisartan before. I stopped taking it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, have you had any surgical procedures?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had a varicose vein procedure, last year.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now some background about your lifestyle.

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...

[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll interpret them after the examination.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, I'd like to check you over now, if that's alright.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathe out slowly.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): The shoulders are painful to move but strength is normal and there is no joint swelling.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me. So where does that leave us? My working impression is polymyalgia rheumatica. [SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I carry on if I feel better?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Report any headache or jaw pain immediately. Don't skip meals, and try to eat smaller portions more often through the day. Please don't wait if you get a new headache or visual changes. That's when to be seen urgently.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, I follow.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book a review in two weeks.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, that's fine with me.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

Transcript (encounter 00737)
[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello, can I just check, is it Mrs Pickering, Joan Pickering? ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): It is, dear, Joan, born in the very same village as the doctor's mother, I'd wager. This is my Helen. ~
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hi. Mum's been dizzy since they changed her blood pressure tablets, that's why we're here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dizzy how, Joan?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): When I stand up, the room goes round and I have to hold the sideboard. It's been going on a while, a fortnight, perhaps longer, I couldn't tell you.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was before Easter, wasn't it? Or after. I can't be sure either, honestly.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine. What does the dizziness feel like?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Light-headed, as if I might faint. I haven't, but it's close.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything with your vision?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): It goes blurry for a few seconds when I get up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any falls?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Not yet, touch wood.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain in the chest.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Palpitations?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my heart's quiet as a mouse.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No headaches, no.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which tablets has she got now, Helen?
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril, 10 mg, once a day. Amlodipine, 10 mg, once a day, that's the new one. And indapamide, 1.5 mg, in the morning.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Any allergies, Joan?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Codeine, when I was a girl. It made me terribly sick. I've avoided it ever since.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Other health problems?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, and arthritis in my hands.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Surgery?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): A hysterectomy, in 1985.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family illnesses?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who's at home?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with Helen and her husband now, since the stairs got too much.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And before you retired?
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was a seamstress for forty years.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your pressure lying down first. Blood pressure lying is 148 over 84.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now stand up for me, slowly. Take your time. Standing, it's 108 over 64, and your pulse is 78.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I do feel odd. ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit down, Joan. That's quite a drop. Temperature is 36.5, oxygen 97 percent, and your weight is 62 kilos.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is that bad? ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): It explains the dizziness. Let me listen to you.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, and the lungs are clear.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's no swelling in the ankles, and the mouth looks a little dry.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't drink as much as I should. ~
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your breathing, Joan?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, I'm fine for breath.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blood pressure is dropping too low when you stand, which looks like the new tablet, but I can't rule out you being dried out as well.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What happens now? ~
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange an ECG, a blood test for kidney function and salts, and a urine test.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): All today? ~
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'd also like to fit a 24-hour blood pressure monitor.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring her back for it. ~
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Drink plenty, stand up slowly. I'll decide about the tablets once I've seen the results, so please change nothing for now.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Understood. ~
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, dear. Lovely to meet you. ~

[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr Krishnan. Headache, is it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. I have been having headaches since many years, but for the past two weeks... well, actually, it is three weeks now. The pattern itself has changed.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): How?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): They are worse in the morning time, a pressure sort of pain. And I have vomited on two mornings.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): The old headaches were migraine?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Those were on one side, and light used to bother me. These feel different.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blurring of vision? Any weakness in the hands or legs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. Vision is clear, and there is no weakness. Yesterday morning I felt a little giddy, only for a few minutes, then it passed.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Medicines?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I take Suminat 50 milligrams when a bad headache starts, almost four times in a week nowadays. For a milder one I take Crocin, two tablets.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still on the preventive? Inderal?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I stopped the Inderal in March. It was 40 milligrams once a day, but I was feeling very dull, so I left it.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the naproxen from the old note?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I never took that, doctor. I did not even buy it.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergy?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): None, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Drink?

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. Follow my finger. Pupils are equal and reacting. No neck stiffness.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Squeeze my fingers. Power is normal in both arms and both legs. Plantars are down-going.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a relief. My wife remains anxious about the snoring, but I do feel she is overstating it. I have a review meeting at the office after this, so I hope we can finish in good time.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Examination is normal. This may be a change in your migraine. I cannot rule out a pressure problem inside the head.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. Kindly advise me what is to be done.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the morning headaches and vomiting have not settled in two weeks, I will arrange a CT scan of the head.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): May I continue the same tablets until then?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Keep Suminat 50 for the severe attacks, not more than two days in a week. Crocin for the mild ones, maximum four tablets in a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): And the Inderal, should I restart it?

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ag, sorry, this computer is crawling. Give me a moment... okay. What can I do for you today?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): A cough. How long are we talking?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It started after the flu. That was six weeks ago. The flu itself went, but the cough stayed, the whole six weeks.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's at it all night. I sleep down the passage and it still wakes me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, it's worse at night. I lie down, this dry tickle starts, and then I can't sleep. Is that a bad sign? Should I have come sooner?
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say the night bit again. I clicked the wrong window.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Night-time, when I lie down. In the day I cope, it's just annoying. At night it's hectic.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm with it, or any blood?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly dry. In the morning there's a little bit of clear stuff, not green. No blood. I check every time, I'm frightened of seeing blood.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And fever, right now?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not now. I was hot and shivery with the flu, but that finished. Nothing like that anymore.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Or short of breath?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. And I'm not short of breath, not even on the stairs at work. It's only the cough. Why the heart questions? Is it my heart?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just covering the list. Have you lost weight?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't lost weight. My appetite is fine, I'm eating the same.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thembi, your work trousers are hanging. You showed me the belt this morning.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually... ja. The clothes are loose. I took the belt in. I just didn't think of it as weight loss when you asked. Yoh. Is this cancer? People say cough plus weight is cancer.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, don't rush me into a name. This screen has frozen again. One moment.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Please don't go quiet on me. Is it cancer or not? I need you to say.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been like this all week, same questions, and Google at two in the morning. We even argued in the bakkie coming up the hill.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): I missed half of that, the fan on this machine is loud. The clothes, say it once more?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I said no, and then it clicked. The trousers are loose, two holes on the belt. So something has come off. I can't tell you how many kilos.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any travel lately? Out of the province, or overseas?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No travel. Work and home, that's my life. I haven't been near an airport in years.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone around you sick with TB? Fair question with a cough this long.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't know a single person with TB.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What about cousin Naledi in Pietermaritzburg? Auntie said they started her on TB treatment. You drove through and took her food.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): That was not TB. Auntie always makes it bigger. It was an ordinary chest infection, and I stood at the gate, I never went inside. So, no contact. I'm sure of that.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm only repeating Auntie. She was quite definite about the TB tablets. I don't want to fight, but that's what she said.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't decide that from here. We'll park it. Medicines... the file says amlodipine, ten milligrams, every morning, for your blood pressure.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? No, doctor. It's five milligrams. The sister at the clinic cut it down. Five, every morning.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box I fetched from the chemist says amlodipine ten. I can still picture the label.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): That box is the old one. Please don't write ten. I take five milligrams, one tablet in the morning, and I don't skip days.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So my screen says ten and you say five. I'm not guessing. I'll leave the dose off until we see the bottle. You are still taking it, though?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, every day, for the blood pressure. It's been years. Could the cough be from the amlodipine? I read that some tablets make you cough.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Some pressure tablets do that. Amlodipine usually doesn't. I'm not pinning this cough on the tablet, and I'm not pinning it on anything else yet.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what are you thinking? The flu that never left, TB, a tumour? Just tell me which one, even if you're not sure.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I won't do is pick one today. Post-viral cough, reflux, a lingering infection, TB, a mass, that whole list floats past. I am not writing any of them down as what I think this is. There isn't enough in front of me.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She also wants to know about work. She does the admin at the primary school, and she's worried about the children.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the school, say that again? I was reading an old note.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I do admin at the primary school, and I've been going in. Must I stop? If this is TB I shouldn't be near the kids, né?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not quarantining you on a guess. Come, let me listen. Deep breath in... and out. Once more.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breath sounds are clear. I don't hear crackles, and I don't hear a wheeze.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Clear is good, isn't it? Then why is the cough still here after six weeks? Clear doesn't mean it's nothing. Does it?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Clear only means I can't hear a pneumonia sitting here. I want a chest X-ray, and I'll book it at radiology.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): An X-ray. Is the radiation a lot? Will the medical aid pay, or is it cash? And how long before you actually see the result?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's an ordinary chest film, not a big dose. Medical aid usually covers it when the indication is this cough. The report often comes back in a day or two, longer if radiology is stacked.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): If it's bad, will you phone, or must I just wait and stew? I can't do two weeks of not knowing.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the film together. If you start coughing blood, or you get short of breath, don't wait for me, go to casualty.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay. What must I bring? And which amlodipine dose are you going to put on the file?
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bottle from home so we can see whether it's five or ten. I'm not changing the tablet today. Keep taking whatever you've actually been taking.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll look tonight. There might be two boxes in the cupboard, eish. We'll bring both.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Last thing, sorry. For the night cough, can I prop myself on an extra pillow? And is a mixture from the chemist safe, or will it clash with my tablet? I don't want to make this worse.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.

- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.

Transcript (encounter 00784)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi. Um, it's the anxiety. It's been bad again. I can't switch my head off at night.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what happens at night.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I get into bed and my mind races. Work, money, everything. I lie there for two hours, then wake at four, and I'm back on the treadmill.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like this?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About six weeks. Since I changed jobs.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any physical symptoms with it?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My heart pounds, my chest feels tight, and I get sweaty hands. And I'm not eating much.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any panic attacks, or thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of panic attacks, on the train. But no, no thoughts of harming myself.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Sertraline, 50 mg once a day. I've been on it three months.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it helping? ~
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, in the daytime. Not at night. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I had depression, years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Wisdom teeth out, three years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have a drink to calm you down? ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): A glass of wine, a couple of nights a week. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 88, blood pressure 124 over 78, temperature 36.6.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it high? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Slightly fast, but normal. Any breathlessness, or chest pain that worries you?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): No, just tightness when I'm anxious. Nothing otherwise.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I'd say this is a flare of your anxiety, on top of a big life change, with sleep suffering.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it go? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It usually settles with the right help. I'd like to arrange a blood test, to rule out something physical like your thyroid, and check your vitamin levels.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like you to try a sleep routine, no screens an hour before bed, a notepad by your bed to write the worries down, and keep caffeine before noon.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): The notepad's a good idea. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm also going to refer you for talking therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, which is very effective.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): How long's the wait? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few weeks. In the meantime, there are breathing exercises on the practice website.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll look them up. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks, to see how you're sleeping.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~
