[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Observations first, then the doctor will see you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, lovely. We were stuck forever at the robot by the garage. Load shedding, lights dead, everyone hooting.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He coughed from the house to here. I'm his wife. I booked this.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Arm straight, please. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse eighty-eight, oxygen ninety-seven percent, and temperature thirty-six point eight.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): That pressure ok? I've been on the tablet for ages. My girl keeps telling me to walk, but she's at varsity doing teaching, she forgets what depot shifts are like.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor can go through that with you. Head on in.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sit. What can I do for you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cough. Started after the flu, and it's six weeks now. I counted it from the long weekend.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Worse at a particular time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Night time, ja. Soon as I lie down it gets hectic. Daytime at the depot I cope, I just step out the office.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He wakes me every night. I thought it would fade after the flu. It hasn't.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Phlegm?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It's a dry cough.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not now. When the flu hit I was burning up and my whole body was sore, but that settled after a few days. The cough is the bit that stayed.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Short of breath on walking?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I get to the spaza without stopping. Mind you, the bread price there is a joke now.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the cough?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Weight loss?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I haven't lost any weight.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His work trousers are hanging off him. I had to put a tuck in last week.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, ja, they are loose. I have come down a bit. I only noticed when she said.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Recent travel, or contact with TB?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't been anywhere, and I don't know anyone with TB.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not quite true. We went to his cousin in KZN in March. The clinic was treating him for TB. He was coughing right there in the lounge.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, it was a quick stop, I dropped a cake for the old lady and we left. I don't believe it was TB. Nobody told me that.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit eight years ago. Was a pack a day on the long-haul run, Durban to Jo'burg, and I stopped when our girl was born. Best decision, besides the wedding, on a good day.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): On a good day, he says. Don't start.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm joking, doc. She's a saint. Mostly.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tablets?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine five milligrams, one in the morning, for my blood pressure. Been years.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every single day, no misses?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any antibiotic for this?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Clinic gave me amoxicillin at the start of the flu. Five hundred milligrams three times a day for five days. Finished the whole box. Cough didn't care.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Previous chest X-ray?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, about four years back, day hospital. They said it was borderline. Didn't give me a figure, just borderline, and I never followed up. I had to renew the truck licence, the queue was mad that week.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Borderline in what way?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I honestly don't know. That's all they said. Borderline. Then they sent me home.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me listen.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear. No crackles and no wheeze. Your throat looks fine.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it my heart? The neighbour's cough was his heart, he landed in hospital. He still hasn't paid me for that bakkie tyre, but anyway.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting a name on this. No guessing today.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. What then?
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I want a chest X-ray. I'll order it for today.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And we come back when?
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week and we'll go through the film.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still work the depot shifts?
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, carry on working. If you get short of breath, a fever, or you cough up blood, come straight in. Don't wait out the week.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): More antibiotics in the meantime?
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Keep taking the amlodipine as it is. I'm not starting anything new today.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): If the form is done I can book that chest X-ray at radiology before you go.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): It'll be ready at the desk. One week here for the result.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): One week. Ja. We'll try be on time if the robots are actually working.
[SEG0059] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he comes. And I'll bring the old clinic card if I can find it in the drawer. It's a mess in there since the move.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, if we find that old clinic card we'll bring it. The hall cupboard is still packed from the move two years ago, shame.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): The card would help if you find it, but don't delay the X-ray for it.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks, hey. We'll see you in a week.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Marcus, quick stuff before Dr. Shah comes in. Pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-four, heart rate seventy-six, and the fingerstick just now was two fourteen. You'd already had coffee, so that isn't a fasting one.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen? No, I draw up twenty-four. Every night, twenty-four units. Unless the pen clicks different than the vial did, I switched a while back and nobody—
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey Marcus, I'm Dr. Shah. I caught the tail end of that. What's been worrying you most?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The sugar, honestly. And my feet. And I keep reading I'm going to go blind, is that, I mean, am I already—
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll talk about your eyes and your feet, I promise. Tell me how the diabetes has actually been day to day.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Messy. I drive a delivery route, like ten hours, and on work days I skip the shot because if I take it I get shaky before I can eat. Nights too, sometimes I skip, no, wait, nights I take it. I'm getting this wrong.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's untangle it. When you do take the Lantus, what time, and how many units do you dial?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Bedtime. Twenty-four units, I stop the dial at twenty-four. What I skip is the night before a work day, so I won't get shaky on the route. Other nights I take it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): I need to flag this. His order and the med list both still say eighteen units of insulin glargine nightly. There's no twenty-four anywhere in the chart.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the label at home is wrong, or the chart is. Should I bring the box? And can the wrong dose mess up my kidneys, because that's the part that scares me?
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bring the box, yes. I'm not going to say your kidneys are damaged off a mismatch like this. High sugars could be the skipped shots, or the dose not matching the order, or meals in the truck, and I won't pick a cause today.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): So not kidney failure? My uncle ended up really sick and I keep thinking that's next, and if you were going to change something I want to know before—
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not kidney failure, not from today. What I was going to do is raise the Lantus by four units and see you back in a month.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Raise it? On twenty-four or on eighteen? That doesn't even—
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're right to stop me. I'm walking that back. No dose change today. Adding insulin when we can't agree on eighteen versus twenty-four is how people get hurt.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. So then what? Do I just keep guessing which number to dial?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't change the number on your pen until we see the box. No increase. First step is bloodwork, a hemoglobin A1c and a basic metabolic panel, and then we decide the dose.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): A1c is the three-month one, right? Last time they told me seven-something, or maybe it was eight, and I didn't write it down. Was that last winter, or the winter before? I can't tell you.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, the three-month average. We'll get a fresh one and not lean on a result you can't place. How's the metformin going?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That one I don't skip. One thousand milligrams by mouth, morning and again with supper. Only the insulin is the problem.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other prescriptions besides those two?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, in the morning, for my blood pressure. Been on it for years. I was taking fish oil too, but I stopped that months ago because of the burps.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad you mentioned stopping the fish oil. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I always get scared I'll react to something new, but I've never actually had an allergy.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Tell me about your feet. Any open sores, redness, anything that isn't healing?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No sores. I look, most nights. The toes tingle, pins and needles, worse right after the boots come off. Walking doesn't hurt my calves.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did that tingling start?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. Maybe when the heater broke, which isn't a real answer. It wasn't like this when I was younger.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Does the tingling mean I'm going to lose a toe? My uncle had type two, like me, and they took his toe. I check for black spots that aren't there.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tingling is a reason to protect the feet, not a toe already lost. And you haven't actually seen black spots?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No black spots. I just picture them. Sorry, I ask a lot of questions when I get scared.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ask all of them. Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was a kid. Nothing after that. And I never smoked, not once, if you're about to ask.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I was, thank you. What about alcohol, and who's at home with you?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer on Sunday, sometimes two, not every Sunday. I live by myself, so that's the whole story.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): How about the eyes? Any blur, floaters, or a curtain coming across the vision?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings are fuzzy until I've been up a while. No floaters, and no curtain. Rubbing them doesn't fix it. Is fuzzy the same thing as retinopathy, because I googled it and—

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So you'll still send me somewhere? I can't do dilating drops on a delivery day, I wouldn't be safe to drive. Can it be a Monday? How soon is soon?

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your feet while you're here.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Skin is intact, no ulcers on the soles or between the toes. Pulses at both ankles are easy to feel. The monofilament feels dulled on both big toes, and it's normal on the balls of the feet.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Dulled, like the nerve is already dead? If I stop skipping shots does it come back? And these shoes I bought online pinch across the toes, do I throw them out?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't promise the feeling comes back, and I didn't say the nerve is dead. Throw out the pinching shoes. Check both feet every day, moisturize, and don't walk barefoot, even at home.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the shaky thing, though? When I do take the shot and then can't eat, I get shaky and sweaty, like on the highway. Is that a low? That's the whole reason I skip.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shaky and sweaty before you can eat can be a low, yes. I still don't want the whole dose skipped. Carry crackers in the truck, pull over, and check if you feel that way. The unit number stays put until the pen and the chart match.

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can come back to the back. Chest and breathing first?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing is fine. The back is both sides, end of the day, from sitting, not a sharp thing.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Now you've got me thinking the ache is my kidneys. You mentioned kidneys and I can't let it go. Is it?

[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Even in the depot parking lot? And if I toss the pinchy shoes, tomorrow I only have the work boots. What if they rub?

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. Sorry the waiting room was so full this morning.

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When is it at its worst?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or sweats in the night?

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed?

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any travel abroad recently, or contact with anyone who has tuberculosis?

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I take one small glass of wine with dinner on a Saturday, and that is all.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you working at the moment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I am retired. I left the Department five years ago.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Medicines, then. What do you take regularly?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, by mouth, one tablet every morning, for my blood pressure. I have been on it for years.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else in the last while, even a short course?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): During the flu the out-of-hours doctor prescribed amoxicillin. He first said two hundred and fifty milligrams, then he corrected himself to five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days. I finished every dose. I am not taking it now.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough mixture or inhaler?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No inhaler. At night I take one spoonful, by mouth, of a brown cough bottle from the chemist. I am sorry, I cannot recall the name of it. It scarcely helps.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife takes metformin for her diabetes. I believe it is five hundred milligrams, but it is hers alone, and I have never taken it. My sister often urges me to try biotin, as she does, and I have not taken that either.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any drug?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): None. I have never had an allergic reaction.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any history of asthma, or anything else ongoing besides the blood pressure?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No asthma. The blood pressure is the only thing that continues. I should mention that about two years ago the hospital did a chest x-ray, and they said it was borderline, something to do with the size of the heart. Nobody followed it up with me.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. That is correct.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach, waterworks, the rest of you, any trouble there?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Those systems are entirely in order.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Before I examine you, you look as if the morning has already been long.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Indeed. I left the house in plenty of time, and still the traffic on the N11 was at a standstill. I was twenty minutes just getting past the Bray turn.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Kilkenny will do that to a house. Was the lunch at yours?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): At my daughter's, in Rathmines. She made a roast, and the small fellow ate nothing but the potatoes. We stayed on for the crossword, which he is already better at than I am.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): They always are. I still buy the paper on a Saturday out of habit, and the sports pages are the only bit I finish.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the same. I will not pretend I understand the cricket they put on the back page in summer, but I read it all the same. It is a harmless way to spend the evening.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Harmless indeed. Right. Shall we come back to yourself?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. Doctor, I ought to correct something I said: I told you I had not lost weight, but fastening my coat just now I saw I have taken the belt in a notch and the trousers are loose. I have lost some weight, and I could not tell you when that began.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting that right. We will keep it in mind, though we cannot date it. Is there anything else?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): One thing, if I may. I still do not believe I have had contact with tuberculosis, for I have not seen my cousin Declan since Christmas. [SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I follow you. We will not call that contact, and we will not put the name tuberculosis on it either, because nobody in this room actually knows. Let me examine you.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your blood pressure today is one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four. Your pulse is seventy-six, and it is regular.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): The temperature is thirty-six point eight degrees. Your oxygen level is ninety-seven percent, and your breathing rate is sixteen.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I think that is better than the chemist. They had me at around one hundred and fifty over ninety-five a month ago, though I did not write it down.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will use today's figures. The chest is clear. I do not hear crackles, and I do not hear a wheeze.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): The throat is a little red. There are no swollen glands in the neck. The heart sounds are normal, and there is no murmur.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): I am glad the chest is clear. Does the redness matter at all?
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): A little redness can linger after a viral illness. I am thinking this through out loud with you. A cough that goes on for six weeks can have a few explanations, and I am not going to put a name on the cause today. Naming one now would only be guessing.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): I quite understand. I would sooner you were sure.
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I will do is order a chest x-ray. It is to have a proper look, not because I have decided there is anything in particular on it.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that be soon, Doctor?
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will ask reception to arrange it this week. If the film shows something that needs a sample, I might send sputum then. I am not ordering the sputum today.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): And as regards medicine? I did finish the antibiotic.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not prescribing another antibiotic. It would not settle a cough of this sort at this stage, and I want the picture first. You may keep taking the spoonful of that cough bottle at night, though we do not know its name, and please do not start your wife's metformin or your sister's biotin.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I should never do that. What ought I to watch for?
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you cough up blood, or the shortness of breath gets worse, or a fever returns, do not wait. Come back here, or go to the emergency department, the same day.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do so. And when should I come back to you in the ordinary course?
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we will go through the x-ray together. If the appointment for the film has not come through by Friday, ring the surgery and we will chase it.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, and I am most grateful.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Please come in, sir. I will check the pressure and pulse before the doctor calls you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, sister, thank you. We left quite early actually, but the fast train was held up at Matunga, so I was worrying we would miss the token, and still we are only a little late.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sit straight and give her the arm. You were talking the whole way in the auto also.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Kindly keep the arm loose. Blood pressure is 148 over 92. Pulse is eighty-two. Oxygen saturation is 98 percent. Doctor will see you now.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): 148 over 92, is it. At home the small machine shows something around 130, but my son bought that during lockdown and I don't trust it fully anymore.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I am Dr. Mehta. Do sit, both of you. Tell me, what brings you in today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Just a check-up, doctor, nothing dramatic. My wife has been on at me since Diwali that at sixty-three one should not only wait for a problem to come. I am still working, accounts for a small transport firm in Dadar, so I keep postponing these things.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): A check-up is perfectly reasonable. How have you been feeling in yourself, day to day?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Day to day I am alright. I sleep, I take my meals, morning tea and two biscuits, office by train, home by seven. If she has made poha I eat that, otherwise just the tea. I don't feel sick as such.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, he is leaving out the stairs. At the station he stops halfway now and holds the railing.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): That is only because the staircase is steep, Sheela, and the crowd pushes. It is not a pain. I am not having chest pain.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. When you do stop on those stairs, what exactly do you notice, if you would not call it pain?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): If I have to be very honest, there is a tight feeling. When I climb the stairs, or if I walk fast to catch the train, the chest feels tight, like a band across it. I slow down and it eases. I would still not call that pain.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he goes quiet. He will not admit the same thing at home also.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this tightness been happening?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I was going to say from January, after the cold, but that is wrong. It is more recent, after the summer, so about three months. I kept blaming late dinner and gas, all that, and I carried on.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): And it comes only when you exert yourself? Not when you are sitting quietly?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not when I am sitting, no. Television, the office chair, lying down, nothing happens. Only climbing stairs or walking fast.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does that tight feeling spread anywhere, to the arm, the jaw, the back?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stays across the front of the chest. It does not go anywhere else.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any sweating, giddiness, or a real shortness of breath along with it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Sweating, no. Giddiness, no. I am a little more out of puff from the stairs themselves, but I would not say shortness of breath. If I stand still it settles in about two minutes.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the heart, does it race or thump at those times?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no palpitations. I even counted once on the platform and it was steady.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me about your medicines. What are you taking these days?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): For the pressure I take amlodipine. I had it in my mind as five milligrams, but no, the strip is ten milligrams, one tablet every morning after breakfast. The physician changed it some time back and I keep forgetting the new number.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the aspirin he is supposed to take, he treats it like an optional sweet. Some days yes, some days no.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ecosprin, seventy-five milligrams. The old doctor said take it for the heart. I do take it, but on and off. If the stomach feels heavy I skip, and some mornings I simply forget, so it is not every day.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else that was written for you, even if you are not on it now?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin, twenty milligrams at night, for the cholesterol. I stopped it in March. The calves were aching, so I left it on my own, and I have not restarted. There was also clopidogrel on one slip, but I never bought it and I never took even one tablet of that.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the statin has been off since March, and the clopidogrel was never started. Any allergy to a medicine, or to a food, anything like that?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No allergy, doctor. Nothing I know of. I had penicillin years ago for a tooth, no rash, no problem at all.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): And old illnesses I should know? Sugar, thyroid, any heart trouble in the past?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Sugar is not there, the last test was normal, and thyroid no. No heart attack, no angioplasty, nothing of that sort. Only blood pressure, for eight years, and last year they said the cholesterol was high, which is why the statin was given.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father had a heart attack, around seventy. His mother had pressure right till the end.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, my father died of a heart attack at seventy, and my mother had high BP. I don't smoke, I never have. Alcohol only if there is a wedding, one small peg, not a habit. We live just the two of us now, the children are in Pune and Dubai.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): You are still going in to the office every day?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, six days. The walk to the station is maybe ten minutes if I go slow. I have cut down on fried snacks after she shouted about the cholesterol, but festivals are festivals, I will not pretend I refused every laddoo.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you. I will listen to the heart and the lungs, and look at the ankles. Just breathe normally.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Our neighbour had a bypass last year and he said this listening part is nothing, so I am not worried about it. Only the stethoscope is cold, that is all.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, I do not hear a murmur, and the pulse is regular. The lungs are clear. There is no swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, a tight feeling when you climb or hurry, with blood pressure for years and your father's heart attack, may be angina. I am not certain, it is only a working impression, and the tests have to tell us more.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. I know that word from my father. But it goes away in two minutes, so I kept telling myself it is only gas from late dinner. If you say we should check, we will check.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): We should. I want an ECG, and bloods as well, fasting lipids, blood sugar, kidney tests, and a haemoglobin. Not because I have already decided it is the heart.
[SEG0045] person_1 (NURSE): I can take him for the ECG after this. The lab is doing walk-in samples till one o'clock.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had tea and biscuits this morning. Can fasting still be done today?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Tea with a little milk and two glucose biscuits, around seven. If the fasting is spoiled I can come tomorrow morning without eating. I have done that before for the insurance papers.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lipids and sugar are better fasting. Since you have eaten, we will do the ECG today, and you come tomorrow morning, nothing by mouth except water, for those bloods. The haemoglobin and the kidney tests can go in the same sample.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow morning, empty stomach, only water. I will come by eight, before office. Should I take the morning amlodipine with water, or skip that also?
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Take the amlodipine with a sip of water, as usual. For the Ecosprin, please take seventy-five milligrams every day now, after food, not on and off. If the stomach pain becomes severe, stop it and tell me.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Every day, seventy-five, after food. I will keep the strip on the dining table so I actually see it. And the atorvastatin I should not restart on my own, yes?
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do not restart the statin until we have the lipid result and we talk. If this tightness ever comes while you are resting, or if it lasts more than a few minutes and does not ease when you stop, you go to emergency. Don't wait for my clinic.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will see that he does not run for the train. He will argue, but I will be there.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. For now, avoid hurrying on the stairs, and if the tightness comes, stop and rest. We might arrange a treadmill test later, only if the ECG is abnormal or this tightness is still troubling you. Not today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Treadmill I have seen on the clinic pamphlet. I can manage it if you say so. My knees are alright, only the left one clicks in the cold, nothing major. Sorry, I am talking too much.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): You are telling me what I need. Come back in one week with the reports, both of you if you can. We will sit and go through the ECG and the bloods properly.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): I will book the ECG now, and I will give you the lab slip for tomorrow morning, fasting.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): One week. If the reports come earlier as an SMS, should I still wait the full week?
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep the one-week visit even if the message comes sooner. If you feel worse before that, don't wait for me, go to emergency, as I said.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will come. Thank you, doctor. He needed somebody else to say it, not only me at home.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor, and thank you, sister. I will take the tablet properly, and I will not chase that train. Three months I brushed it aside, that was foolish, I can see it now.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): You came, that is the important part. ECG first, then home, and we meet next week.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): My leg is swollen and painful, and I'm terrified it's a blood clot. I read about it last night and I haven't slept.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can hear how worried you are. Let's go through it carefully. Which leg is it?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The right calf. It's tight and sore when I walk.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you first notice it?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Two days ago? Or three. I'm honestly not sure, I was away for work.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been travelling or sitting for long periods? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): A long drive on Monday, about six hours. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or breathlessness?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. A bit worried, but no breathlessness.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any redness, warmth or a recent injury to the leg?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No injury. It's not red. A bit warm, maybe.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you or anyone in your family had a clot before?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not that I know of.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the blood thinner, rivaroxaban, 20 mg, once a day, with dinner.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Why were you prescribed that?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a clot in my leg three years ago. I was told to take it for a year, and I just carried on.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking it every day, including this week?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I think so. I missed two doses on the trip, maybe three. I'm not certain.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for being honest. That matters. I'd like to look at your leg. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): The right calf is swollen, about two centimetres bigger than the left, and tender along the vein.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it a clot? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): It could be, and it could be a muscle strain. I can't tell which by feel alone.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): What do we do? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to have an ultrasound scan of the leg veins today, and a blood test for clotting.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Today? Okay. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll phone the department now. Please keep taking the rivaroxaban every day.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. I won't miss any. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get chest pain, breathlessness, or cough up blood, call an ambulance.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the system's crawling. Give me a tick. What are we doing today?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When were you last in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The possums wrecked the veggie patch, and the tap's leaking, so between that and— oh, the clinic. A year? Bit over, maybe.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): About a year. Anything specific, or a general going-over?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): General, I suppose. Blood pressure's the thing they always bang on about. I've been good with the tablet.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which tablet? Wrong screen. Say that again?

[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, the little white ones. On and off, when I remember. Grandkids were down from Geelong and the week went sideways.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Geelong was lovely, waterfront, fish and chips, the kids were feral by four.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): The dose, sorry. I lost you, the screen's jumped again.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Hundred milligrams, I think. That's what the box says.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I walk the dog every morning by the river. Kelpie cross, Pip, pulls like a train.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The vet can't fit her in till Thursday. Her nails are a disgrace, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, breathing. Sorry. I'm alright unless I rush, then I'm a bit puffed. I'm sixty-two, I put that down to age.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on a cholesterol tablet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Was. Rosuvastatin. I stopped it in March, the muscle aches were shocking.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength was that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? Or twenty. Don't remember. They also wrote ezetimibe and I never filled the script, never took it.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Most times when I'm rushing. Not when I go slow. That was it.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. Can't stand the smell. The wine is one glass on a Saturday if we go out.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. That's a bit of a shock.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): What if it keeps happening?

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come in, take a seat. The nurse has had a quick word and says you're here about your hair, but I'd rather hear it in your own words.
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. It's thinning.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinning where, would you say? All over, or in one patch?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): The top, mostly. The crown, where my parting is.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how long have you noticed it for?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Six months. About that.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Was there something that made you spot it, or did it just creep up on you?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): My wife pointed it out. Then I saw the photos from my sister's wedding and, well.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Is it more that hairs are falling out, or that they're getting finer so you can see more scalp through them?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Both, a bit. It's coming out in handfuls when I wash it.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Handfuls in the shower. Is that every wash, or just now and then?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Every wash.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Think of your scalp like a lawn. Each hair grows for years, rests, drops out, and a new one starts from the same spot. Something can nudge a lot of them into the resting phase together, and then you lose a clump at once.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): The other pattern is more like a lawn slowly going thin because every blade comes back a little finer each season. That one is down to the follicle itself.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that the one I've got?
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd be guessing if I said, and I'd rather not guess at you. What I can tell you is that there are sensible things we can do whichever it turns out to be.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Before anything else, a blood test makes sense. I'd like to check your iron stores and your thyroid, because both can quietly affect hair and both are easy to put right.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. When would that be?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take it on your way out today. It's about two minutes with a needle, no fasting needed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile I'm going to start you on minoxidil foam. Carrying on with the lawn idea, it's a bit like fertiliser: it wakes the follicles up and lengthens their growing phase.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I put it on wet hair?
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dry scalp is best. Once a day, half a capful, rubbed in wherever it's thin, then wash your hands thoroughly.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Once a day. Right.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Be warned, it can make you shed a bit more for the first month or so. That's the old resting hairs making way, and it's a good sign rather than a bad one.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Hm. So worse first.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): A little worse first, yes. Most people need around four months before they see any difference, so please don't judge it too early.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Four months.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a photo of your crown in the same light today, and then again every month. It's far more reliable than trusting your memory in the bathroom mirror.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I can do that.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): And be kind to what you've got: no harsh brushing or tight hats. Ordinary shampoo is fine, you don't need anything fancy.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Not a problem.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Did you want to ask me anything before you go?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Will the bloods take long to come back?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually a few days. The results will be on your record by then.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind the step on your way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, love, I'll grab your obs before the doctor. Hop on the scales.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): Ninety-seven kilos. Blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse seventy-two. Sitting, and quite steady.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Any medicine allergies I should put on the file?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day. I'm Dr Shah. Good you've got your daughter with you. What's brought you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which knee, and what sets it off? Stairs are often the giveaway with this sort of pain, so I'm listening for that.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Stairs.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the right knee. Going down the stairs sets it off, coming up is fine, and it wakes him at night.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long's it been like that?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Years.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not years, Dad. Since August, after the trip. Eight months.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the timing loose, about eight months to a few years. Better a range than a date we made up.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): How bad is it? And I'm wondering about swelling, and about stiffness in the morning.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling, though?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes. Not really.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll treat both of those as maybes, not facts. Does the knee lock, or give way?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it? Gel, tablets from the chemist?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Gel.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Voltaren gel. He's meant to put it on the knee twice a day, but he skips the morning most days. Nagging hasn't fixed it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Diclofenac gel, twice a day on paper, and I'm not sure it actually happens. Tablets as well, from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which tablets, what strength?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Voltaren. Twenty-five. Think.
[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Those are the fifty milligram Voltaren, Dad. One when the pain's really bad, not every day.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Strength's not agreed, twenty-five or fifty, so I won't write a dose. By mouth, only on the bad days. Any stomach problems with them? Reflux, ulcers?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Before that, were you on a script anti-inflammatory?
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Naproxen. Two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, for the knee, from his old GP.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still taking the naproxen?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped. March.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March. That's discontinued, not something you're on now. Did you ever actually start the glucosamine the chemist suggested?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Never started, so it stays off the list. And you're still on the amlodipine?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Side note while I remember. I take biotin for my hair, that's mine, not his. Mum, his wife, has diabetes and she's on metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day. His amlodipine is five milligrams every morning for the blood pressure, ongoing for years, and he lives with me and Mum, retired last year.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your biotin and your mother's metformin do not go on his chart. Her diabetes I'll record as his wife's history. Hypertension ongoing, amlodipine five milligrams by mouth every morning. Now the knee itself.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right knee. Tender along the medial joint line, crepitus when you bend, flexion a bit short of full, and no effusion that I can feel.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Working impression is osteoarthritis of that knee. Going down stairs is mechanical and it fits. Night waking means I can't fully rule out an inflammatory flare, so that stays a possibility, not a firm label.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weight's ninety-seven kilos, and that's a lot of load through a sore knee. Easing off a few kilos would help the joint. Mechanics, not a lecture.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets heartburn, you know. He said no stomach problems.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Heartburn. After tablets.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so there is heartburn, and it comes after the diclofenac tablets. The earlier no doesn't hold. When did the heartburn start?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): No date, then. Any chest pain with it, pain into the arm, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): No chest pain and no breathlessness, which is reassuring. I'd like you to ease off those Voltaren tablets because of the heartburn, keep the gel if your skin tolerates it, and start paracetamol, two five-hundred milligram tablets, up to four times a day, for the knee.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The other doctor mentioned physio, or a needle into the knee. Which are we doing?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not deciding today, and here's my thinking. We might refer you to physio for the stairs and the muscle support. We might do a steroid injection into the knee if the night pain is the bit you want settled faster. If we went for the injection I'd want a plain x-ray of the knee first, but I won't book the x-ray unless we choose the injection.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks either way and we'll settle physio or the injection. Ask reception to book that on your way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. I'll grab a blood pressure before the doctor sees you. 136 over 84, pulse 58, and the scales have you at 89 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Sit yourselves down. What has you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The tiredness, doctor, though if I start properly I'll wander. I do the accounts at the co-op, the month-end is a killer, I'm 53 in March, and I've been putting the whole lot down to the job and to getting older.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's asleep in the armchair before the nine o'clock news, most nights. I had to drag him in.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I was getting to that. I couldn't tell you when the tiredness began — last winter, or the one before, one or the other. I'm no use after half four, and the backlog at work just sits there.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the fatigue's been there a good while, and you can't pin the start. Are you cold with it as well?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Freezing, even with the heating up and a jumper on in the kitchen. That's been the same stretch of time, whatever length it is, hands worst of all, and the weight —
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry — the jumper is year-round. He had it on in June.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): The weight, yes. You've me at 89. I was twelve stone a few years back, about 76 kilos, so that's the best part of two stone, and I haven't really changed the eating, only more tea and biscuits at the desk because the days run long.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight up, cold, tired. What about the bowels, any change? And has your mood dipped, or is it just the energy?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): The bowels are a misery. Constipated, every three or four days, hard stools, and I'm after trying prunes and then senna from the chemist. The mood I'll come to, because the senna is a small saga in itself —
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much senna, and how long have you been on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Two tablets at night, only the last fortnight, and it's done nothing. I read the packet twice so I wouldn't take the wrong amount, and I still feel blocked.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been very flat as well, and the garden's gone to —
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the mood you asked about. I'm low. No interest in the garden and I used to live out there. I don't think I'm depressed, I just put the flatness down to being wrecked from work.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low, but not depression in your own view. Any thyroid trouble in the family?
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had the underactive thyroid, for years.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Eltroxin, they called the tablets, right up until she died, God rest her. I think her sister might have had something similar but I never got that straight, so I won't swear to it. I had a blood test myself once and they told me it was borderline.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that blood test?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't date it if you paid me. Before the pandemic, or just after, or somewhere in between. They said borderline, I'm nearly sure of the word.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said normal, Seán. It's in the sideboard at home. You've called it borderline for years and it wasn't.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Was it normal? I was certain they said borderline. Sure maybe I have it wrong — I do mix the old results up.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, we won't hang anything on that old result, since you remember borderline and your wife remembers a normal letter, and neither of you can date it. Let me say back what I have. Tired and cold since last winter or the winter before, weight from about 76 kilos up to 89, bowels every three or four days, mood low but not what you'd call depression, mother with an underactive thyroid, senna two at night for a fortnight with no joy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the bones of it. I still think the co-op hours are half the story, mind you, and the age.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): They might well be. On examination your hands are cool, the pulse matches the 58 the nurse got, and I can't feel any enlargement or lump in the thyroid itself.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Is a normal feel a good thing? My mother had a goitre late on — or was that someone else. No, it was her, I'm sure of that much.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): A normal feel doesn't rule an underactive thyroid in or out. This could be hypothyroidism, or it could be the workload and age catching you, and I can't tell those apart from the chair.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you'll do a blood test, will you?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will. I'll order a thyroid function test, and a full blood count as well, with the tiredness gone on this long. Not this minute — the nurse will book the phlebotomy.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning is free, if that suits ye. I can put the form through now.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is the audit, I can't do morning, the regional manager is in and I'll be stuck at the desk till lunch. Afternoon I could manage, if there's a slot, though the car park is desperate after three —
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Afternoon, so. Half two.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Leave the senna off, since two at night for a fortnight hasn't shifted things. Plenty of water, and don't write the whole thing off as age until we have the numbers.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): If it is the thyroid, is it the same tablet my mother was on? I don't fancy being on something for life if I can avoid it, though I know people are, and she managed grand on it for years.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't start any tablet until the result is back, and we'll talk it through then. Come back to me about a week after Thursday, once the results are in.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll root out that old letter so you're not depending on his memory of it.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll take your observations before you go in. Sleeve up there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, grand. Is it much longer? The head is pounding and I've been clock-watching outside.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): He's nearly ready. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, temperature thirty-six point seven, oxygen ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one thirty-eight bad? Could the blood pressure be what's driving the headache?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Only mildly up. The doctor will go through it. In you go.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit down. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The headaches. I've had migraine for years, but it's changed, and I'm really frightened about it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Changed how?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse in the morning. I wake up and it's already pounding, the whole head, and I've been getting sick with it.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A month at least. I'm awake with him from about five.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not a month. It's a fortnight, two weeks. I'm nearly certain.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll call it a few weeks and not fight over the day. Vomiting every morning?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not every morning. Only a few times. I can't tell you when the vomiting started, it crept in, maybe last week, I genuinely don't know.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in an arm or a leg?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. If I did get weakness, what would that mean? Should I be checking?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): It would mean the emergency department. Speech slurred? Seeing double?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Speech is normal and there's no double vision.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stiff neck?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the neck is fine.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He snores the house down as well, and he's tired all day. Asleep on the couch after the tea.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore. She's exaggerating. And I'm not tired. I'm grand once the headache lifts.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do snore, loud, most nights, and you are tired. I've watched it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not having that row in here. Can we stay on the headache? I was googling tumours half the night.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the migraines been there?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Since my twenties. I'm forty-two, so about twenty years. My dad had migraines too, the same sort of thing.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, when one starts. I've been taking it nearly every day lately, which is too much, and that worries me as well.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box at home says a hundred milligrams. He keeps telling people fifty.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought it was fifty. Maybe the chemist changed it. I haven't checked the new box, so I can't swear to the dose.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else for the pain?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, maybe three if it's desperate, most days. Is that dangerous? Could it be causing the morning headache?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Daily paracetamol can keep a headache going. Were you on a preventer?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Propranolol, forty milligrams twice a day. I stopped it in March, it had me wrecked. They offered topiramate after and I never took a single capsule.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): This might sound stupid, but my sister takes biotin every day for her hair. Would it help if I tried some? She also wants me to ask about her mother's tablets.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My mother takes metformin for her diabetes. I only wondered if that kind of thing did anything for headaches.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. The biotin is your sister's and the metformin is her mother's. Neither is yours. Anything else you're on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. So do I stop the paracetamol today? Am I allowed any sumatriptan at all?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut the paracetamol right back, not every day. Keep the sumatriptan for a proper attack, not every morning. I'll have a look at you.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pupils are equal and reacting to light. There's no swelling at the back of the eyes.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the pressure thing, isn't it? So that's clear? Does that mean I'm alright?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): It makes very high pressure less likely. It doesn't close it. Power is normal in both arms and both legs, and the reflexes are present.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coordination is fine, finger to nose is accurate. No neck stiffness. Your gait is steady.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you think it actually is? Don't soften it, please.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a change in the migraine, with medication overuse likely on top. I wouldn't rule out raised pressure, given the morning vomiting.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're scanning me today, then?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled in two weeks, or the vomiting gets worse, we might arrange a brain scan.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Might, so it's not booked. If I wake up worse on Sunday, do I just wait?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): New weakness, confusion, or a sudden terrible headache, you go to emergency, you don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in a fortnight.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I feel a bit better? And would the scan be an MRI or a CT? I'm awful in tight spaces.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): The fortnight visit stands either way. If we do a scan it would be an MRI, and only if things haven't settled. Nothing is booked for imaging today.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the two-week review in the book at the desk. Mornings are easier.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning, please. Is there anything else I should watch for, or am I overthinking it?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting that won't stop, confusion, a thunderclap headache. Don't start the biotin, and leave the metformin alone.
[SEG0054] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And you're not going to touch the snoring at all?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): There is no snoring, and I am not exhausted. I wish you'd drop it.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sleep can wait. Emergency if anything sudden happens. Otherwise two weeks.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sharp, right at the base of the thumb side, worse if I try to turn the hand over.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you move your fingers? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I can wiggle them. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medical conditions I should know about?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Just asthma.

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand. The X-ray will answer the question quickly. I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the wrist, today.

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Radiology is down the corridor. They'll fit you in. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. And in the meantime? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep it elevated on a pillow, and use a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for twenty minutes at a time.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't use the hand to lift anything. A sling would help for a few hours.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll ask the nurse. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): For the pain, you can take paracetamol, nothing more than the label says. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take the X-ray result back to the front desk, and they'll find me. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Will you look at it today? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. If the X-ray shows a fracture, I'll refer you to the fracture clinic right away for a cast.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. And if it doesn't? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we'll treat it as a sprain, with a wrist splint. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): That I can handle. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good luck with the presentation. ~
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks. I'll need it. ~

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's book an echocardiogram to look into exertional syncope.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll do it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's get an ECG, for syncope. No exertion for now, I am arranging urgent specialist tests. A short walk every day, even twenty minutes, will help more than you'd think. [SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, take a seat. What can I do for you?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm, I'm here because of stiff aching shoulders and hips. I'm hoping you can tell me something definite. I'd rather know what's going on than keep guessing.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): what do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): well, I'm on iron tablets, once a day. Naproxen i take it 250 milligrams, twice a day for the knee pain i'd been on diclofenac, not any more though, I stopped
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): when did this begin?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): it's been about four days, I'm fairly sure
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to to mind.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): honestly a couple of times a week. Pretty severe if I'm being honest. It's worse with mornings. A neighbour of mine said I should see someone about it
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other symptoms with it?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): sorry what was I saying it usually comes with difficulty getting out of bed the difficulty getting out of bed? That's been for two months
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): right any a mild temperature as well?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): yes, about the same, three days. About mild temperature, a three out of ten, I suppose. It's all the time
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): have you been feeling tired and low?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Two months, I'd say. With feeling tired and low, moderate, I'd say.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had stiff aching shoulders and hips before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you get headache or weight loss?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): none of those, no
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): have you had any visual changes or jaw pain on chewing?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah no visual changes or jaw pain on chewing none of it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels, any trouble?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): nothing unusual, you know, no
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): are you in work at the moment?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I work in a bakery, early starts.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): is there someone at home?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you do any exercise?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I swim twice a week.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does your family have any medical conditions?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): my mother had a stroke. My uncle has high cholesterol
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): do you have any long-term conditions?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I have low haemoglobin for two years. I'm not great at remembering details so bear with me. Arthritis in my knees for about ten years.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay yes low haemoglobin and arthritis in your knees are known to us good to have that clear. Are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): okay, so I think I reacted to some antibiotic once, years ago i don't remember which one, or what happened exactly
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can I check a few measurements before we carry on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright bear with me while this finishes...
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: SpO2 98 percent on room air heart rate 67 temperature 36.6. And BP is 119 over 81.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): alright over here please and I'll take a look
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): hold that for a second
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): The shoulders are painful to move but strength is normal and and there is no joint swelling.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): okay, thinking it through, my working impression is polymyalgia rheumatica. We shouldn't forget rheumatoid arthritis. Let's get blood tests, for proximal stiffness
[SEG0044] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book that for Thursday at 10 am
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): let's use prednisolone, 15 milligrams, once a day, reducing course you take it by mouth that should help with polymyalgia rheumatica
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): can I collect it from my own pharmacy?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): report any headache or jaw pain immediately see me again in two weeks
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): that's fine with me
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): right, I'll do that thank you, doctor

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, not at all, please sit. What seems to be wrong?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's burning pain in the upper tummy, mostly.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the timeline, when did it begin? Bear with me, I'm just building up the picture.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Probably three weeks. Yeah.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): What aggravates it, if anything?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): I notice it more with an empty stomach.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been feeling full quickly?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I have. As for feeling full quickly, I'd call it moderate.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss, black stools or vomiting blood at all?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No weight loss, black stools or vomiting blood, none of it.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any difficulty swallowing?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any difficulty swallowing.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your heart given you any trouble?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): My heart's been fine, as far as I know.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your skin been okay?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Skin's normal.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about any past illnesses or ongoing conditions.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Arthritis in my knees, for nearly five years. I've had heart disease, yes.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. Alright, arthritis in your knees, that matches what I have here.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you list what you take, tablets, creams or inhalers?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): It's paracetamol, 650 milligrams, when needed. I told myself I'd wait and see, and here I am. I'm on clopidogrel, 75 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few questions about your lifestyle now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I only drink at family occasions. I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day. I do a yoga class on Thursdays.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can I check a few measurements before we carry on?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nearly done with the readings...
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: saturation 99 percent, pulse 64. And blood pressure 127 over 78, temp 36.8 degrees.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, shall I start the examination?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to your chest now.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your upper tummy is tender in the middle with no guarding.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me.

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Months is a big range. Closer to two, or more like half a year?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The weight. I've put weight on, my work pants won't button. And, this is kind of gross, I'm constipated.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not gross at all. About how much weight, and what's the bowel pattern?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe twelve pounds. I didn't exactly weigh myself. I go every three or four days now, hard stools. I used to go every morning.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been safety-pinning the waistband. That's new for her.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your mood been with all this?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I don't cry or anything, I just don't care about stuff I liked. I figured that's the job and getting older, you know?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any hair loss, dry skin, a lump in the neck, or changes with your periods?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Periods stopped a couple years ago, menopause. Skin's dry, yeah. No lump. Hair's thinner, though I color it, so it's tricky to judge.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or feeling like you might pass out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She nods off on the couch after dinner. She never used to.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): That's true. Oh, and my mom had thyroid trouble. Took a pill for it her whole life. They checked mine once and it was borderline, they said.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline. Any sense of when that was, or what the number was?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I want to say two years ago? No number stuck. They said borderline and left it. I never started a thyroid medicine.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Huh. I would've sworn they said borderline. Anyway.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister sent iron tablets in the spring. Bottle's still sealed in the cabinet. She never took a single one.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the iron was never taken.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, never. The senna I did use, one tablet at night for the constipation. I stopped it in March because it was cramping me up.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Senna, one tablet at night, stopped in March. Anything you take now? Any allergies, to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Just a multivitamin, one a day. No allergies that I know of. Oh my gosh, though, the drive over was ridiculous.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): We sat on the bridge forty minutes, and a guy in a pickup had the country station so loud the windows buzzed. Then a huge flock of geese went over, hundreds of them, heading south.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Made me think of my granddaughter's school play last month. She was a tree, construction-paper leaves and everything. I teared up, the happy kind. Sorry, I wander off.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Paper leaves in the cup holder for a week. Weather's been the same way, coat on, coat off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No harm done, geese aside. You've been tired and cold since the fall, up about twelve pounds, with hard stools every three or four days, a flat mood, dry skin, thinner hair, and naps after supper. Your mother had thyroid disease, the twenty twenty-three TSH was normal on the chart, and you never started thyroid medicine or the iron. Senna stopped in March, you take a multivitamin daily, and you have no allergies.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's the picture. I still think it's just the job and my age, though.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Work and age can absolutely wear you down. I'm also thinking this could be an underactive thyroid, and I'd rather check than guess. I want a TSH, a free T4, a blood count, and a basic metabolic panel.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Can they stick me today?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the lab has a slot when we're done, yes, otherwise tomorrow morning. You don't need to fast. Coming before breakfast is fine if it's easy, not a requirement.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I start the senna again, and when am I supposed to come back?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't restart the senna. If the constipation is really bothering you before the labs are back, psyllium once a day is fine to try on your own, and I'm not prescribing it. Ease up at work a little this month if you can, and I'll see you in two weeks for the results either way. Call sooner if you get chest pain, if you start vomiting with the constipation, or if you feel markedly worse.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, got it. I'll try to leave the geese out of it next time.
