[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What has you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this knee, doctor, the right one. Going down the stairs is a holy show, and then of a night it starts up on me again.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the stairs, in your own time.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): There's fourteen steps down to the hall, and the third from the bottom is the killer. I go down sideways, holding the rail like an old crab. Coming up isn't nearly as bad, which is odd.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Five weeks. Well, no, I'm wrong — we had the communion early in the summer and I was grand then, so it's eight weeks. Definitely eight weeks.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what is it like at night?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I get to bed grand enough, and then around two, maybe half two, it aches deep in the joint. The pillow between the knees was a waste of money, it goes flat. I end up sitting on the edge of the bed until it eases.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It puffs up a small bit by the evening, over the kneecap. It doesn't lock, thank God. And it hasn't given way on me. I was worried after Josie next door went down in the supermarket, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heat in the joint, or a fever with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. And it's not hot if I put my hand on it. Just sore, and a bit puffy, as I said.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where exactly do you feel the pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): On the inside of the right knee, and under the kneecap on the way down the steps. If I sit too long at mass it stiffens up, and the first few steps after are desperate.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been doing for it yourself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The gel from the chemist, diclofenac, the one percent. I rub a finger's worth into the right knee twice a day — actually, no, it's three times a day, morning, after the dinner, and before bed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets along with the gel?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol by mouth, two of the five hundred milligram ones, most mornings. And now and again the diclofenac tablets, by mouth as well. I thought they were the twenty-five milligram, but I looked at the box this morning — they're fifty milligram.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often would you take the diclofenac tablet?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every day. Maybe two evenings in the week, if the stairs have been bad. I never swallow two of them together. My sister takes hers every day for her back, but I'm not doing that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble from them at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all. I was careful about that, because my mother had an ulcer from tablets years back, and I didn't want the same.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What else are you taking, prescribed or from the chemist?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, amlodipine, for the high blood pressure I've had for years. It was five milligrams for ages and then they put it up — no, sorry, it's ten milligrams now, by mouth, every morning.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I do miss it the odd morning, if I'm rushing to the half eight mass. Not often. Most days it goes down me.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the plan is every morning, but you're not dead sure it happens every single day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the truth of it, yes.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else sitting in the press?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon. A spoonful by mouth when I need it, usually in the evening.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, is it?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yes. I said no stomach problems and I meant no pain in the stomach itself, but I do get heartburn of an evening, the last few weeks. If I take the diclofenac tablet and lie down on the couch for the news, it burns up behind the breastbone. A spoon of Gaviscon settles it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you put any date on when that heartburn started?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. It crept up on me. Not years, just lately, and I can't pin the day at all.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, black stools, or food sticking on the way down?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): None of that. No vomiting, the bowels are grand, no black stools, and nothing sticking.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No allergies that I know of.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can I ask about your weight? It matters for a knee.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I know, I know. I'm after putting on a bit since I stopped the bowling. Too many biscuits with the tea, if I'm honest, and no one in the house to give out to me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The note from the nurse this morning has you at ninety-one point five kilograms.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Those scales are miles out. I weighed myself at home yesterday, eighty-six — no, eighty-seven kilograms, in my socks, before the breakfast. I'd swear to the eighty-seven.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it's ninety-one point five on our note and eighty-seven on yours, and we won't settle which is right today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Put the eighty-seven down as the true one. I still had the coat on for your one, I'd say. Theirs always reads high. Still and all, eighty-seven is what my own scales said.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep both figures. How are you managing around the house and out of it?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I live on my own since Paddy died, three years now. I was a primary teacher, retired ten years. I walk to mass most mornings, only about ten minutes and flat, though the hill home is another story. I gave up the bowling in the spring.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the knee now, if you're agreeable.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. It's the right one. The left never bothered me.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender along the medial joint line of the right knee. There's a small effusion, nothing dramatic, and crepitus when I bend it. It straightens out fully, and there's no redness.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the exact spot, yes, when you press there. I got the same catch coming off the path outside the credit union last week.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this sounds like osteoarthritis of the right knee, wear and tear. I'm not calling it certain — it's my working impression from the story and from that examination.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had the two knees done, so I was half waiting for it. She was eighty-two for the second one. I'm seventy-four in November, so I've a bit to go yet, please God.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have an operation yourself, on the knee or anywhere else?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataracts, the both eyes — the left one three years ago, and the right the year before that. Nothing ever on the knee. No scope, no surgery there at all.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): For this knee, two roads are worth a chat. Physiotherapy, to build the muscle above the knee, or a steroid injection into the joint. I don't want to decide that for you today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Would the injection be done here in the treatment room? Josie had one and she was flying for months, though she also said the first week was worse, so I don't know which part to believe. And is the physio the place down on the Mall?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either one is reasonable. Physio if you'd rather avoid a needle, the injection if the night pain is what you want eased sooner. We might do one, we might do the other. Nothing is booked.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I think about it, so? I want to ask my daughter. She'll say I'm being dramatic, but she doesn't have my stairs.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): You think on it. Nothing goes ahead until you say the word.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I picked the physio, how many times would I be trailing over there?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Usually a short block of sessions, but we won't book it unless you want it. Same story for the injection — only if you decide you want it.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, keep the gel three times a day, that's fine. Go easy on the diclofenac tablets with that heartburn — take one with food if you take it, and don't lie down straight after.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll do that. I'll leave the Gaviscon by the couch so I don't have to go hunting in the press.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Easing even a small bit of weight off the knee would help, whichever number we believe. No crash diets. A bit more of the flat walking, and on the stairs try leading with the good leg on the way down.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Down with the good leg. I'll try it. I already hold the rail, ever since Mrs Kearney fell, and I'm not proud about it.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks. We'll make the decision then, physio or the injection, once you've had time to think.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Should I be writing down the nights it wakes me?
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you like, a simple note of which nights it wakes you. It's not essential.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): What about an x-ray? They x-ray Josie every time she sneezes, near enough.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might x-ray the knee if it's not settling by then, or if we head towards an injection. I'm not ordering one today.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so. And the amlodipine — I stay on the ten milligrams?
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, stay on the ten milligram amlodipine every morning, and try not to skip it on the mass days. That one is doing a different job to the knee tablets.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): I will. And just so the file is right, the diclofenac tablet is the fifty, not the old twenty-five. I don't want the wrong strength written in.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fifty milligram diclofenac, now and again, with food. The gel as you are already using it. Paracetamol in the mornings is fine alongside the both of them.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Perfect. I'll go out the long way and skip the stairs. You've been very decent about it, doctor.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind yourself on the way out, and I'll see you in six weeks.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, please God. I'll have picked one or the other by then, or I'll have talked myself out of the pair of them, knowing me.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, the tablets are not working. Still the room is spinning every time I turn in bed. I have not slept properly for days.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, let's go through it step by step. When you say spinning, the room moves around you, or you feel unsteady?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The room moves, like a merry-go-round. It only lasts some seconds, maybe a minute, but it is so frightening. I hold the bed with both hands.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds unpleasant. And when did this first begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About five weeks back. First I thought it was because of the heat, or low sugar, so I ate something and lay down, but it came again.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often does it come now?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Every morning, when I turn on my side to get up. Sometimes also at night. Mostly when I turn to the right.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mostly to the right, interesting. Does anything else bring it on, apart from turning in bed?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Looking up at the shelf in the kitchen. Yesterday I looked up for the salt box and I had to catch the counter.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does anything make it settle, besides waiting?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Closing my eyes helps, and keeping still. That is all. Doctor, I saw a video on WhatsApp saying such things are from a brain tumour. Is it so?
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those forwarded videos cause more worry than they ever cure. Nothing you've told me so far points to something dangerous, but let's carry on with my questions.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, okay. Please ask.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting with the spinning?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting, only a little uneasy feeling in the stomach, and that passes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any ringing in your ears?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no ringing. My hearing is the same as always, my husband still says I don't listen, ha ha.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, that's a universal complaint. Now, you came to see the other doctor two weeks ago, and he started something. What are you taking?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Betahistine, 16 mg, three times a day. He said it is for the dizziness.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And you've been taking it properly since then?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, morning, afternoon and night, with food. I have not missed one, I even set an alarm on my phone.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that's useful for me to know. Are you taking anything else, any other tablets or supplements?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, only that one. Should I increase the dose? My neighbour says take double and it will work faster.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't double anything on a neighbour's advice. Stay on the dose you have for now. It can take a few weeks to show its full effect.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): A few weeks? But I am so scared to sleep, doctor. What if I fall and break something?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a very reasonable fear, and I'll give you some practical tips for it in a moment. First, tell me about your health in general. Any long-term conditions?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I get migraines sometimes, not often, maybe four times a year. And neck problem, cervical spondylosis, the X-ray was done long back, but I take no tablets for it.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right, I'll note both of those down. Let me check your numbers now.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 128 over 80, and your pulse is 74 beats per minute.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it okay? The last doctor said my pressure was a little high.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a perfectly good reading today. No need to worry about it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Then why is the spinning happening? Can you tell me what it is?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't want to guess yet. What I'd like is to arrange a hearing and balance test, called audiometry, so we can see how the ears and balance system are working.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it a long test? I have to cook for my family when I reach home.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): About forty minutes. You'll wear headphones and press a button when you hear a beep. The front desk can book you a slot this week.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I will do it. And in the meantime, what should I do about the falling thing?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Three simple things. Sit at the edge of the bed for a minute before you stand. Turn slowly rather than jerking over. And put a night light on the way to the bathroom.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Sit first, turn slowly, night light. I will write it down. My daughter will fix the light today only.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. And when you look up at the high shelf, get someone else to bring things down, so you're not tilting your head back.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I will ask my son to move the salt box lower, ha ha. It is always on the top shelf.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, a simple fix. I'd like to see you again in three weeks, once the test is done, and we can look at everything together.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. And if the spinning gets worse before that?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you notice weakness in an arm or leg, trouble speaking, double vision or a severe headache, go to the emergency department straight away. Otherwise, continue as you are.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I will remember. Thank you, doctor. I was so scared, now I feel little bit calmer.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that's what I wanted. Keep taking the tablets, and the best of luck with the cooking.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. Bye.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): no problem at all, come in what's troubling you?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Okay, you know, so morning, doctor. I'll stay and fill in anything that's missed.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that'll be useful. Pull up a chair.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been dealing with skipped beats.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Since last weekend, that's when it began.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): It's on and off. I notice it more with lying down and caffeine. Maybe a five out of ten on a bad day. I get some relief from deep breaths. Right, I've also had a flutter in my chest, for about three months. Let me think, I had being a bit anxious before. That's settled now, though.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, and what about shortness of breath or chest pain?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, um, none of those at all.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): a few quick ones: fainting or dizziness?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't had fainting or dizziness, no
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, neurologically, anything strange?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): erm, no, that's all normal
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything different when you pass water?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): no, that's all fine
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any long-term conditions?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, I have heart disease, for two years. Yeah, I've had an irregular heartbeat for five years now. My sister suggested writing things down, but I forgot. I have low haemoglobin. Actually, I have an underactive thyroid, for about a year. My family kept telling me to get it checked.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sure. Right, so an underactive thyroid is already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, um, not that that I know of.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): actually, I remember she had some kind of reaction to diclofenac before i couldn't swear to it
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't remember that
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll note both of those. What operations have you had, if any?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had part of my thyroid removed, years back.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you list what you take, tablets, creams or inhalers?
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): let me think, she is on clopidogrel, once a day, I give it to her
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): so, how much do you take?
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): it's 75 milligrams
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): roughly how long on that one?
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): for nearly five years hmm, um, she is on apixaban, 5 milligrams, twice a day for the heart rhythm, I give it it to her well, um, it's iron tablets, once a day, doctor it's Eltroxin, 100 micrograms, every morning for my thyroid, doctor
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Before this I was on aspirin; that's been stopped.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about smoking?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I have about eight cigarettes in a day.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, are you active?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I walk the dog every morning
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): who lives with you?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): My partner and our baby.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): alright, tell me about your eating
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): any inherited conditions that you know of in the family?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): My uncle has high cholesterol. Let me think, you know, my cousin has psoriasis.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Time for your numbers, if that's okay.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, keep your arm relaxed for me...
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature is 36.9 degrees, BP is 120 over 68, pulse 69.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll need to examine you for this, it won't take long
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me if that's sore.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your pulse is regular and your heart sounds are normal.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can relax now.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Having listened and examined, my working impression is harmless extra heartbeats. Another possibility is an anxiety-related palpitation.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm, I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's harmless extra heartbeats, and we'll know more once the an ECG is back. Let's book an ECG to look into palpitations. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed. Cut back on coffee and energy drinks and keep a diary of when it happens. We'll catch up if it carries on after a month.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): right
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): does all of that make sense?
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, um, okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I think it's my turn.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): that's fine, sit down. Tell me why you came
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, it's a cough that eases on holiday. I don't know what's causing it. I took the morning off to come in today.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): it's, It's all the time a eight out of ten, I suppose
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): any other symptoms with it?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Wheeze at work goes along with it, most of the time. I've also had itchy eyes at work, for about three months.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): is it there all the time or does it come and go?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd say all the time.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much does it limit you?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): It's severe, honestly. The wheeze at work? That's been for three days.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed fever, weight loss or ankle swelling?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever, weight loss or ankle swelling, none of it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): nothing like coughing up blood?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): definitely no coughing up blood
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): okay, any pins and needles or loss of strength anywhere?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): no, that's all normal
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): any medical conditions, anything you've been treated for?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing I can think of.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): so, do you do any exercise?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I swim twice a week.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you on your own at home?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with my elderly mother.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Before we go further, any allergies?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not to my knowledge, no.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there any regular medication you use?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing at the moment.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): No, uh, not at all.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note down your vital signs first
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): okay: pulse is 84 beats a minute, height 180 centimetres, oxygen saturation is 99 percent, BMI works out to 30.2, blood pressure 113 over 82, respiratory rate 16, temp 37.0 degrees, weight 98 kilos
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): they help me see the whole picture, more shortly
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to check you over now, if that's alright.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathe out slowly.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): there is a little wheeze at the end of each breath out
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so my impression is this: I think we're dealing with occupational asthma at this stage. So, to recap quickly. You've had a cough that eases on holiday, and no fever or ankle swelling.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Exactly.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll request spirometry, it'll help with wheeze. I want serial peak flow readings done, that's for work-related wheeze. What I'm giving you is beclometasone inhaler, 200 micrograms, twice a day, long term. That should help with asthma. Record peak flows at work and at home for four weeks. I think occupational health should see you too. Keep an eye out, and if the symptoms get worse, call us the same day or go to emergency.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, um, I'll bear that in mind.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please come and see me in four weeks. Right, that's the plan. Do you wanna ask me anything?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): That's clear, um, thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, come on back. I'll grab vitals before Dr. Shah sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure, just go easy, bending's the part that gets me. Third-floor walkup, no elevator, and I hauled a couch up those stairs like an idiot.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I told him to wait for the movers. I'm Lauren, his wife. He never listens.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 128 over 82, pulse 76, temperature 36.8 Celsius, oxygen sat 99 percent, and he's breathing 16. You can stay sitting.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 128 okay? Guy at work, Ray, his was like 160-something and he made it sound like he was dying, so now I'm paranoid about those home cuffs.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): 128 over 82 is fine for today. Dr. Shah's finishing a note, she'll be right in.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. Back pain is what I have on the schedule. What's been going on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Low back. It's a deep ache across the bottom, a little more on the right, about a five or six most of the time. If I lift a case it grabs and jumps to an eight, and I have to stop. Warehouse work is cases of drinks all day, and then we moved, so it's been boxes on boxes.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did it start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the annoying part. A few weeks, or since the move. And the move, um, I want to say after Halloween, or maybe closer to Thanksgiving, or I'm mixing it up with last year. I really cannot tell you the date.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't look at me. I had it as September and then I remembered the lease was later. I can't date it either.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, so we leave the start date open. Is the pain there every day?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, every day. Stiff in the morning, maybe twenty minutes, then it loosens up. Lying flat on the floor feels better than the new mattress, which was a total ripoff, don't get me started.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Besides lying down, what helps?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen takes the edge off. A hot shower helps a little too. Oh, and the new floor squeaks and the dog loses his mind, totally unrelated, sorry.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's alright. Let me ask the things that would worry me, one at a time. Any numbness or tingling in the legs, feet, or groin?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, my left foot falls asleep if I'm on the forklift too long. That's old, though, for years, and it wakes up when I walk it off. It's not new shooting pins and needles down the leg, and the groin is fine.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): So longstanding foot numbness with sitting, not a new radicular pattern. Next, your bladder. Any trouble starting, leaking, or not knowing when you have to go?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Peeing is completely normal.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I started telling Lauren I dropped a couple pounds because the kitchen was in boxes and we lived on cereal. There's no scale, though, so I was kinda making up a number.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did not lose weight. Same jeans, same belt hole. He skipped two lunches and turned it into a documentary.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, she's right. I haven't lost weight.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): So no weight loss. Last one, any fever, chills, or feeling flu-ish?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no chills. I feel well otherwise. The beagle got into the packing paper and I was up late, but that's not sick, that's just a beagle.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any leg weakness, any change in your bowels, or numbness where you sit?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. Bowels are regular. Nothing numb down there.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. I'm not hearing the dangerous features. How are you actually taking the ibuprofen?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I buy the 200 milligram tablets. I swallow three, so 600 milligrams, two or three times a day on the bad days, not every day. Usually with coffee, which I know isn't food.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any other pain medicine, prescription or somebody else's?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Lauren had tramadol for a tooth. I took one of hers once and I was useless on the forklift, so never again. I'm not taking her pills.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Please don't. Those are mine, and they're almost gone.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Understood. Any allergies to ibuprofen or other medicines?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No drug allergies. Penicillin and ibuprofen are both fine.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any medical problems, surgeries, or family history that matters for the back?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Surgeries, no. I'm pretty healthy. My dad had a bad back, but he roofed for forty years, so that might just be the job. Oh, and they X-rayed my back once and said it was borderline.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me more about that X-ray. What did borderline mean, and when was it?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Urgent care, I think, or the work clinic, I mix them up. They said borderline, like a little wear, nothing dramatic. Last winter, or the winter before that. I cannot remember which, and they never gave me a number or a report.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I wasn't there. I just remember the word borderline, and he went to work the next day.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): So an old back X-ray called borderline, no report here, and the year is fuzzy. I'll treat that as your recollection, not as a measurement we can use. Let me examine you.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): The muscles on both sides of the low back are tender, the right a little more than the left. The bones in the midline are not tender.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise doesn't send pain down either leg. Strength is full, sensation is intact, and your walk looks normal.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the pressing is sore right where it grabs. Am I gonna end up with screws like Ray? He still complains, and he also owes me twenty bucks, which is unrelated but it bugs me.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, this fits mechanical low back pain, a strain from the warehouse lifting and the move. No fever, no bladder change, no new leg findings, and the exam doesn't show a pinched nerve. I can't fully exclude a small disc irritation, but nothing here says surgery.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, good, because I can't take six weeks off. Peak season is coming and my supervisor already side-eyes my bathroom breaks.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bed rest would actually work against you. Stay active, skip the heaviest lifts for now, keep the cases around waist height, and bend your knees. Heat after work is fine.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep the ibuprofen at 600 milligrams by mouth, up to three times a day on bad days, but take it with food instead of just coffee, and skip it when the day is easy. Don't go past that dose.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): With food, got it. Stomach's been fine, no heartburn or anything.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll hide the tramadol, and I'll nag him about breakfast. He stands all day too, if that matters.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Standing and lifting both matter. I'm going to refer you to physical therapy for your core and for lifting mechanics. They'll call you to set it up.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): PT, alright. Do I need another X-ray? Last time borderline sounded scary and then nobody did anything.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it's not better in three weeks, come back and we'll do a lumbar X-ray. Come sooner if you get leg weakness, numbness that sticks around, trouble with your bladder, or a fever.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. What if it just disappears next week? Do I still have to come?
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Only if it's not better. If it settles, cancel. For now I'm calling it mechanical low back pain, provisional, from the story and a reassuring exam.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll put it on the calendar as a maybe. And he is not lifting that dryer, I don't care.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, alright. Thanks. If the beagle asks, the couch won.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): The nurse will have the therapy referral on your way out. Take care of that back.
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the referral and walk you both out. Watch the step by the desk.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. I was told to come back, because my throat swab came back positive. The nurse phoned me yesterday.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, I've got the result here. Group A strep, a bacterial throat infection. How are you feeling now? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit better than at the weekend, but my throat is still very sore. And my glands are swollen. ~
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did it start? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Five days ago. Fever, headache, and a terrible throat. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any rash, or difficulty swallowing your saliva?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash. I can swallow, it just hurts.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Just paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your throat. Open wide. ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Ahh.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tonsils are red and swollen with white spots on both, and there are tender swollen glands under your jaw.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): It looks bad? ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's typical. I'd say this is strep throat, bacterial tonsillitis, as the swab confirms.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Can you give me something? ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'll prescribe penicillin V, 500 mg, four times a day, for ten days.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days? My friend had five. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): For strep throat, ten days is the full course, to clear it and prevent complications. Finish it all, even if you feel better in two. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything about the antibiotic you'd like me to explain before we go on? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's clear enough. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, temperature 37.6, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. A mild temperature, as expected. Rest, drink plenty, and use paracetamol for the pain. Salt-water gargles help too.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I go to work? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay off until you've had two days of the antibiotic, and your fever has gone.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't swallow, drool, have a very stiff neck, or a one-sided swollen throat, come back at once.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in a week, if you're not completely better.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four months of back pain. And is it constant, or does it come and go?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly it's there when I bend. Tying my boots is the worst part of the day.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me what you take for it. Be honest, nobody's grading you.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen. The 600 mg ones, I take them two or three times a day. Well, two, usually, but three on the bad days. I've got a bottle in the truck, one in the kitchen, one in my jacket.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Huh. So it's the pills doing it, not the back.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): The pills are the likely culprit, yes. From what I'm seeing, it looks like the anti-inflammatories are straining your kidneys. It's early, and it's usually reversible.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Reversible. That's the good word. How early?

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. It's yellow like always. Well, darker in the morning, but everybody's is.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's normal. Do you remember if anyone ever told you about your kidneys before?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I get kidney stones, every few years. I passed one on a fishing trip once, worst day of my life.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's helpful to know. Anything else on your medical history, the sort of thing you'd say if someone asked you?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure. I'm supposed to watch it. Oh, and I had my appendix out as a teenager, you were going to ask that.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I was heading there. Appendix as a teenager. What do you do for work, with that back?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Construction. Framing houses, I've done it for twenty-two years. No, twenty-three. Whichever, long enough.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heavy on the back, that explains it. And any alcohol?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): A beer or two after work. Weekends maybe four.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Let me get your blood pressure and pulse while we're talking.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 138 over 84, and your pulse is 70. Not bad at all.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Better than last time, I think. I forgot to take my coffee this morning, that probably helps.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fewer cups never hurts. So, here's the plan. I'd like to repeat the creatinine blood test, so we can see whether the number is moving. I'll order that today.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I have to fast again?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fasting needed. I'd also like a urine test, to check whether any protein is leaking through the filter.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Same as last time, the little cup?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): The little cup. You can leave both at the lab on the way out.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. And what do I do about the back? I can't just not take anything.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the ibuprofen, all of it, including the bottle in the truck. Use heat on the back in the evening, keep moving, and I'll have the physiotherapist's number for you at the desk.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): The bottle in the truck. Yeah. Fine. I'll bring it in the house and throw it out.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Also, check labels on cold and flu medicines, because a lot of them contain similar stuff.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Got it. I never thought about the cold stuff.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people don't. Any other questions for me?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the one thing, what was it, oh, can I still lift at work?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lift with your legs, keep loads close to your body, and listen to the back. If it screams, put it down.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha, the back screams plenty. Thanks, doc.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anytime. Look after those kidneys.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): In the morning there is some phlegm, clear, or a little gray. Later it is mostly a dry tickle. Bothersome, though I would not call it severe.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the phlegm?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. None that I have seen.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it wake you at night?

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's been ten days, I'm fairly sure.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you describe it a bit more for me? How strong it is, what the pattern is, what helps.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It settles a little with paracetamol. I'd say on and off. So, and I've been feeling sick as well, for about four days. I've also been sweating a lot. I had muscle aches before. That's settled now, though.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a high fever with shaking chills before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, a couple of years ago. It settled by itself back then.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shall I check your blood pressure and pulse?
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: respiratory rate 21, pressure 119 over 70, SpO2 98 percent on room air, pulse is 108 beats a minute.

[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you in a second, make yourself comfortable.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me feel here.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): The spleen tip is just palpable and the chest is clear.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can relax now. Have you had any rash, yellow eyes or confusion?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash, yellow eyes or confusion, none of it.

[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not a single one.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your urine normal, no changes?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): My partner and our baby. I grab fast food at lunch most days. Not much, I mostly stay in these days.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Sertraline. I take it once a day.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the dose?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): It's 50 milligrams. Dolo. I take it 650 milligrams, when I get the fever.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I've never been operated on.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you react to any medicines or foods? Any allergies?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I'm allergic to nickel.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in your past medical history I should know?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Depression, for five years.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so my impression is this: It points towards a fever after travel that must be treated as possible malaria. Typhoid fever is still possible.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): What are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like a fever after travel that must be treated as possible malaria, but I'd like to confirm. I'm going to order blood cultures, for fever.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): When would that take place?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood tests is what I'd like next, for fever. Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers and keep drinking. Please come and see me after the results today. That's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): I think I understand everything. Thanks.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, take a seat. What can I do for you?

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you tell me when it first started?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Around ten days... no wait, it's more like two days. I did try to ignore it for a while.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much trouble does it give you?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd call it severe.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you get it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Honestly, all the time.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll just record a few vital signs.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit still for a moment...
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: temp 37.4 degrees, oxygen saturation is 92 percent, pulse is 97 beats a minute, blood pressure 119 over 77, respiratory rate 25.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll explain what these mean in a moment.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now I'm going to do a short physical check.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): You are pale, breathing fast and bringing up fresh blood with every cough.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, you can sit up now.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, a few quick ones: chest pain or fever?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't had chest pain or fever, no.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any weight loss?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Definitely no weight loss.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything on the skin I should know about?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing on the skin, no.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, any allergies to tablets, food or anything in the environment?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No allergies at all.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any chronic illnesses?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I have diabetes.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Yes, diabetes is known to us, good to have that clear. What's on your current medicine list?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Glycomet, 500 milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you live by yourself?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I share a house with my brother.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you active?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I walk the dog every morning.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing, I haven't had any operations.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Having listened and examined, the most likely explanation is life-threatening haemoptysis. Let's book urgent blood tests to look into bleeding.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): That makes sense.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's use tranexamic acid, 1 gram, now, single dose. That's for haemoptysis. Lie on the bleeding side and I am calling the emergency team. See me again straight away.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, you know, I'll be back.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care now.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, I'm worried. I've been waking at night in a sweat, shaking, and my meter says my sugar's low. It's happened three times this month.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me, that's important. What does the meter say, when it happens?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Two point eight, once. Three point one another time. I ate some biscuits and it came up.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you lose consciousness, or have a fit, when it happens?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no, I don't pass out, and I've never had a fit. I wake up myself.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's go through your treatment.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Insulin glargine, 20 units at night. Metformin, 1000 mg twice a day. And gliclazide, 80 mg twice a day.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And do you take the gliclazide even when you haven't eaten?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I try to, but if I skip dinner, I sometimes skip it as well. I'm not always sure what I've done.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for being honest. I'll note that the gliclazide is meant to be twice a day, but you're not always sure. Any allergies?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medical history?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Type 2 diabetes, fifteen years. And high blood pressure.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Cataracts, both eyes, three years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): What time do you have your evening meal, and how much? ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): It varies. Sometimes seven, sometimes nine. Lighter, lately, since I've been trying to lose weight. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the clue. Gliclazide pushes your body to make insulin whether or not you've eaten, and on top of the long-acting insulin, a lighter dinner can send your sugar too low at night. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's the tablets? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's the combination. I'd say these night-time lows are most likely due to the gliclazide and insulin together with smaller meals.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stop something? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to cut the gliclazide to 40 mg twice a day and keep the insulin the same for now. Eat a small snack with carbohydrate at bedtime.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Will it get high? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your sugars may run a little higher, which is safer than lows. I'd like to arrange an HbA1c blood test, to see the longer-term picture.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Fair. What if it happens again? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Treat with fast sugar, fifteen to twenty grams, a glass of juice, retest in fifteen minutes, then eat a snack. And ring us with your readings.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll write it on the fridge. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please do. If you ever can't wake properly or can't treat it yourself, your family should call 999.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thank you, doctor. Should I carry something sweet in my pocket? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, glucose tablets or jelly babies, always. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come through. Your partner's happy to wait outside until you're ready, he said.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, leave him, he's glued to his phone. I'm a bit all over the shop, sorry. We've been up since six because the dog was barking at the bin truck.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All good. I'll just do a blood pressure and pulse before the doctor. You're not feeling faint sitting there?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Not faint, no. It's this spotting and the cramps that got me in.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy-four, pulse eighty-six. I'll grab the doctor.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this thing's decided to update itself. Right. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm pregnant, and I've been spotting. Brown, not heaps. And crampy, low in my belly, like a period. I reckon I'm about eight or ten weeks but I honestly don't know.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, it just pinged. Say again how many weeks?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): About eight to ten? The last period was around Diwali, or after. I can't pin the day. We had family over, there was so much food, my auntie made that carrot halwa, I ate way too much, totally off topic, sorry.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. When did the spotting start?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a few days. Maybe since the weekend, or a bit before that. I keep losing track of which morning I first saw it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cramps, did they start then too?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, same sort of time. They come and go, not all day. Worse when I'm on my feet. I do reception at a physio in Parramatta, so I'm up and down all arvo, and the M4 this morning was a car park.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any heavy bleeding, clots, soaking through a pad?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. It's just a bit of brown when I wipe.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the pain more on one side?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. It sort of moves around.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shoulder pain, or dizziness?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No shoulder pain. I went a bit woozy in the shower yesterday but it passed, I just stood up too quick. My sister's like that, she's anaemic, forever telling me to eat spinach.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the wooziness isn't hanging around?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, gone.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nausea? Vomiting?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Not vomiting. The neighbour's curry last night was a bit much but I still ate, we had leftovers for tea.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain or burning when you pass urine?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think so. I haven't actually checked with a thermometer.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Folic acid. Um, the one milligram— no, wait, GP put me on five milligrams, once a day, because we were trying. And Elevit, the pregnancy one, most mornings. I skipped a couple when I felt off, but mostly I take it.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen jumped. Folate dose again?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. I had penicillin as a kid for tonsillitis and I was fine.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Oh, and I've got asthma, had it since I was a teenager, but it's quiet, I haven't touched the puffer in months.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Asthma, quiet, noted. Do you smoke?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. And I stopped drinking when the test turned positive. We live together, me and my partner, over in Westmead. He's still outside, poor thing, he hates waiting rooms, reckons the magazines are from 2004.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to butt in. He's asked if he can come in now. And ultrasound have a slot at two today if you want it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah send him in, he can just sit. I'm properly anxious about this, hey. I barely slept last night, just going over worst cases. He's not going to talk, he goes quiet at the doctor.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's understandable. I'm not calling this a miscarriage. It might be a threatened miscarriage, or it might just be benign spotting this early. With the dates all over the place we need a look.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. The home test was positive, two lines, about three weeks ago I think, or maybe a bit less, I didn't write it down.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll do a pelvic ultrasound today, that two o'clock slot, and bloods today as well: a pregnancy hormone level, a full blood count, and your blood group.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to keep taking the Elevit and the folate?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep both going, same as you are. No new tablets from me today. Take it easy, no heavy lifting this week, and if you're standing all day at work see if you can sit more.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I can ask my boss. She's pretty good. We had a staff morning tea yesterday, someone brought lamingtons, I had two, which is probably not the issue but I feel guilty about everything now.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lamingtons won't have done this. If the bleeding gets heavy, you soak a pad within an hour, the pain gets severe, or you feel faint, come straight to emergency, don't wait for me.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Straight to emergency. Okay. And if it's just this same spotting?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then I still want you back here in a week with the results, even if it settles. Don't skip that one.
[SEG0049] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll book the ultrasound for two and put the blood forms through to pathology downstairs so you can go after this.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. If my partner looks pale it's just him, not me. He nearly fainted at his own blood test last year, dramatic.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll keep an eye on you, not him. Any questions before I let you go?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I think that's it. I'll try not to google myself into a state before two.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, my sister coughed for months on the lisinopril until they swapped hers. I was blaming the grandson, though. And the load shedding, eish, I can't even boil the kettle half the time, so the honey-and-lemon thing is hit and miss.

[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Nurse, what's on the medication list while I find the right tab? I've clicked into someone else's letters.
[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Repeat script is metformin one gram twice a day, and insulin glargine, Lantus, 28 units at night.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not right. I do, um, 24... no, 22. They cut it after I went hypo at my sister's barbecue, last autumn. 28 was the old dose.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again, I was in the wrong box. Was it 22?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): 22. I dial 22 on the pen. Well, most nights I do.
[SEG0009] person_4 (NURSE): The chart still says 28 units once nightly, doctor. If someone changed it, they never updated this.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He tells me 22, and I've watched him dial it a few times. I'm not there every single evening, mind.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which nights are you not taking it, then?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Early shifts. I'm on the forklift at the depot from six, so on a work day I skip the injection. Don't want a hypo halfway up a rack. Weekends I'm good, I take it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the metformin, you're actually swallowing that?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a thousand milligrams in the morning and again with my tea. Don't miss those, they're just tablets. Been on them years.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): My mate Dave's on some weekly jab and he will not shut up about it. We were meant to go fishing Sunday, only the rain was filthy, so that was that.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. What were those home sugars? Someone's scribbled a figure and I can't read my own writing.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting it's, um, one-eighty-something. Well, actually I looked this morning and I can't remember if it was 186 or 181. I don't write them down, the book's under the batteries and the dog lead.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-eighty? Say that again, is your meter still in the old American numbers?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It comes up 180, or 186, something round there, before breakfast. I never changed the setting. After meals I don't bother, life's too short.
[SEG0020] person_4 (NURSE): Finger-prick in the room this morning was 11.4. Blood pressure 146 over 88, pulse 78, weight 91.5 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ta. Any thirst, or getting up at night to wee?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirsty, yeah, I'm on the squash all day. And I'm up once or twice in the night, which is new these last few months. Knackered with it, if I'm honest.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's shattered. Asleep in the chair before the news most nights.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feet. Any numbness, tingling, sores between the toes?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, feet are fine. I walk the dog every evening, no tingling, nothing like sores. Had a verruca years back, gone now.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes? Any blurring, or have you had the screening photos?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Eyes are all right. Photos last spring, letter said all clear. I squint at the telly but that's wanting new glasses, I've been on about that since Christmas.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look while this thing restarts. Skin on both feet is intact, no breaks, the pulses are there, and the monofilament sensation is normal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, penicillin or otherwise?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Penicillin's fine, never had a rash or anything.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the diabetes been? Remind me, the summary box is blank.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Diagnosed about eight years back. My dad had it too, type two, he was on insulin near the end. Mum's side, nothing of the sort. Linda still buys the chocolate digestives, mind, I have the one with my tea.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to conclude the dose is wrong. It might be the injections you skip on shift days, or 22 units might simply not be enough, and I can't separate those two from here. The home numbers are too woolly to hang a decision on.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll send you for an HbA1c today, before anyone changes the insulin. Nurse can do the blood on your way out.
[SEG0035] person_4 (NURSE): Chair's free, I can take it before half ten. Just the HbA1c, yeah?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. And Graham, don't just skip the injection on work mornings. If the forklift and hypos are the worry, we can shift the timing, but missing it is muddying this. Write the fasting figures down for a fortnight, actual numbers.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks and we'll go through the result. Reception will book it, assuming this computer's alive.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is fine, long as it's not an early. I'm on earlies all next month. Cheers, then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Knee playing up, is it?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, it's the right knee, and I'm seventy-one so I probably should have come sooner, but I kept thinking it would settle. It really grabs when I come down the back stairs at home, the wooden ones with the wobbly rail, and I have to hang on like I'm on a ladder.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee only?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right is the one I came about. The left gives a little niggle if I've been round the shops all morning, but I wouldn't have booked for the left, it's nothing beside the right.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Karen, her daughter. I drove her so she didn't have to do the stairs at the station.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, um, that's the annoying part. I cannot date it. It was last winter, or, well, actually it might have been the winter before that, and I couldn't tell you the month.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've asked her. She goes round in circles. I can't put a date on it either.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Worse coming down stairs?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Much worse coming down than going up. Going up I'm just a bit stiff at the first step, but coming down I take them one at a time, sideways sometimes, and if I rush because the kettle's boiled it really bites on the inside of the knee.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night-time?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I wake, usually round two, and the right knee is aching deep in the joint. Most nights this past fortnight. I shove a pillow under it and that takes the edge off, then I can get back to sleep, though I'm not what you'd call fresh.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've checked in the morning light, and it doesn't swell and it isn't red. It just looks like my usual knee.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Locking, or giving way?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No locking, and it hasn't given way under me. I'm slow on it, but it holds.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She tripped on the hose last week. That was the hose, not the knee buckling.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Voltaren gel from the chemist, the diclofenac one. I rub a decent blob into the right knee morning and night, I don't measure it. And when the stairs have been rotten I also take the diclofenac tablets you can buy at the counter, not a script.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablet strength, and how often?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac, twenty-five milligrams. One tablet, maybe two or three times in a week, not every day. I try not to take the tablet the same evening I've already put the gel on, but some nights they overlap and I know that's probably not clever.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach trouble with them?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no stomach problems. I have them with toast or a bit of yoghurt and I've been fine on that front.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The scale at the clinic last month said ninety-six kilos, and I'm one metre sixty-two, so yes, I'm heavier than I was. Before I retired from the library I sat in the low eighties, and the kilos crept on with the desk and then with not walking.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ninety-six kilos. That load goes straight through the knee.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Speaking of not moving, the freeway this morning was a car park. We sat by that big servo for ages and the bloke in front was eating a pie at the wheel.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): And the radio was the cricket from Adelaide, and I was trying to tell Karen what a slip cordon is, and she kept changing the station to some gardening show.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I still don't see why everyone claps a maiden over. Anyway the weather's supposed to turn this arvo, big storms coming up from the south, so we want to be home before the dog starts hiding.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Little Ollie, my grandson, he's cricket mad. He bowls a tennis ball down their hallway and takes out the photo frames, and his mum rings me to complain as if I taught him the grip, which I suppose I did.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He rang last night, under-tens won by four runs, and now he wants a new bat. That's the whole saga from the car. Nothing to do with the knee, before you ask.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): A few minutes, that's all. I get up, it's tight, I walk to the kettle, and by the time the tea's poured it's loosened. Not an hour of hobbling, just those first steps.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hips or back?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Hips are fine and the back is fine. It's just the knee.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said the stomach was fine.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I did say that, and I meant no pain in the tummy or being sick, but I do get heartburn. A burning behind the breastbone, a couple of times a week, worse if I lie down straight after tea. It's been a few months. Since about March I can place that one better than the knee, though I don't know if it's the tablets or just me.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything for the heartburn?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon, the liquid from the chemist. One dose after tea when it comes on, not every night. It helps enough that I haven't needed anything stronger, and I haven't mentioned it till now, which is silly of me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll look. Tender on the inner side?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, ow, that's exactly the spot, the inside of the right knee, not the kneecap so much.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender medial joint line, right knee. No effusion. Flexion is limited at the end. Ligaments feel steady.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): It catches a little when you bend it that far, a small clunk more than a pain. The night-time one is a deep ache, different from that catch.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like osteoarthritis. Wear and tear in the right knee. Working impression only. I wouldn't call it definite without an X-ray.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Could the gel be giving her the heartburn?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can't say. Oral diclofenac can cause heartburn. Ease off those tablets.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, I'll leave the tablets alone. I'd rather the heartburn went than keep taking them two or three times a week. Can I keep the gel, though, because that actually dulls the stair pain for a few hours?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel's fine. Morning and night, right knee only.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the morning one after my shower so it soaks in before the trousers go on, and the night one in my pyjamas, and the smell is a bit menthol but I've got used to it. I won't put it on the left, since you said right only.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Next options are physio, or a steroid injection into the knee. Not deciding that today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather not leap to a needle if some proper exercises might sort the stairs, but I'm not ruling it out. My neighbour had a knee injection and she was walking the dog the next month, though that's her knee, not mine.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She hates needles. She'll still do whatever you actually recommend, she just talks herself in circles first.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park both. Physio or an injection only if it's still limiting you. Come back in six weeks and say which way you want to go. If the heartburn picks up, stop the tablets sooner and ring the clinic.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the job.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Picker in a warehouse. Lifting cartons, some around twenty kilos, on my feet for an eight hour shift. Been doing it for years.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. I'm hearing three months from you and about five from June, and I can't pin a start date either of you is sure of. I'll hold it as roughly three to five months.
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): That seems fair. I apologize for the muddle.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): No apology needed. Walk me through a typical night.
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): I get into bed near eleven. I may doze after midnight, then I am awake around three and I do not really get back to sleep. I am tired all the next day.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And then he naps in the armchair after lunch, which I swear makes the night worse. Also the dog's been stealing his pillow, but that's, well, not why we're here.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dog out of the chart. Is that low energy there most days, Mr. Hale?
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes. Most days. I stay polite about it at home, but it is wearying.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the interest, if we drop the word completely?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): I said I was fine, and that was not the whole truth. I have lost interest in the workshop. I still read the paper. I am not indifferent to every single thing.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also won't see people. His friend called twice and he just let it ring.
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): I did see Robert last Sunday, briefly. I would not say that I will not see anyone.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): One visit isn't the old social calendar, but I won't inflate it. Do you feel hopeless about the weeks ahead?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Flat, I would say. Not hopeless. I still expect the days to keep coming.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I need to ask something I ask anyone when energy and interest fall off like this, and I'll ask it gently. Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): No. I have not. I want to be quite clear that I have no thoughts of harming myself.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I believe you. Any chest pain, or trouble getting your breath, along with the fatigue?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And no shortness of breath.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines on a regular basis?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): Nothing regularly. I would prefer to keep it that way, if possible.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, to a medicine or to anything else?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sometimes low energy is a blood test and not just the mood. Did anyone ever check your thyroid, or say you were anemic?
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Two years ago my previous physician ordered a thyroid test. They said it was borderline. I was never started on a medicine for it, and I do not have the number.

[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes. That would be acceptable.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His father died of a heart attack, if you need that. And Daniel was laid off from the bookkeeping job in April, so he's home all day.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Useful, thank you. Mr. Hale, do you smoke, or drink alcohol?
[SEG0038] person_4 (PATIENT): I do not smoke. I might have a small glass of wine on a Sunday, and nothing more than that.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looking you over, you're well groomed, your speech is clear, and I don't see a tremor in the hands. You do look tired. Nothing acute is jumping out on this quick exam.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, this looks like a depressive episode, and I mean a working impression rather than a final label, with the grief and the job loss underneath it. I also can't fully rule out a thyroid contribution, given that old borderline test, so that stays on the differential until the lab speaks.
[SEG0041] person_4 (PATIENT): I understand. I would rather not begin a medicine today, if you feel that is reasonable.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is reasonable, and I won't start one today. If you're still this low when I see you in four weeks, we could start sertraline at fifty milligrams. We can decide that then, not in this room.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Between now and then, the useful steps are ordinary ones. Pick a single wake-up time and keep it, even after a bad night, and skip the long nap after lunch. If any thought of harming yourself shows up, you call the office or you go to the emergency room, and you do not wait the four weeks.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll help him with the wake-up time. Sorry, the parking garage took twenty minutes off my temper, which is not relevant, I know.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm putting in a referral to our behavioral health counselor, so the two of you aren't carrying this alone. The thyroid blood draw can happen today if the nurse is still around.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk him to the lab once you're finished. We're still drawing for a bit.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Mr. Hale, I want to see you in four weeks either way, not only if you feel worse. We'll look at the thyroid and only then talk about whether sertraline makes sense.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the care you have taken with this.

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had bowel cancer.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): See me again if it isn't working in a week. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, alright, thanks, take care.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Yes — redness at the lower end, a little yellow discharge, and the edges are still together. There is no gap, and nothing I can feel as a collection of pus. It is tender, just as you found.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not from what I see today. No opening of the wound, and no drainage. We will swab it, change the antibiotic, and watch you closely.

[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, come either way. And if the redness spreads or the fever returns before that, do not wait for the two days — come straight in.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday is all right. My husband can drive me. The baby is feeding well, by the way — that part has been a blessing. I was more frightened about the wound than about myself, if that makes sense.
