[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in and sit down there. You look worn out, if you don't mind me saying. How have you been keeping?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. I'm grand. It was the wife who booked this, not me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. What had her worried, would you say?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The sleep, mostly. She says I'm up half the night and I've no energy the next day. I told her I'm fine.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you fine, though, or is that the short answer to make it go away?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Well. I'm tired — knackered, actually — and I can't get interested in anything, the telly or the garden or the lads. Months of it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Months is a while. Can you put any kind of date on when it started?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't a clue, honestly. Last winter, or the one before, around when I was let go from the depot. Could've been after Christmas, could've been before — I can't give you a date.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's all right, we don't need the exact day. The job — a redundancy, was it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Twenty-two years in the one place and a letter. I'm still rattling round the house like a spare part.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'd take the stuffing out of anyone. With the sleep, is it getting off, or waking early, or the both?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The both. I lie there till two — well, actually nearer three some nights — with the mind going ninety, and then I'm awake again around five. Not every night. Most nights.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And through the day, the energy?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I could be on the couch from eleven and still feel useless. Half the time I don't even switch the telly on.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): The loss of interest — is the mood low along with it, or more just numb?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Low in myself. Snappy with the wife, which isn't fair, and I don't ring anyone. Dinner doesn't taste of anything — I'm not even hungry in a... no, the eating's the same, I'm just not enjoying it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the appetite itself hasn't changed, and no weight loss that you've noticed?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Eating the same. Weight's the same. She's still cooking for four.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I have to ask you something straight, the way I ask everyone in this spot. Any thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that — I'm miserable, not stupid, and I wouldn't lay a hand on myself. The two kids are still in the house, for God's sake.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you can say it plain. Anything else in the body — chest pain, shortness of breath?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, breathing's grand. It's the head and the get-up-and-go, that's the whole of it. The spaniel's been walking herself, a dog with more of a routine than me.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): She'll cope. Are you taking any medicines just now?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the blood pressure one. Ramipril. That's it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse read it off the sheet for me just now — ramipril five milligrams, once every morning.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That's wrong. It's ten. Ten milligrams, and it's been ten a long while. She has the old number, so don't write five.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the strength blank till we check it against the repeat script. Nothing else — no sleeping tablet, nothing over the counter?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't take anything else. I nearly said the wife has something for her own sleep, but that's hers, not mine. I never took it.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to a medicine, or to anything else?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Never had a reaction that I know of.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke? And what about drink?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked in my life. A few pints of a weekend, same as always. Maybe the one extra since the job went. Not every night, before you ask.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are the days filled, if you're not in work?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Signing on. The odd walk when the dog makes a show of me. Otherwise the kitchen and the racing on the radio. Fierce boring.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're looking tired even while we're talking, and the speech is a bit flat. No restlessness, though, and no shake in the hands.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, well, I didn't sleep, so. Sorry if I'm sharp. The waiting room was roasting and yer man on the phone wouldn't give it a rest.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No apology. From what you've told me, this has the shape of a low mood after the redundancy — the sleep, the interest gone, the energy gone. I wouldn't put a firm diagnosis on it today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing it, then. Grand.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not losing it. We could think about a small dose of sertraline later if this hasn't lifted, but I'm not starting any medicine today. I'd rather see what a few ordinary weeks do.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather no tablet. Not yet. Tablets for the head... I don't know. Maybe if I'm still like this.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a fair way to leave it. Try to get out of the house once a day, even twenty minutes, and keep the bed for sleep instead of lying awake stewing. If a thought of harming yourself ever does show up, ring the surgery that same day or go to the emergency department — don't wait it out.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I hear you. I'll tell the wife, she'll be on my case anyway.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in four weeks, better or not, and we'll decide about a tablet then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi. Sorry, I'm a few minutes late, the lot out front was full.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oh, don't worry, that lot is a nightmare on Thursdays. And this rain, it was sunny an hour ago. Did you end up parking on the street?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Garage across the road. Eleven dollars.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ouch. Well, you're here now. Your chart says it's your diabetes check, the sugars have been creeping up. Is that how you see it?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. The numbers on my meter are higher lately.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How high are we talking, roughly? What do you see in the morning?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Around one-sixty. Used to be one-ten.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's a real change. Have you noticed anything in yourself, anything that feels different?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm thirsty a lot. More than normal.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thirstier than normal. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): About one month.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about the bathroom, are you going more often?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Up at night to pee. Twice, sometimes three times.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twice or three times a night. Is that new as well, or have you always been a night-time person?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): New. I used to sleep straight through.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Got it. Any blurry vision, like you can't quite focus on the page?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Eyes are fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Remind me, when were you diagnosed with the type 2 diabetes?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Three years ago. And high cholesterol, same time.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, type 2 diabetes for three years, plus the high cholesterol. And you're managing with diet alone, no pills so far?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Just diet. The walks stopped when it got cold, though.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the diet. I'm always curious what people actually eat, not what they think they should say.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Lots of rice. Bread. My wife makes banana bread on Sundays.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Banana bread, I love banana bread, I won't hold that against you. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And alcohol, do you drink?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of beers on the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's moderate. Okay, let me check a few numbers. I'll take your blood pressure, then we'll put you on the scale.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure comes out at 134 over 82. A touch high, but I'd want it again before I worry. Step up here for me, please.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight is 94 kilograms. Last year you were 90, so a few kilos have crept on over the winter. Now, take your sock off, I want to look at your feet.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Which one?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Left first. I'm touching a few spots with this thin little thread, tell me when you feel it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Yep. Yep. Yeah, I feel that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, sensation in both feet is normal. And the pulses at the ankles are strong, so the circulation looks fine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): That's good, right?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Very good. So here's my thinking. It looks like your blood sugar control is slipping, mostly from the winter routine, the extra rice and bread, and the walks stopping.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): So I need pills?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not yet. Let's get an accurate picture first. I'd like to order an HbA1c, which tells us the average of the last three months. We'll draw it today at the lab downstairs.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Is that all?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd also like a urine test for protein, since diabetes can affect the kidneys over the years. You can give that sample on your way out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, go back to walking, even twenty minutes after dinner, and try swapping half the rice for vegetables. Banana bread, one slice, not three.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): My wife won't like that.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell her it's doctor's orders. Let's meet again in two weeks, when the results are back, and talk about whether medicine makes sense.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Great. Take care of yourself, and if the rain stops, maybe skip the garage next time.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Thanks, doc.

[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Since when, the morning one?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know, doctor. Could be three weeks, could be a month. I cannot put a date.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Two times this week, morning only, with the headache. Not daily.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Every time I pass urine it burns, doctor, and I have to go much more often. At night I am getting up twice.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, this is the third time this year I am getting this same problem. It is becoming a habit, I feel.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. No fever. I even checked with the thermometer at home.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine, or pain in the back?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood, doctor, and the back is not paining. It is only the burning and running to the toilet.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): You mentioned this is the third time this year. Were those episodes much the same?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, similar only. Um, well, actually, maybe it is the fourth. I forgot one in the summer. I am sorry, my count is not exact.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please, no apology needed. Did you take anything for it before coming?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I am embarrassed to admit this, doctor. I took my elder sister's leftover antibiotic — those white and yellow capsules, the urine ones. I cannot recall the name.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you telling me plainly. How did you take them, and are you still on them?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): One capsule in the morning and one at night, by mouth, for two days. Then the strip got over, so I stopped. I did not purchase them myself.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet, for the discomfort?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I took Crocin yesterday, two tablets, when the burning was too much. I have not taken it today, so I have stopped for now.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. Nothing of that kind. I am perfectly fine in that respect.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): At the office I forget, doctor. Maybe four glasses only, which I know is less. The meetings run long.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I am sorry, doctor. I was shy. There is a little itching since yesterday, but there is no discharge. I should have said so at once.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A little heaviness, doctor, just above the front. Not severe. My husband said I should not delay the visit, so I came today itself.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good that you came. Let me press gently on the tummy. The lower abdomen is soft, it is a bit tender just over the bladder, and there is no guarding.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I will follow that. Kindly say when I should come back.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in three days. If you develop fever or the burning becomes severe before that, come sooner, do not wait.
[SEG0036] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mrs Deshmukh, I will collect the urine sample in the side room — both the routine and the culture, as written. If it is not coming, drink a little water and we will wait.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I can try just now. Thank you for your kindness, doctor. I will be careful with the tablets.

[SEG0006] person_4 (PATIENT): My ear hurts. I don't like it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, Finn. Which ear is the sore one?
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): This one. The right. Will you hurt me?
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll only look with a little light, it shouldn't hurt. Mum, how long has it been sore?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): About a week— no, sorry, three days. Monday night was the first bad one. I'm getting my days mixed.
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): Am I poorly?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A bit, love, he's only three. He's been screaming with it after bedtime for two nights, and last night he wouldn't settle till gone three.

[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any gunk or discharge coming out of the ear?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's gone off his food. He only wanted a bit of toast this morning.

[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): In a minute, Finn. Mum, was anything actually leaking from the ear?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, no, nothing leaking. Sorry, I went off somewhere else.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting or diarrhoea?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting and no diarrhoea. Wees are fine. He's drinking, he's just not eating much.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cough, the cold, his breathing?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Snotty cold last week, mostly gone. Still a bit of a dry cough, not chesty. No wheeze. He's not breathless.
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): Can I go to nursery? I miss painting.
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's tomorrow, we'll ask. Doctor, is the cough part of this or something separate?

[SEG0034] person_4 (PATIENT): Medicine is yucky.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My uncle has high cholesterol.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please sit back down. Putting it all together, the most likely explanation is perimenopause.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, is this serious, doctor?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's reasonable to be concerned, but right now perimenopause is my leading thought, not anything worse.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want a blood count done, that's for irregular periods.

[SEG0068] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0069] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0070] person_2 (DOCTOR): See me again in three months.
[SEG0071] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll book it on my way out.
[SEG0072] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0073] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Rahman. Sorry about the wait, the list has got away from me this morning. You're Mark?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking we'll be here all morning if we litigate the date. Somewhere between two and four months, and I'll leave it at that. Dates aside, Mark, is the sleep actually bad?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Trouble getting off to sleep, waking early, or both?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. Mind won't stop.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Still awake at two, then awake again near five, and shattered all day. He just sits.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is that tiredness there all day, Mark?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): All day.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): The interest Helen mentioned. Football, friends. Has that faded?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Won't put the match on, won't ring his brother, and five-a-side on a Thursday has stopped. He used to love it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Suppose.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit low.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about appetite?
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Awful. Half his dinner goes back in the pan. He's hardly eating, I don't care what he says.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Feels normal to you, the eating?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It isn't. I wash the plates.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you two contradict each other on appetite, and I'm not choosing a winner. You hinted at weight, Helen, but with no number I'm not writing a weight change down.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Next question is a direct one, Mark, and I'm sorry to ask it. Any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that you'd rather not be here?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any plan along those lines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's never said anything of the sort. I'd have had him here long before now.

[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Omeprazole. Twenty milligrams, no, sorry, the box is ten milligrams, once every morning, for heartburn. He skips mornings. Don't ask me how many, I can't keep count.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sometimes you skip it?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The GP printed a sertraline script once, fifty milligrams, and he never fetched it from the chemist. Never took a single one.

[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you know the thinking, if we medicate later I would use sertraline fifty milligrams once daily. [SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): A few things worth doing yourself. Get up at the same time whatever the night was like, keep the phone out of the bed, and a short walk on the days you can manage. [SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Didn't watch.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Highlights only, on my end. Beautiful cover drive, then on came the covers. Standard summer.
[SEG0065] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Standard Leeds, weather and traffic both. That's all that was.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Back to it, I'd like a full blood count and a thyroid function test. [SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0072] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His father had a heart attack at about sixty. I'm sure of that. Depression in the family, I don't know, so I won't guess.
[SEG0073] person_4 (DOCTOR): Father, heart attack, around sixty. Rest unknown. Are you working at the moment, Mark?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Warehouse supervisor until they made him redundant. He's at home with me now. Hardly drinks, a beer of a Saturday if there's football, and he's never smoked.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0077] person_4 (DOCTOR): Living together, not in work since the redundancy, a weekend beer at most, never a smoker. I want you back in three weeks, a firm appointment, not a come-back-if. We'll have the bloods and only then decide about sertraline. Reception will give you the card as you leave.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0079] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll see that he turns up.
[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): You got past I'm fine, Mark. That was worth the visit.
[SEG0081] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks.
[SEG0082] person_1 (NURSE): Whenever you're ready, Mr Hale, we'll do those samples next door.
[SEG0083] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Come on then, love. We'll get it over with.

Transcript (encounter 00635)
[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning Callum, come in. I've got your GP's letter here, and I remember you saying last time that the back was easing a little. Is that still the story? ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Sort of. It's odd, really. My back pain gets better the more I do, which my mum says is the wrong way round.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not wrong at all, it's actually a clue. Remind me how long it's been going on?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Let me think. It started gradually, around when we moved flat, so about eight months now.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): And where do you feel it?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Low down, right across the bottom of my back. Sometimes it shoots into my right buttock.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's it like first thing in the morning?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Awful, I'm stiff as a board. It takes me a good hour to loosen up and I can barely get my socks on.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it ever wake you at night?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, I get night pain, usually around four. I have to get up and shuffle about the kitchen.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if you've been sitting a long while, say at work? ~
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Worse. Sitting is the enemy. But a swim or a bike ride and it's far better, so exercise helps it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): That pattern matters. Let me ask about some other things. Any red or painful eyes?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes have been fine.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any diarrhoea or blood when you go to the toilet?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, nothing like that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or weakness in your legs?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No numbness, my legs work fine. It's all just the back.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies to medicines that I should know about?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no allergies that I know of.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now your background. Are you well otherwise?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): I get skin trouble, psoriasis, on my scalp and my elbows. Since I was about nineteen.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's worth knowing. Anything else?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Migraines now and then, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I had my appendix out when I was fifteen. That's all.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does anyone in the family have back problems?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My dad does. He has ankylosing spondylitis, he's had it for years. It's why I came in, to be honest.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's helpful. Do you smoke?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): About ten cigarettes a day, I know, I know.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted. And what about alcohol?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I only drink a couple of pints of beer on a Saturday.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a delivery driver, so loads of sitting. That's probably why it's worse some weeks.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): And you mentioned swimming. How often?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I swim on Tuesdays and Thursdays before work. It's the best bit of my week.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Let's check you over. Your pulse is 66, blood pressure 124 over 78, temperature 36.7, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 14 a minute, and weight 78 kilos.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all fine? ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): All normal. Can you bend forward and try to touch your toes for me?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): That's as far as I go. It pulls right here. ~
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, I can see bending forwards is reduced, and it's tender when I press over the right sacroiliac joint.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Ouch, yes, that's the spot. ~
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now take a deep breath in. Your chest expands fully, which is good.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good for the back? ~
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): It tells me the ribs and spine up top aren't stuck. I can also see patches of psoriasis on your elbows.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, they come and go. ~
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your breathing or chest at all?
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, my chest is fine.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now, I can't rule out an inflammatory back condition at this stage, which would fit with the morning stiffness and your dad's history. We need tests to separate it from ordinary mechanical pain.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): So it could be what dad has? ~
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): It could, but it's early. I'd like to arrange an MRI of your sacroiliac joints, and we'll do blood tests including a marker called HLA-B27.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the MRI noisy? ~
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Very, you get earplugs. I'd also like to get an X-ray of your pelvis.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine by me. And will you give me something for it? ~
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, let's start naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food.
[SEG0056] person_1 (PATIENT): Any side effects I should watch for? ~
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stomach upset mainly, so I'll also start omeprazole 20 mg once a day to protect your stomach.
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. And the swimming, I should keep going? ~
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Absolutely, keep swimming, it's part of the treatment.
[SEG0060] person_1 (PATIENT): Brilliant, that's a relief. ~
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in six weeks to go through the results.
[SEG0062] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks, great. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning. Before we start, can I just check your name? Is it Mr Desmond Achterberg?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): That's me. Desmond is fine, though. Nobody calls me Mr Achterberg except the bank.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Desmond it is. Your GP asked me to take a look. What's your own understanding of why you're here?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Honestly? It's my left foot, and it's probably nothing. My daughter nagged me into coming.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Daughters usually have good instincts. Has anything stopped you doing what you normally do?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. I still walk the dog every morning. I just wanted her to stop going on about it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good for you. Now, a few questions about the nerves. Do you have any weakness in the leg?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): No weakness. It has never given way on me or anything.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about your balance? Have you had any falls lately?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't fallen. I'm steady enough, thanks.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last of the nerve questions. Any trouble with your bladder or bowels?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, those are the ones I worry about most. Do you have any other health conditions?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Type 2 diabetes. Diet only so far, the GP keeps an eye on it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does anybody else in the family have diabetes?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): My father did. He had diabetes for years before he passed.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for telling me. Do you smoke?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): About ten cigarettes a day. I know, I know.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to nag, your daughter has that covered. What about alcohol?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of pints on a Saturday at the club. That's my lot.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair. And are you taking any tablets at the moment?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Not a thing. I keep away from them where I can.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): None that I know of.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'm going to check your blood pressure and pulse, then test the feeling in your feet.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Is this going to hurt?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Blood pressure is 136 over 84, and your pulse is 72.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pretty reasonable. Now close your eyes and say yes each time you feel this wisp of cotton wool touch your foot.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Yes. Hang on. Was that the toes? I couldn't tell.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. The feeling is reduced in the toes of your left foot, compared with the right.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. Well. Is it serious?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me explain it plainly. Nerves are like electrical cables, and years of high sugar can wear away the insulation, so the signal gets fuzzy. It looks like early nerve damage from the diabetes.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Can it be fixed?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can be slowed down a lot. Step one is bloods. I'd like to order blood tests, for your sugar control and your vitamin B12, since a low B12 can do something similar.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Today?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take them on your way out. Then I'd like to see you in two weeks, to go through the results together.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Right. I'll bring my daughter, she'll want to hear it for herself.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please do. And look after those feet in the meantime. Check them every evening, and wear slippers indoors.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care, Desmond. Give the dog my regards.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two and three weeks, then. We'll call it that and not argue over the calendar.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now, have you been unusually thirsty, or getting up in the night to pass water?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I'm not up in the night at all, and I'm not thirsty any more than usual.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that's reassuring. While we're chatting I'll read out your numbers from today.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 132 over 84, which is fine, just a touch on the upper side. And you're 86 kilograms on the scales.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the weight a problem? I've put on a few kilos this year, I know, I know.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I just want to know what we can do at home, doctor. He won't stop fretting and it's wearing both of us out.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's exactly the right question. From what we have so far, this looks like pre-diabetes, and it's been caught early, which is the best time to catch it.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Early. So it can go back to normal?
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): For many people, yes. Steady changes make the biggest difference. Walking for thirty minutes most days, and swapping sugary drinks for water. Nothing drastic.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Thirty minutes, I can do that. Do I need tablets for it?
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at this stage. Let's see what the small changes do first.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): And if I get it wrong? Slip up on a weekend or something?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then you carry on Monday. One weekend doesn't undo anything. It's what happens over months that counts.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll walk with him in the evenings. Gives me an excuse to get out of the house anyway.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely, that's a team effort. Now, I'd like to see you again in three months so we can see how things are travelling.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Three months. Right. Should I book that at the front?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the girls at the front desk will sort a time on your way out.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. Sorry again about being late, I'm a bit of a flustered mess today.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): You've done well to ask your questions. Go easy on yourself, and on the internet.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Come on, love, let's find that car and have a walk down to the shops.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Righto. Cheers, doctor.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A little peach one. I quit it a while back, on my own.

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, Mr Gallagher. The booking note says 'contact of a TB case, wants checking'. Is that why you're here today?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): It is, aye. My daughter made the appointment. I said I was grand, but she wouldn't hear it.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good for her. Tell me what happened, from the start.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): My father was diagnosed with TB last month. They told us in the hospital, and the nurse there said the family should all get looked at.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): That must have been a shock. How is he doing, if you don't mind my asking?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): He's on the tablets now, and he's in good form. Giving out about the hospital food, so he must be better.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, always a good sign. And how about you? Have you noticed anything yourself, anything at all?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It's nothing really. I've a bit of a cough, that's all.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): A bit of a cough. How long have you had it?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, I'd say. It's a dry sort of thing, and it's worse first thing in the morning.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it a dry cough every time, or do you bring anything up?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Dry, mostly, it just tickles.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Anything else? Even something you think is silly.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): My voice has gone a bit hoarse, since Monday. The wife says I sound like a corncrake.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): A corncrake, lovely. Is that the only thing?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a bit tired in the afternoons, but sure, I'm not twenty any more.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Tired in the afternoons, is that new, or has it been like that for a while?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): It's been the past week or so. Maybe it's the early mornings with the lad's football.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe so. Have you had any coughing up blood?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Not a spot.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you. Let me ask about your general health. Do you have any conditions I should know about?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): I've an underactive thyroid, years now, and a bit of eczema on my hands. That's the lot of it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): And for the thyroid, what do you take, and how much? Do you know the dose?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Levothyroxine, every morning. Maybe 75 micrograms? Or is it 100? I can't mind, to tell you the truth. The chemist fills the little box for me.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's grand. We can check it on the system later. Any operations in the past?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): My appendix out, when I was fifteen. A summer I'll never forget, I missed the whole of the county final.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, a hard price. Now, I'm curious about something. Your father was diagnosed, and you've seen him recently. How much time would you spend with him each week?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, every Sunday for dinner, a couple of hours. And I'd drop in on Wednesdays. But since the diagnosis I've stayed away, only the phone.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sensible. Well, before I examine you, can I have the nurse give me the numbers she took earlier?
[SEG0030] person_3 (NURSE): Of course, doctor. Blood pressure is 124/80, pulse 78 bpm, temperature 36.9 °C, oxygen saturation 98 %, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Ahhhh.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your throat looks a little red at the back, nothing dramatic. Now take some deep breaths in and out while I listen.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your chest is clear all over, no crackles, no wheeze, and the air is going in well on both sides.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): So I'll live, is that it?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think you'll live for a good while yet. What I think is going on, and it is only my working view, is a post-viral cough, a lingering cough after a cold, with the hoarse voice that goes with it.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): A cold? I never even had a cold. Well, the lad had one a few weeks back.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): That would fit. Colds are often passed round the house, and the cough can hang on for weeks after the cold itself has gone.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): And the TB? Does it rule it out?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't want you to feel I'm dismissing your father's illness, and being close to him was the right reason to come in. I'd just say that nothing I found today alarms me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, I can tell you. The wife has been at me. Is there anything I should do for the cough itself?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Plenty of warm fluids, honey and lemon is as good as anything, and rest your voice. Don't whisper, mind, because whispering strains it more than talking softly.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if you ever start to cough up blood, or you get fevers and sweats at night, ring the surgery that day, don't wait.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I will, yes. I'd not wait with something like that.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks, to see how the cough and the voice are getting on. The desk will give you a time.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, grand. Will I tell the daughter?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell her she did the right thing, and that she's earned a cup of tea off you.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): She'll be delighted. Thanks, doctor, thanks, nurse.
[SEG0048] person_3 (NURSE): Mind yourself, Mr Gallagher. Mind the puddle at the door.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a second, it just kicked me back to the login screen. Okay. You're in for the repeats, but say again what you wanted. I only half caught it at the door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The repeats, yes, but the real reason is my right knee. It's a deep ache, worse on the stairs, stiff for about twenty minutes every morning, and I wake at night to shift it. Walking the dog loosens it, and a bag of ice helps a little. I came hoping you might give me something stronger than what I'm already on.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee. How long has it been like that? One more time, I was in the wrong chart.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I almost said three months. No, scratch that, it's been five months, since around the new year, because I remember not being able to kneel down and fix the cabinet hinge in the kitchen.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five months. Any swelling, or does it give out under you?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, and it doesn't give out. My wife looks at it every night like she's going to find something, and there's never anything puffy. I keep telling her she's worrying over a knee that's just loud and sore.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pharmacy list is up whenever you want the doses. I can't print it, the printer's jammed again, so we'll just read off the screen.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. What are you actually taking for the knee? Go slow, this page keeps jumping.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen, five hundred milligrams, one tablet twice a day, by mouth, with food, for the knee. Breakfast and dinner. I don't skip that one, I even set the bottle by the coffee maker so I see it.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): What I have on the pharmacy list is naproxen two hundred fifty milligrams twice a day. Not five hundred.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): That doesn't match the bottle in my cabinet. I read it this morning, orange label, five hundred milligrams, sitting right next to the coffee. I've been looking at that bottle for months.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't, uh, don't re-litigate it while the chart's frozen. We'll leave the naproxen exactly as it is. No dose change from me today.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still using Tylenol with it? Say the strength, I don't trust what I half typed.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Five hundred milligrams, no, sorry, I always mix that up with the regular extra strength. They're the eight-hour arthritis ones, six hundred and fifty milligrams, two tablets three times a day when the knee is bad, by mouth. On a quiet yard day I might not take any.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two of the six-fifty, up to three times, only when it's bad. And the stomach pill? I just typed twenty by mistake, ignore that. What do you take?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams, no, that's the old dose. It's forty milligrams of omeprazole every morning, by mouth, for my stomach, because of the naproxen. You raised it a while back and I tossed the twenty bottle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every morning, though? You actually get it in every morning?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. If I'm rushing out to the hardware store I skip it, so don't put down that I'm perfect with it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Sort of noted. Blood pressure pill still the same? Repeat it, I lost the line.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, every morning, by mouth, for my blood pressure. I don't miss that one. The pressure problem's been going on for years, and I line that pill up before the omeprazole, ironically.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Lisinopril ten daily matches our list. Omeprazole forty matches too. Naproxen is the only one that doesn't.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies? The alert bar still isn't loading, so I have to ask out loud.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Penicillin was fine when I had that tooth, and there's nothing else.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The tooth was a whole picnic disaster, temporary crown popped off into the potato salad at my nephew's graduation, everybody staring, but that is not why I came and I should stop.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, skip the potato salad. What stronger medicine were you picturing, exactly?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Hydrocodone, the Norco my neighbor has, five-three-twenty-five. Just a small number for the nights and the stairs, not to take every day. He says they wipe out his back pain, and his back sounds worse than my knee, so I thought a few wouldn't be crazy.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. I'm not prescribing hydrocodone. This still sounds like your knee osteoarthritis acting up, and a narcotic isn't the right tool, especially with those Norco tablets also carrying acetaminophen while you're already on Tylenol.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I figured you'd say no. They told me osteoarthritis after the arthroscopy, that was twenty nineteen, they trimmed the meniscus in the right knee. So that diagnosis is already on the books, it's not something new I made up today.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, the old scope. I'm not ordering an x-ray. Nothing you're describing sounds like a fresh injury.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any burning in the stomach, or black stools, on the naproxen?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning, and no black stools. I check, which is probably more information than you wanted about my bathroom. The ice I do with a bag of frozen peas most evenings after the dog.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the ice after the longer walks. Don't put any other anti-inflammatory on top of the naproxen, no drugstore ibuprofen. Stay with the Tylenol the way you said, two of the six-fifty when the knee is bad, and don't go past that in a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't buy ibuprofen, and I won't take the neighbor's Norco even if he offers it out of that kitchen drawer. That's his mess. I'll stick to the peas and the pills you already know about.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I'll renew the lisinopril ten milligrams and the omeprazole forty milligrams the way they are. I'm not touching the naproxen until your bottle and that list say the same strength.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can leave a note for the pharmacist that naproxen needs a strength check, two fifty on our list versus five hundred on his bottle. I won't rewrite the label myself.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, leave that note. Come back in six weeks for another med check. If the knee suddenly locks or swells up hard before then, don't wait it out, call us.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, I can do that. I'll bring the actual naproxen bottle so nobody has to argue from memory, and I'll keep walking the dog, just slower on the way back up the hill.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bottle, yes, that'll help. I have to reboot this machine before the next chart. We're finished for today.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll walk you toward the pharmacy window and drop that note in. Watch the mat by the door, it's curled up.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Appreciate it. If the computer eats the renewals, I'll call, but I think I followed everything, even the part where I don't get the stronger pills.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, it was pouring. Sorry, doctor, to come back to your question, I do not take alcohol.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, please book the ECG. I am ordering thyroid tests as well, TSH and free T4.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and no weight loss. My motions are normal, doctor.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Until the reports are back, stop the energy drinks completely, cut coffee to one cup a day, and stop the vaping. If the palpitation starts, breathe in for four counts and out for six. Please practise that twice a day also, not only in the moment.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I will follow your advice, doctor. Giving up the vape before meetings will be difficult, but I will try.
[SEG0051] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shall we come back once the reports are there?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Come for a review in two or three days, when the ECG and the thyroid results are ready. Please ask reception to book it on the way out.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I quit smoking around ten years ago. Nothing, I'm teetotal. I'm a plumber, lots of bending and kneeling. I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day. I hardly move around during the day.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Not to my knowledge, no.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy? These questions might sound routine, but they matter.

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): About two months.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in your past medical history I should know?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I have an irregular heartbeat.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been any bleeding?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No bleeding.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath, vomiting or confusion?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no shortness of breath, vomiting or confusion.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your chest okay generally?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): No problems with breathing.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, any pins and needles or loss of strength anywhere?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, no weakness or anything.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note down your vital signs first.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit still for a moment...
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: temperature 36.9, heart rate 65, pressure 125 over 72.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll interpret them after the examination.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll need to examine you for this, it won't take long.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathe out slowly.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft and you look comfortable and thin.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, thank you, you can get dressed. Taking everything into account, I'd lean towards cancer pain needing better control. I'd also keep opioid-induced constipation in mind.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it dangerous, doctor?

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you smoke, this is a good moment to think about stopping, and we can help you with that. I think the palliative care team should see you too.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure, where do I go?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll want another look in one week. Alright, I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I do apologise for taking up your time, but I have been left with sore ribs since a dreadful bout last week.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning. No need to apologise. Which side is it, and when exactly did it start?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The right side, low down towards the back. It began one week ago, quite suddenly, in the middle of a coughing fit.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Does anything make it worse?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, when I cough, and also a deep breath. Laughing is rather out of the question at the moment.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it a sharp pain or more of an ache?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Sharp, I would say, but only at those moments. In between it is a dull soreness. Moderate overall, though it does keep me awake if I roll onto that side.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Are you coughing up any blood?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that, thank goodness.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And are you short of breath at rest, or going upstairs?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not at all. My breathing seems perfectly all right, it is only the pain that catches me.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you taken anything for it?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't, I am afraid. I am not fond of tablets. I only take amlodipine, 5 mg every morning, and I have not changed that.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine, carry on with that. Any allergies I should write down before we go further?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none that I am aware of. I have never had a reaction to anything.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Have you had any operations in the past?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the one. I had my appendix removed about twelve years ago, and it all went smoothly.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. And do you smoke, or have you ever?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up smoking in my fifties. It was the best decision I ever made, if I may say so.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Well done. Right, I'll take a few readings so I have a baseline.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your pulse is 76 beats per minute, and your oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that satisfactory?
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfectly. Temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius too. So nothing there that worries me.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): That is a relief. My daughter was convinced I had done something terrible to myself.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me lay out the options. We can wait and see, we can get a picture, or we can do both. I'd like to arrange a chest X-ray today.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Would that be necessary? I should not like to waste anyone's resources.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's not a waste. After a hard cough, a picture settles the question, and then we can plan properly.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): In that case, certainly. Where do I go for it?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Radiology is down the corridor on the left. Reception will give you a form, and it's usually quick.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Splendid. And in the meantime, is there anything I ought to be doing?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Hug a pillow against your side when you cough, and keep walking gently. Resting completely tends to make it stiffer.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): A pillow. I would not have thought of that.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try short, shallow breaths first, then build up to a few slow deep ones every hour or so.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Every hour, understood. Shall I come back to see you afterwards?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, let's see you again in two weeks, and we'll go over how it's settling and what the picture showed.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): In two weeks. I shall ask the receptionist to book it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good idea. She'll find a slot for you on your way out.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the pain gets worse before then?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ring the surgery straight away. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): I will not. Thank you very much indeed, Doctor.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind the corridor floor, it's just been washed.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you. Goodbye.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. I'm here because my partner says I've got a temper, and I need to sort it. I don't want to lose my job.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for coming. Tell me what's been happening.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I get short with people. At work, at home. Small things, someone leaves a door open, and I blow. I shout. Then I feel terrible.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): A year? Maybe longer. I can't say when it started. It got worse after Christmas.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything changed in your life? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): A new boss. A new baby, eight months ago. I'm not sleeping, and money's tight. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your sleep?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Four hours a night, broken.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No, I'd never. Not anyone.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Propranolol, 10 mg, when I feel wound up, but not sure it does anything. Something for my stomach, omeprazole, 20 mg. And I take St John's wort, maybe 300 mg, a day.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I need to stop you there, because St John's wort interacts with a lot of drugs. So it's 300 mg, as you recall it. Any other conditions?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Acid reflux. That's all.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink, or use any substances?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): A few beers at night, to switch off. Four, five. And lots of coffee.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what do you do for exercise, or to relax?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing. No time.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 84, blood pressure 138 over 88.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that okay? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Slightly raised, which fits with stress and the alcohol. Any breathlessness, chest pain?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Putting this together, irritability and outbursts for a year, poor sleep, a new baby, work stress and heavy-ish drinking, I'd say this is stress-related irritability, probably with sleep deprivation and alcohol feeding it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all? I thought I might be bipolar or something. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing you've described points that way. But I'd like to check your thyroid and a few other things, because they can cause irritability.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cut the beer to a couple of units, not every night, and stop the St John's wort, it can interact with other things. Cut the coffee after midday.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like you to try a short anger-management course, and talking therapy.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Will that help? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): It does, for most. I'd like to see you again in three weeks.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Thanks. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Have a seat, both of you. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I have had headaches for many years, but the pattern has altered, and I felt I should come in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Altered in what way?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They are worse in the morning. I wake with the pain, and on some mornings I have vomited, which is quite new.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was coming to the tablets, but it can wait. The vomiting, as I said, did not happen with the old headaches.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the original headaches been with you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-ish years. I was told they were migraines, though I could not name the precise year I was given that label.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And this morning pattern — can you put a time on when it changed?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid I cannot. Last winter, or perhaps the winter before that. It crept in, and I never marked the date.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll leave the date open. Before the pain, do you get lights, or a warning—
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he snores. Terribly. And he's wrecked in the daytime, asleep in the chair after tea.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore, and I am not especially tired. With respect, it is the headaches I have come about.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted, and we'll park that disagreement. Back to what I asked — any flashing lights or a visual warning nowadays?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no flashing lights. Not with these. The older headaches sometimes had a little shimmer, but that has gone.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any neck stiffness, weakness in an arm or a leg, or a fit?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness, and I have never had a fit. My neck is not stiff.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does look dreadful some mornings, just before he's sick.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is the vomiting?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Perhaps two mornings in a week. Not daily. I had started to say, about the medicine, that lately it is less—
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He lives on those tablets.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Less what? Finish that thought for me.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Less reliable, I was going to say. I take sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, by mouth, when a migraine starts. And paracetamol, a thousand milligrams, rather often.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the hundred milligram sumatriptan, I've seen the packet. And the Panadol is every single morning, two tablets, before he's even dressed.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, but the sumatriptan is fifty milligrams. I do sometimes take a second tablet if the first has not worked, which I know was not what was intended.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. I'm hearing fifty from you and a hundred from your partner, so I'm not going to invent a dose. Bring the box and we'll settle it. The second tablet means you're not really on the plan you were given.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That is fair. I take nothing else. I do not smoke, and I drink very little — a glass of wine at the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We nearly turned around, you know. The Monash was a car park from Chadstone out.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): It was grim this morning, wasn't it. I only saw the tail of the cricket. Did you catch it?
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most of it. The batter was poking about for an hour and then he middled one, straight to deep midwicket, and the catch stuck. I nearly spilt my tea.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not a cricket person, I confess, but the delay was extraordinary. We were sitting near the exit for an age, watching the weather come in.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Proper Melbourne grey. Anyway, we've used up your time on the freeway and the cricket. Sorry, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. Let me get a blood pressure and do a quick nerve check while I think this through.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-six over eighty-four, and your pulse is seventy-six. Pupils are equal and reacting, no facial droop. Power is full in the arms and legs, reflexes are brisk and even, and your gait is steady. I'm not seeing any focal signs.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm turning it over as I go. The long story still fits migraine best, but a new morning headache with vomiting — I can't rule out raised pressure inside the head. And if the snoring your partner describes is real, sleep apnoea could be adding to the tiredness, though you've set that aside.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I would rather we did not make too much of the snoring. I sleep perfectly well, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. You two don't agree, and I won't force it. I don't scan every migraine, but if the morning headaches and the vomiting haven't settled in a fortnight, I would like a CT of the head.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should he knock the sumatriptan off until then?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it cold if a bad migraine hits, but skip that second dose, and ease the paracetamol back — more than a couple of days a week can feed the headache. I suspect medication overuse is part of this picture.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I shall keep the paracetamol for genuine need only.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any brain tumours or aneurysms in the family, or migraines?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had migraines. No tumours that I know of.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in a fortnight either way, and if it hasn't eased we'll book that scan then. If you get a sudden thunderclap headache, new weakness, or you can't keep fluids down, go to emergency rather than waiting.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall do exactly that. I am grateful you explained your reasoning.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the sumatriptan box next time so you can read the strength yourself. And I'll get him here, freeway or not.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would help a lot. We'll sort the dose off the packet. Mind how you go.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I woke up on Tuesday with a stiff neck, and it's not eased. I suspect I slept on it badly.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you any numbness or pins and needles in your arm or hand?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing in the arm. It's only the neck and a little into the shoulder.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any injury before, a fall, a car accident, lifting something heavy? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I did spend the night on my friend's sofa, which has a pillow like a brick. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, the sofa. That tends to be the culprit. ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I did think so. Is it serious? ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Almost never. Let me check you over to be sure. Temperature first. ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature 36.6, pulse 70.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now I'm going to see how far your neck moves, so tell me where it pinches. Look left.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): That's fine. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now over your right shoulder. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow. That's it. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, no fever and no worrying signs. This is a muscle strain from the awkward position. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): How long will it take to settle? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually three to seven days. It should be a bit better each day. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I rest it? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not completely. Gentle movement is better than keeping still. A warm pack on the muscle for twenty minutes helps.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I have a wheat bag. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Use one pillow that keeps your neck level, not two. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll get rid of the brick. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care with sudden movements, and avoid carrying a heavy bag on that shoulder. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): And should I come back? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only if it's still bad after a week, or if you get weakness or numbness in the arm, a fever, or a severe headache.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thank you. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hope the neck loosens up. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): G'day, doc. Bloody nuisance, this, I'm up four times a night for a pee, and my wife's had enough, she's moved to the spare room, and the dog's been sick too, we had to take him to the vet on Monday...
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry to hear about the dog. Four times a night. How long's that been going on?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Six months, mate, give or take. Started with two times, now it's four.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when you're at the toilet, how's the flow?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Weak. Slow to start, and then it dribbles. I stand there like a statue.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything after you've finished?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, dribbling after. Down the leg, embarrassing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any burning when you go?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No burning.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No blood, I've checked. Well, I think I've checked. No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you thirsty all the time?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah, not really.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Back pain?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No back pain. That's the one thing that's fine.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, 5 mg, once a day. I take it every day, religiously. Well. Except when I'm out on the boat, then I forget it for a couple of days.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So not quite every day. Allergies?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Bactrim. I react to it, but don't ask me how, I can't remember what it did.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Conditions?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, gout, and kidney stones, years back.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Kidney stone removed, in 2009. Hernia, in 2015.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Dad had prostate cancer. My brother has diabetes.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Retired farmer. Still go out to the sheds every day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drink?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Four beers, Friday and Saturday.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your numbers. Pulse 70, blood pressure 144 over 88, temperature 36.7, oxygen 98 percent, breathing 14, weight 92 kilos.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Bit high, eh? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): A little. Hop on the bed. I'm feeling your tummy.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Cold hands. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your abdomen is soft, and I can't feel your bladder, so you're emptying it reasonably.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Reasonably? ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm also going to do a rectal exam. It's quick.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, here we go. ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): The prostate is smooth, but enlarged.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Is that why? ~
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): And there's no swelling in your ankles. Any trouble breathing, mate?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, my breathing's fine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): An enlarged prostate fits, but I can't rule out diabetes or kidney trouble yet.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it cancer? ~
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): It could be nothing. I'd like to arrange a PSA blood test, and an ultrasound scan of your bladder and kidneys.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): When? ~
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): This week. And I'd like to start tamsulosin, 400 micrograms, once a day.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it stop the toilet trips? ~
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): It should help. Cut the beer after dinner, too.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, that's the hard part. ~
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Cheers, doc. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, grab a seat. Sorry about the wait — we've been flat out this arvo.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): That's alright. Um, I don't know, doctor, I feel a bit silly coming in. I've just been so tired.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. How long's it been?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. Six months? Maybe longer, I can't pin the start. I figured it was work — I'm a project manager, desk all day, deadlines are brutal. And I'm fifty-two, so maybe it's just age.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could be either. Is it that you can't get going, or you're wrecked after the day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, sort of. I sleep heaps, nine hours easy, and I still wake up tired. It's not that I can't get to sleep.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feeling cold as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I blamed the office aircon. Well, actually it's at home too, even with the doona on. A few months.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your weight?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I've put on that much.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes fitting the same?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. Jeans are two sizes up, so yes I have. Five or six kilos. I don't know exactly — I gave up on the scales.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the bowels?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Constipated, honestly. Maybe three times a week, and it used to be every morning. No blood in the stool.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain with that?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain really. Just slow, hard to get going. Sorry, that's grim.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your mood sitting in all this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I don't enjoy the footy or dinner with my sister like I did. I pinned it on work being hectic. I don't know if I'm depressed, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you taken anything for the bowels, or for your mood?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Coloxyl, from the chemist. One tablet a day for about a week, then I stopped because it didn't do much. Nothing for mood. I never have.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Tired, cold, weight up, sluggish bowels, low mood — that pattern can be an underactive thyroid. Any thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had it. Underactive, I think. She was on tablets for years. She died a few years back, so I don't know the fine detail.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And has your own thyroid been checked?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Years ago, yeah. The old GP did a blood test and they said it was borderline. I never followed it up. I don't know the number, and I couldn't say when it was.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so we've got 'borderline' as you remember it, not a number I can rely on. Has anyone ever actually diagnosed you with a thyroid condition?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I'm pretty well apart from this. Oh, random one — I reckon the parking meter's about to run out.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your skin and hair?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Skin's a bit dry. Hair, I don't know, doctor. Maybe there's more in the brush. I'm not sure, so I wouldn't trust that.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put down the dry skin and leave the hair. On examination the thyroid isn't enlarged, there's no lump, the heart sounds are fine, and your ankles aren't swollen.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So is this just age? I don't know, doctor. I had a coffee on the way, if you're doing bloods — do I need to fast?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fast, the coffee's fine. I'm not calling it hypothyroidism today. The working idea is an underactive thyroid, given the symptoms and your mum, but burning out at work stays on the list. I won't start thyroxine on a guess.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I just want to feel like myself again.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll order a thyroid function test and a full blood count today. If those thyroid numbers are out of whack and this hasn't settled, we might do an ultrasound of the thyroid — I am not booking that now.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And the, um, not going to the toilet. Anything I should do meanwhile?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep your fluids up and add some fibre, pears or oats. If your mood drops hard, or you can't get out of bed, come back sooner or ring the clinic, don't sit on it. Otherwise let's see you in a couple of weeks once the results are in — reception can book that as you leave.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so high cholesterol and high blood pressure are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. What operations have you had, if any?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had a wisdom tooth extraction under sedation, five years ago.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin, 20 milligrams, maybe, at night.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you happen to bring the box or the paperwork?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, um, not with me. I'll bring it next time. Ramipril. I take it 5 milligrams, every morning.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's what's prescribed, but I'm not sure she takes it every day.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Neurologically, anything strange?

[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that normal?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll look at it together shortly.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, over here please and I'll take a look.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hold that for a second.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can feel a couple of small glands in your neck, not tender.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, no problem.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hold that for a second.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft and I can't feel any lumps.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me. So where does that leave us? The most likely explanation is an unexplained weight loss that needs a proper work-up. I can't rule out a chronic infection yet.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): What are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's an unexplained weight loss that needs a proper work-up, and we'll know more once the a chest X-ray is back. Stop me if I've got anything wrong. You've had no real appetite for nearly five years, and no itching or blood in the stool.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): That's it, yes.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): We should do a chest X-ray for cough and weight loss. I'd like to arrange blood tests for weight loss.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I need to prepare?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weigh yourself once a week at the same time and note it down. We'll refer you to the chest clinic.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): So, sure, where do I go?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, will do.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the symptoms get worse, or you feel really unwell, please come to the emergency department.
[SEG0056] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, yes, I'll bear that in mind.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): Good, thanks, I'll see you then.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): See you soon.

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take the purple inhaler properly, twice every day, not three days a week. Keep the blue one for when you are breathless or wheezy. And I would like to refer you to the smoking cessation service, if you are willing.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): I would be grateful for that help. I know I ought to stop.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange a chest x-ray as well, with the smoking history and the recent infection.
