[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning. It's these patches. Itchy ones, on my elbows and knees. I've had them a few months.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me more about them. What do they look like?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Red, with a silvery flaky bit on top. They look daft.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do they flake a lot?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Aye, I find bits in the bed. And they itch like mad, mainly at night.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had anything like it before? ~
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. First time. ~
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any changes to your nails, pitting, ridges, anything?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nails are fine.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And are your joints okay, any pain or stiffness, especially in the morning?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Joints are fine.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What work do you do?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a scaffolder. I'm outdoors most days, and gloves and knee pads, so the knees are rubbed a lot.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): That could be making them sorer. Let me have a look. Roll up your sleeve, and your trouser leg.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): There you go. ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm not going to put a label on it today. I'd like to treat them first and see how they respond. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Fair enough. What's the treatment? ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to start you on a steroid cream, betamethasone, apply it to the patches once a day for two weeks, thinly.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Just to the patches? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just the patches, nowhere else. Wash your hands afterwards. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Does it stop the itch? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): It usually does within a few days. And I'd like to arrange a skin scraping from one patch, to make sure it's not a fungal infection.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): A scraping? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): A tiny bit of the flaky skin, painless. I'll do it now. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on then.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Done. You'll hear if anything shows. Moisturise every day, with a plain thick cream, even when they're better.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm not much for creams. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It makes a big difference. Try it for a fortnight. ~
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And if it doesn't work? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then come back and we'll think again. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon. Have a seat. What's the problem?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my stomach, and I'm not sleeping, and I'm knackered the next day. They feed each other, really, the pain stops me sleeping and then I'm useless. I'm a bookkeeper, and I've been leaving the office early when it flares, which isn't like me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where is the pain?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Upper tummy, dead centre, just under the breastbone. It comes in bouts, especially late afternoon, a dull ache that sometimes burns, moderate rather than doubling-over. A big meal or coffee makes it worse, and a snack doesn't settle it. I wondered about my gallbladder, a colleague had hers out, but it's not off to the side.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't date it. Since Diwali or after, maybe. My neighbour had everyone round, there was so much food, and I remember pressing on my stomach in her kitchen, though it might have started before that.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Constant, or in bouts?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Bouts. It goes quiet, then it's back, especially late afternoon. I'm usually on the spreadsheets then, which is probably irrelevant, sorry.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I feel a bit sick now and then, queasy, but I haven't actually been sick. No blood either, not that there's anything to bring up.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Black stools, or blood in the stool?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Once a day, brown, formed, nothing dramatic. Sorry, that's a lot of detail about something very ordinary.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lost any weight?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. My clothes fit the same, and I was about eleven stone at Christmas and I'm still there.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No temperature, and I haven't felt hot or shivery. I've still got a thermometer from covid in the drawer, unused, which says it all.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sleep?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I drop off, then I'm awake around two or three, maybe four hours altogether. I was going to say weeks, well actually it's longer than the stomach, last winter or the one before, I can't date it. Sometimes the burning wakes me, other nights I'm awake first and then I notice the tummy. I lie there scrolling about ulcers, which is stupid, I know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, acid coming up?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, if I lie flat. Two pillows help a bit, and if I slide down in the night it comes straight back. I've started sleeping almost sitting up, which plays havoc with my neck, but that's another story.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Breathless?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not breathless. My uncle had a heart attack in his fifties, so I did panic one evening, but it doesn't go into my arm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Trouble swallowing?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, food goes down fine. I had a scratchy throat for a week in the autumn, a cold, long gone, my nephew had the same thing.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ulcers or bowel cancer in the family?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had a stomach ulcer years ago, on tablets for ages. No bowel cancer, not that anyone's mentioned.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. One cigarette at a party when I was sixteen, I coughed for an hour, and that was that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Socially. An odd glass with friends, that sort of thing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much in a week?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, if I'm straight about it, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I open it while the pasta's on and it just goes. Socially was me making it sound better than it is.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines, including from the chemist?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two tablets, when the ache is annoying, not every day. Ibuprofen as well when it's properly bad. My sister bought me vitamin D, but I don't really take that.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength of ibuprofen, and how often?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The four hundred milligram ones, just one. Maybe three times a week. I take it with a biscuit, which I suspect isn't how you're meant to.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. Penicillin was fine when I had it for a tooth a few years ago.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty-two. Only one. It might have been keyhole or a proper cut, I was too groggy to take it in, just a small scar on the right.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diabetes? Blood pressure?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Blood pressure's been fine at the chemist. I do get migraines, have done for years, though not in the last few months.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lie back. I'll examine your abdomen.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft. Tender in the epigastrium. No guarding, and no masses.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's the exact spot, sorry I flinched. It's sore if I press it myself in the shower as well.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could be acid, could be the ibuprofen irritating the lining, could be the wine. I'm not calling it an ulcer today, and I'm not saying it's your liver. Let's see what the tests say.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're thinking it's just indigestion?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working impression is gastritis, and that's provisional. The poor sleep might be the pain or it might be the alcohol, and I won't split those today.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll start omeprazole, twenty milligrams, once every morning before breakfast, for four weeks. Stop the ibuprofen. Paracetamol is all right if you need something for the pain.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that clash with anything? I read it can thin your bones if you stay on it for years, and I got myself in a state about that at two in the morning.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four weeks isn't years, and we'll look again when the bloods are back. No lecture on the wine. Cut it to a couple of glasses a week, not a bottle a night, and don't eat for three hours before bed.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bloods today, liver function, a full blood count, and a coeliac screen. Come back in two weeks for the results. If you vomit blood, pass black stool, or the pain turns severe, come back sooner.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, one minute, this screen has frozen again. Right, it is moving. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, I am feeling very tired only. From many months it is there, but from exactly when, I don't know.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tiredness. For how long? Please say that again, I was looking at the monitor.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe since Diwali, or after. Or last winter, or the one before. I cannot fix a date.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So some months, start date unclear. The old notes are not opening. What else?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel cold also. My husband says the room is warm, and still I am sitting with a shawl. At the showroom I keep the cardigan on the whole day.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the cardigan part. You feel cold the whole day, is that what you said?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Whole day, mostly. Others in the office are comfortable only.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It has gone up, I think. My salwar is tight at the waist. How many kilos I don't know, doctor. I did not check.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the bowels, are they daily?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Every two days... well, actually every second or third day. Stool is hard, and I have to strain.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every second or third day, hard, with straining. I want to be sure I heard that over the fan. Has that been for the same period?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I think the same time as the tiredness. But I don't know, doctor. I cannot say which month.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): How is the mood?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Low only, not crying-crying, but no interest to do anything. I am putting it on the work and my age, and I am forty-eight. What else can it be, doctor? I don't know.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forty-eight. What work is that? One second, I have to clear this pop-up.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Accounts, in a garments showroom near the market. Long hours, sitting only. Evening time I am completely finished, I don't feel like cooking also.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): You feel the job and getting older explain the whole thing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, what else, doctor? I don't know. After forty everyone is getting tired, no? My sister was also saying that on the phone, but she is alright, she just likes to talk.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not everyone. Is there thyroid disease in the family? The history page is blank, so I am asking fresh.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had it. Thyroid disease, and she took tablets for many years. Hypo or the other one, I don't know, doctor. They just said thyroid.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mother, thyroid disease, on tablets many years, type unknown. Did you ever have a thyroid test?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Once only, some time back. They said it was borderline. No tablets were started.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you repeat that result? This window just refreshed and I lost the sentence.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Borderline, they said. I don't remember any number, doctor. They said it was borderline and medicine was not needed. I don't have the report.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was that test?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I cannot date it. Last... no, I should not guess. If I say a year it will be wrong only.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will leave the year blank. Are you taking any tablets these days, even for pain or sleep?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. Nothing from the pharmacy. Sometimes jeera water for gas, that is home remedy only, not a medicine.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or breathlessness on walking?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing is normal. I am slow, that is all.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, doctor.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the hair falling more, or the skin newly dry? I should have asked before the screen distracted me.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Hair is the same only. Skin is not more dry than my usual. On the bus I was thinking maybe, but no, it is not.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me feel the front of the neck. Look ahead. Sorry, the glove caught.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): The gland is not enlarged. Your hands are cool. Pulse is regular, I make it about seventy-two a minute.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two is okay, no? I was thinking it would be very slow.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): That rate is acceptable, and it does not settle the question. My working impression is a possible underactive thyroid, but I cannot confirm it without bloods. It may still turn out to be the workload, though the cold and the constipation pull me towards the thyroid.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Underactive, meaning that borderline has become a proper disease? I don't know, doctor. I always thought borderline means it is normal only.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. What they told you is not a figure I can rely on, and it is old. I am arranging a fresh thyroid blood test, TSH and free T4, plus a full blood count for the tiredness.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I do it today? I took tea in the morning, is that a problem? I don't know these rules.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tea is fine, fasting is not needed. Go to the lab downstairs after this, today itself. They will take both.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. The old report, should I search the cupboard? It may be there, it may not. I really don't know.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you find it, bring it when you come back. If not, leave it. And don't settle it in your mind as only age and long hours until we see these results.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): The low feeling also, you are saying that can be the thyroid? Sometimes I think I am just bored of the showroom.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can travel with an underactive thyroid. I am not diagnosing depression in this visit. Come back in two weeks for the results, even if you feel a bit better by then.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, yes. I will go to the lab now. Sorry I was late, the parking on this road is a full headache today.

[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Never an antidepressant. I bought melatonin, three milligrams, and stopped after a week. It did nothing at all.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me reflect this back. [SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes. That is accurate. I apologise for saying I was fine at the outset. I am not fine. It has been difficult to state that formally.
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's more than he's told his brother. I'll take it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): My impression, and I stress it is provisional, is a depressive episode brought on in the setting of the job loss. Low mood, lost interest, poor energy and poor sleep for these months. I do not think we should start medication for it today.

If you ever felt unsafe before that, go to emergency or call Lifeline, thirteen eleven fourteen. You've said those thoughts aren't there, and I want the door left open anyway.
[SEG0042] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. We will return in four weeks, and I shall be direct with you.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I'm terribly sorry I'm late, doctor, I got the wrong day on the calendar, I thought it was Thursday. I mean, it's Thursday, but, oh, never mind. ~
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all, Mr Alderton. We have time. How have you been since I last saw you? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Not great, I'm afraid. The stiffness is worse in the mornings, it takes me an hour to get going, and my right hand shakes.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the stiffness is worse first thing, and the right hand has a tremor. Which hand, again?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The right. Sorry, did I say left? The right.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how's your walking?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Slow. I shuffle. My wife says I'm like a penguin.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any falls?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No falls, no. Wobbles, but I've caught myself.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any hallucinations, seeing things that aren't there?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you on at the moment?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Levodopa, 100 mg, four times a day. The last one's at six, and by seven in the morning I'm worn out.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any allergies?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No allergies, none.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your Parkinson's, remind me when you were diagnosed?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Three years ago. Though I think it started a year before.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And you worked as?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I was a bus driver. Retired now.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check you. Pulse 72, blood pressure 138 over 80, temperature 36.5, oxygen 98 percent, breathing 14, weight 74 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): All right? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): All fine. Hold your arms out in front.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see a tremor in the right hand at rest.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, it's a pill-rolling thing. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when I move your right arm, there's stiffness, a cogwheel catch, but the left is normal.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that bad? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's what we expect. I think the stiffness in the mornings is the levodopa wearing off between doses.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): What can we do? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to start rasagiline, 1 mg, once a day, to smooth things out.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it help the shaking? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): A little. I'd also like to arrange a physiotherapy assessment, and blood tests for your kidney and liver function.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the stiffness isn't better in a month, come back and we'll look at the timing again.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): A month. I'll write it down. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mrs Adeyemi, have a seat. How have you been getting on at home?

[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's not alright. Her ankles have been up like puddings, and she has to stop halfway up the stairs.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Puddings. They're a bit puffy by the evening, that's all. Hardly a crisis.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit puffy by evening, noted. When she says you stop on the stairs, do you get short of breath at all?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I just take my time. I'm not breathless.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is, though. She sits on the stair with her hand on her chest. Most days, going up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I sit because my knees are old, not because I can't get air. You're making a meal of it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. In your own time, when did the puffiness actually start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. Last winter, or the one before. It comes and goes. Not worth pinning down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's been worse these past three weeks, evenings especially. Her shoes won't go on.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are you sleeping? Any waking up gasping, or needing more pillows?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep like a log. One pillow, same as ever. She's the one fussing at night.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does cough a bit once she lies down. Dry, not a chesty one.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Everyone coughs. It's the heating. It's nothing.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest with all this?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. I keep saying I'm fine.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's untangle the tablets, then. The box looks as if it's got away from you. Who fills it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do. I live in. Every Sunday I do the dosette. Morning she's got the water tablet and the heart one, and there's a little white one at night that isn't labelled.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The water one makes me traipse to the loo, so sometimes I don't bother. And that little white one, I couldn't tell you. Might be a vitamin for all I know.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet — do you know its real name and the strength?
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Furosemide, forty milligrams, one in the morning. That's what the chemist box says. There's another blister that looks the same, and I think I've been dropping two in some mornings without meaning to.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't take two. I take one, if I take it. She's counting the same tablet twice, that's the muddle.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it's one furosemide, forty milligrams, not two different water tablets. And the heart one?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Bisoprolol. The packet in the cupboard says two point five milligrams.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, mine's the half. One point two five. The hospital doctor halved it. She's still on the old dose, if you ask me.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't guess the bisoprolol today. I'll want that hospital letter before anyone changes it. Has anything been stopped?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The other doctor stopped the ramipril. Said it was knocking my kidneys about. I don't take it.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril five milligrams. It came out of the box ages ago.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when was that, roughly?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. I haven't a clue, really. Whenever that appointment was.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They did print a simvastatin script once as well, but she never swallowed a single one. I didn't even pick up the repeat.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Cholesterol rubbish. My sister's the one on metformin, for her sugar. She's forever pushing her biotin on me for my hair. I haven't touched it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your sister's metformin and her biotin stay hers. We won't put either on your list. Anything else — inhalers, shop-bought bits?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't go in for all that. Paracetamol now and then, if my head's a bit off. That's the lot.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does have the paracetamol, maybe twice a week. Five hundred milligrams, two tablets. I buy them.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I look at your ankles and have a listen to your chest?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's pitting swelling on both sides, up to the mid-shin. Chest is clear, no crackles. Pulse is seventy-six, blood pressure one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Clear chest. There you are. I told you I was fine.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): A clear chest is reassuring, but that swelling is proper fluid. I think this is most likely your body holding on to fluid, possibly the heart not quite keeping up. I can't be certain until we do a few tests.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to change the water tablet. Furosemide forty milligrams in the morning and again at lunchtime, instead of the single dose. Leave the bisoprolol exactly as it is until I see the letter.
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Morning and lunch, forty each. I'll redo the dosette tonight, and I won't double it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): More time in the loo. Wonderful. If I feel like skipping it, I still might.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd really like you to take both doses while we sort this out. I'll send you for bloods, kidney function and a BNP, and an ECG today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods. I had bloods last winter or whenever. Waste of time.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a waste. It tells me the higher dose is safe for your kidneys. If the swelling hasn't eased in two weeks, we might arrange a heart scan.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there. Do you want her weighed at home?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes please, each morning after the loo, and jot the number down. Ease off the very salty food if you can. Come back and see me in a fortnight with the weights and the results. If she's suddenly much more breathless, or the swelling shoots up before then, don't wait, ring the surgery or 999 if she can't speak in sentences.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, if I must. I'm still not ill.

[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can be, with sugars running high. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Blurring, yes, some days, worse when the sugar is high, then it eases off. No floaters, no curtain. When was I meant to have the eye screening? I think I missed the last one.

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you actually swallow it every day?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The metformin, yes, I don't miss that one. The insulin is where I slip.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): We treat it as not agreed, and I am not changing the pen today. Do you inject every single night?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every night. On shift days — I drive the delivery bakkie, those early starts — I skip the evening dose, I'm scared of going low on the road. Maybe three, four nights a week. Is that why the readings are rubbish?

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that sits heavy. It raises our attention, it doesn't mean you are on the same path. Do you smoke, or take alcohol?

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. What do I actually do about eighteen versus twenty-four? And can I still drive the bakkie, or is that finished?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay on eighteen units at night, the dose you have been taking, until the diabetes sister reconciles the card. Don't jump to twenty-four on your own. Driving is all right if you are not hypo — keep glucose sweets in the bakkie.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the summary. [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit wherever's easiest for the back. You look wrecked, the pair of you. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The back. The lower back. It's been murder, and I'm sick of talking about it already.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's like a briar, doctor, and he's not sleeping. We moved house and he lifted every box himself.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sheila, I can talk. It's been a few weeks. Or since the move. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright. Sheila, when do you think it started?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The move was six weeks ago. He was hunched the night we shifted the couch, and I'd say it's been six weeks solid.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, that is not it. I was grand for a while after the move. This is a couple of weeks, not six. I'm not fighting about a couch.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dates for now. Whereabouts is the pain, and what's it like when it's bad?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Low down, across the belt line. Dull, and then it grabs if I bend. Mornings are desperate.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it go down either leg?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Can we not pick at that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park it. Any numbness, or pins and needles, in the legs or round the groin?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No numbness. The legs feel normal.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks. Any struggle to pass urine, any leaking, or not feeling when the bladder's full?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bladder's the same as ever. That's not why I'm here.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Trousers are a bit slack. Not really, though. I'm just off the dinners.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He picks at his food, but he's not wasting away. Appetite's gone with the pain, that's all.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, night sweats, or shivering?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm tired, not sick-sick. Don't write me down as a temperature.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired since when?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the back got bad. I'm not sleeping on it. I'm wrecked the whole day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's up half the night pacing the kitchen, then into the warehouse for seven. And he's been at the tablets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, warehouse operative. On my feet, lifting all day. They haven't a light duty between them, so don't bother suggesting it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking, and what strength?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen from the chemist. I nearly said the two hundred milligram, but no, it's the four hundred milligram ones. Three times a day.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you get the three doses into you, and are you taking them with food?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly with food. I take them. Well, I miss the odd one, I'm not a robot.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The middle-of-the-day one, he misses that half the time. I've seen the blister pack.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not half the time. The odd one. I'm sat right here, Sheila.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else for the pain?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol as well, for a while. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, four times a day. Stopped them last week. Useless.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Operations in the past, or any long-term illness?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. The same spot in the back gave a twinge five-ish years ago and then it settled. Nothing else ongoing.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking, or drink?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Never did, really. A few pints at the weekend normally. Not this month, I'm too sore and too tired.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's just the two of us in the house. The kids are grown and gone, so it's me keeping an eye.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you're with him. I'm going to press along the low back. Say where it's worst.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): There. Right side. For God's sake, that's enough poking.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): The muscles either side of the low spine are tender, and it's clearly worse on the right. The bone itself isn't sore when I tap it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise is clear on both sides, no pain shooting down. Power and feeling in the feet are normal. You can sit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Finally. If I'm sweating it's from standing, not a fever. I already said that.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. In the chair your blood pressure was one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two, the pulse was seventy-four, and the temperature is thirty-six point six.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't come in about blood pressure. Is the back knackered or not?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pressure's fine. This fits a mechanical strain of the low back from the lifting. That's my working impression, not a final label, until we see how it behaves.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has himself told it's broke. Does he not need a scan, doctor?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I said it feels broke. I did not say it is broke. Give over, the two of you.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think it's broken, and no scan today. If it's not settling in six weeks, we might arrange a plain x-ray of the lumbar spine.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. I've had enough weeks. Brilliant.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay on the ibuprofen, four hundred milligrams three times a day, and take it with food every time. You can add the paracetamol back if you want, one gram four times a day, and don't go over those amounts.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep moving, short walks, and heat is fine if it eases you. Don't stay in the bed all day, and no heavy lifting in the warehouse until this settles. I know that's easier said.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Work will love that. I'm not after a sick cert, I'm not that man. And if I lie down tonight, I'm lying down.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): A lie-down is fine, it's all day in the bed that seizes you up. Come back sooner if the pain shoots hard down a leg, or you go numb, or the bladder changes. If it's not better in a fortnight, book back in with me.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, then. I'm going home. Don't tell me to be positive about it. Thanks, I suppose.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, how are your meals?

[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it clear up?

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the system's just thrown a wobbly again. Give me a second. Right, what's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): So my heart's been doing this weird fluttery thing, and I get proper puffed out with it. We nearly didn't get here, the 49 was rammed and some bloke had a speaker on full blast.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I was on the wrong tab. Say that first bit again?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Palpitations. And I get breathless when they come. Mostly when I'm in bed at night.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Alex, his partner, we live together. It's been frightening at night, he sits bolt upright.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it actually been going on?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks. No, hang on, it was before reading week, so six weeks.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks? The screen just refreshed, I missed that. Six?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, six weeks. Not three.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Six weeks, and it's always worse the night before an exam or one of his Monday meetings.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not stress, though. I don't do stress. My supervisor's just obsessed with Harvard referencing, she docked me marks for a comma, which is ridiculous.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do get wound up. Before every exam and those cafe meetings you're pacing the flat and snapping.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. I just like being ready, that's a completely different thing.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): The breathlessness, does it only come with the fluttering?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the breathlessness comes with the palpitations. These six weeks, night-time's the worst, and it's bad before exams and before the Monday meetings. I do a few cafe shifts on top of the master's, so Mondays are stocktake.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain at all?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain, not even a twinge.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you blacked out, or felt you were about to?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I've never fainted. My mate Keiran went down at a gig in March, dramatic, but that's not me.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't fainted. He just grips the duvet till it passes.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or a temperature?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough and no temperature. I feel alright in myself apart from this.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much caffeine are you getting through?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee, about three cups a day. Actually it's five, if I'm being straight. And energy drinks, two a day, no, three, mostly Monster.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, Teams just pinged. How many energy drinks did you say?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Three a day. And five coffees. It's how I get through the reading, sadly.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, three's fair. The recycling's basically a Monster museum.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke or vape?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. I've been doing it two years. Actually no, six years, I started at eighteen and I'm twenty-four.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any asthma, or problems with your heart before this?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mild asthma. I use the brown inhaler, no, I don't, I never got on with the preventer. It's the blue one, salbutamol, two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He forgets it half the time. I'm not convinced he uses it when he actually needs it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies? Medicines, food, anything?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And medicines, apart from that inhaler? The list on screen looks empty, is that right?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the inhaler day to day. Last year the GP tried bisoprolol, one point two five milligrams, no, it was two point five. I stopped it after a week because I felt completely wiped out.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family history? Heart disease, thyroid, that sort of thing? Sorry, this cursor's jumping.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum's got an underactive thyroid. She's also just bought a cockapoo and it ate the telly remote, which is a whole other saga.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell her about that blood test at uni.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh yeah. Last year the uni GP did thyroid bloods and said they were borderline. They didn't give me any tablets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline what, sorry? I lost the end of that.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They never told me a number. Just borderline, and leave it alone.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while this loads. Pulse is regular, ninety-two. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, no murmur. Blood pressure's one eighteen over seventy-six and your oxygen is ninety-nine percent.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-two bad? My watch shouts at me on the bus sometimes, but I think it just hates hills.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ninety-two resting is fine. I think this is probably palpitations stirred up by the caffeine and the vaping, maybe a few ectopics, but I don't want to miss a thyroid problem or an odd rhythm.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll book a twenty-four hour heart monitor, and I'll send you for thyroid bloods.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): The thing is, each flutter only lasts about twenty seconds, and I've got an exam every single day next week. I can't be wired up for twenty-four hours, I'll rip the pads off in the first hour.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He really won't manage a monitor next week. The exams have him all over the place.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, that changes it. Scrap the twenty-four hour monitor for now. I'll do an ECG instead, and we'll still do the thyroid bloods.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the ECG and the thyroid test are alright and the palpitations haven't settled after your exams, we might arrange a twenty-four hour monitor then.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, try slow breathing when it starts, in for four and out for six, especially at night and before those meetings. And cut the energy drinks and the coffees right down, and ease off the vape if you can.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I did download a yoga app in January. Used it twice. The woman was so calm it annoyed me, which is ironic, ignore me.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks and we'll go through the results. If you get proper chest pain, or you collapse, don't wait on me, go to A&E.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Before you go in, I've the observations done. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse is seventy-six, oxygen saturation ninety-eight percent, and the weight is seventy-two kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two, grand, though that cuff was fierce tight and I'm after a strong mug of tea, so I hope it isn't a false reading. I always feel the pressure jumps when I'm rushing for the bus.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come on in, the two of you. I'm Dr. Brennan. What has you here today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the stomach, Doctor, a burning pain, and the sleep has gone to pieces with it. I could write you a book on the ceiling at three in the morning.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The bad pain, I'd put it at three months. She was eating grand back in the autumn, Sunday dinners and all.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months? The burn sits under the breastbone and goes through to the back, worse after rashers or anything fried, and a sup of milk eases it a little. It's been on me since last winter, or the winter before, and I couldn't put a date on it. The Christmas pudding that year was a pure disaster.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. The burn is under the breastbone after fried food, milk eases it, you place the start at last winter or the winter before and can't date it, and your carer has the bad patch at three months. I won't force a single date. Where exactly is it sitting now, and does it travel?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Top of the belly, and through to the back if I've been bold with the fry, which I already said, I know. Not a stab, more a hot coal, and then I'm burping for an hour, which is lovely in company. People pretend not to hear it and I pretend not to notice them pretending.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting with this?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The dinners have been a saga, if you want the truth. Tuesday was stew and I left the onions out because onions repeat on me something shocking, Thursday was toast and tea, and the wine sits on it, and then I'm awake at two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll park the menu for a second. Have you actually vomited, or brought up any blood?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting, and no blood, thank God. There's a sour taste in the mouth, like, but nothing comes up.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the bowels — any diarrhoea, constipation, or black stools?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The bowels are grand, once a day, ordinary brown, nothing black. I watch the colour because my father had an ulcer, Lord have mercy, and they were forever asking him about it.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has the weight dropped at all?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The clothes fit the same, so I don't think so, though I've not stood on the scales at home. The appetite is up and down — brown bread I'll take, a full dinner I often can't, and then I feel guilty for wasting good food.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many hours are you actually sleeping?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Four hours if I'm lucky, all broken, and it's the pain that wakes me. I say a decade of the rosary and then it's Lyric FM until the heating clicks on. Mad, isn't it, the things you do at that hour.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath, at night or otherwise?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not gasping or anything like that. I get myself into a fuss, sure, but the breathing is grand.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked, not even a puff behind the sheds. The drink is only socially, a glass if there's a do on.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ah now, love, that's the polite version. Tell her about the evenings in the armchair.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, it's a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. Red, nothing posh, just with the telly. I didn't want a lecture, but there it is.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): No lecture, I promise, and thank you for saying it straight. A bottle most nights can irritate the stomach and the liver, so the liver bloods are worth doing. What tablets are you on at the moment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): There's the water tablet, the little white one, for the blood pressure. I think the dose is two and a half milligrams, or maybe five, I never read the box properly. And I use the pink Gaviscon from the chemist when the burn is up, and two paracetamol at night sometimes, more for the head than the belly.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't know the name and neither do I, it's just the water tablet from the surgery, years back. She misses it some mornings if she's rushing — I counted three still in the blister on Thursday.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the blood pressure is ongoing, and the water tablet for it has no name to hand, dose maybe two and a half or five milligrams, with some mornings missed. Gaviscon when it burns, and paracetamol some nights, I've got that. Any drug allergies at all?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not allergic to any tablet I know of.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There was penicillin, years ago. She came out in a rash and they stopped it, though she always says it might not have been that.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I was sixteen or so, it was warm weather, and it could have been a heat rash, I honestly don't know. I've avoided penicillin since, just in case, which is probably daft if it wasn't even the cause.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Were any tests done for the stomach or the liver before this?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods at the surgery, and I couldn't tell you when — last year, or the year before that. The nurse said the liver one was borderline, just a shade high, and they left it, no tablets or anything.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): None for me. My sister had the gallbladder out last spring and I nearly went with her for the company, but no, I've never been under the knife.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She bought those herbal sleep tablets too, the valerian ones, and they went in the drawer.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, valerian, from the chemist, I took them for a few nights and stopped. They did nothing for the sleep and they smelled like old hay, if I'm honest.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hop up on the couch and I'll examine the tummy.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): This couch is always freezing, I'll try not to jump. I tense when it's cold, so don't mind me if I do.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft, tender at the epigastrium, no guarding, and I can't feel any lump. The chest is clear and the heart sounds are fine.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Tender, yes, that's the spot, especially if you press just there. I thought you were going to find a lump the size of a turnip, the way it feels from the inside.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): This sounds like acid irritation of the stomach, a gastritis, likely stirred by the wine. I can't rule out a small ulcer, but there's nothing today that says you're bleeding.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): An ulcer is what took my father, so you'll understand I'm spinning a bit. If it's only the acid I can live with that, once I know which it is.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll start you on omeprazole, twenty milligrams, by mouth, one capsule every morning half an hour before breakfast, and we'll do that for a month at least. Keep the Gaviscon for breakthrough if you need it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Before breakfast, half an hour, I can do that if I put the capsule by the kettle. The Gaviscon I'll leave on the bedside locker so I'm not rooting in the dark and waking the whole landing.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering a liver panel and a full blood count, and I'll see you back here in two weeks to go through them. If the pain hasn't settled by then, we might arrange a gastroscopy, a camera test, but only if we need it. If you vomit blood, or the stools turn black, or the pain gets severe, come straight in and don't wait for me.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And the wine — are you wanting it stopped dead?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): No command to stop dead. Bringing it down from a bottle most nights, even towards a glass, will help the stomach and the liver. I'd skip the fried food, and don't take ibuprofen or aspirin for that pain. Bring the water-tablet box to the next visit so we can name it and fix the dose.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take the liver panel and the full blood count next door now. It won't take long.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Honestly, it's a dull ache on one side of the chest, and my family pushed me to come. I looked a few things up online, and that probably didn't help.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): since when exactly?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): it started yesterday
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it constant or in episodes?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): it comes and goes
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): is it it accompanied by anything?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): it usually comes with weight loss mm, the weight loss? That's been for two weeks
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): before we go further, any allergies?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I have any no
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine work habits that sort of thing.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner. No, I've never smoked in my life. I live with my elderly mother. I swim twice a week
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): right any medical conditions anything you've been treated for?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): no, nothing I can think of
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you take any regular medication?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): no I don't take any tablets
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): any coughing up blood, fever or night sweats?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): no, no coughing up blood, fever or night sweats
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): anything on the skin I should know about?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): skin's normal
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): let me quickly check your readings
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay this won't take long..
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: respiratory rate 20 pulse 98 temp 36.9 degrees SpO2 92 percent on room air blood pressure 129 over 77.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): we'll look at it together shortly
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): shall I start the examination?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): breathe out slowly
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): There is dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the right base.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): all finished, thank you
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): from what you've told me and what I found, I'd lean towards a pleural effusion needing a cause
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): is this serious, doctor?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): it's reasonable to be concerned, but right now a pleural effusion needing a cause is my leading thought, not anything worse i think a pleural fluid sample makes sense here, for pleural effusion i think a chest X-ray makes sense here, for breathlessness i am arranging an urgent chest clinic review the chest clinic would be the right next step, I'll refer you
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure, where do I go?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled next month, we'd think about a CT scan of the chest, but not now. Let's plan a check after the scan.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): that's fine with me
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): right, that's the plan do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): take care now

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Parking was a shocker. Two laps, then some ute sitting in the disabled bay. Thanks for fitting us in, anyway.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): They're digging the front up again. Come through. Dave, and Jen, yeah?
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his partner. I booked it. He wasn't going to.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Because I'm fine. This is a waste of your arvo, seriously.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're here, so we'll use the time. Jen rang about your sleep and you being flat. Dave, your words, what's going on?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing much. Bit tired. She worries about everything.
[SEG0007] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He is not sleeping. I lie there listening to him roll around half the night, and the next day he's a write-off.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): I sleep. Just not brilliantly. Settle down.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not brilliantly how? Getting off to sleep, waking up, or both?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Um. Both, most nights. I lie there ages, head going. Then I'm awake again at four, sometimes half three, and that's me done.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like that?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Couple of months. Well, actually, no. The job finished in November and it started straight after, so it's five months.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five months. And before November you were sleeping okay?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Had to. Early starts at the depot. Out like a light.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What happened with the work? Short version.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Council depot, forklift and the yard. Redundant. Restructure, they reckoned. Nothing going in town except night fill at the supermarket, and nah.
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's put a few applications in. Then he won't look at it for a week. Just sits.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Eleven years I was there. Nah, twelve, I always forget, I started in the March so it's twelve. And can we not do the Centrelink thing? Those forms do my head in.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll skip Centrelink. Energy through the day, how's that?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm alright. Bit sluggish first thing. Everyone is.
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): First thing, he says. I had Biscuit out at seven, she's the kelpie, and he hadn't even shifted. Some days it's lunch before he's really up.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Footy, the shed, your mates, walking the dog. Are you still getting any enjoyment out of that?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'm fine with it. She's exaggerating. Mates are busy, that's all.
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother offered Crows tickets and he said no. He hasn't been once. He used to live for it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): They've been ordinary all season. Look, I don't get the buzz. I put the telly on and I can't be bothered. The thing in the shed's just sitting there half finished.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the interest has dropped off. Not only the energy.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): If you're writing it down, yeah. Don't make it a huge thing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Under that, the mood. Sad, flat, teary, short with people?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Not sad. I'm not sitting there crying. Flat, if you need a word. I get snappy with her sometimes. Not proud of it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The quiet worries me more than the snappy. He'll just go still.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Appetite? Weight? Any change you've noticed?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Appetite's fine. I eat.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He pushes it round the plate. Last night half the snags were left. It's been like that for weeks, don't let him tell you otherwise.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): I wasn't hungry last night. One night. I eat enough. I'm not wasting away.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not writing wasting away. I am noting the two of you don't agree, and I'll park it. Any neck pain, headaches, dizzy spells?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Neck's a bit sore off the couch. No dizzy spells. I chuck a couple of Panadol and the neck comes good.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ordinary Panadol, paracetamol? How often?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, not the strong ones. Couple of times a week if it's nagging. Not daily.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the water tablet. He still takes that every morning, tell the doctor.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the name and the dose?
[SEG0041] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's indapamide. His water tablet. Two and a half milligrams. Chemist wrote it on the repeat.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): No, it's five. Five milligrams. Little white tablets, I read the box last week. She's got it wrong.
[SEG0043] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cupboard box says two point five. You were half asleep.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not picking a winner between two point five and five while you argue. Bring the actual box next time, or a photo of the label. Anything else you take regularly?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'll bring the box. That's it otherwise, the water tablet and the odd Panadol. I don't like pills.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Other history. Blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, any operations?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Blood pressure, yep, that's the point of the water tablet. Been years. No diabetes, no asthma, and I've never had an operation.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last you heard, was the pressure behaving?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Chemist reckoned it was good. Don't ask me the number, it's gone. Ages back.
[SEG0050] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You should know about his mum. She was treated for depression for years.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): That was after my brother. Long time ago. Mum's fine now. We don't have to unpack it.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't unpack it. Helps to know it's been in the family. Do you smoke, Dave?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand the smell.
[SEG0054] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has a beer with tea, though. Say that bit.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many on a normal night?
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): Two. Light beers. Same as when I was working. I'm not drinking to get to sleep.
[SEG0057] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two's about right. I'll agree with him there.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who's at home?
[SEG0059] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just us and the dog. She sticks to him, which he pretends means nothing.
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): Dogs do that. Can we get on with it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): One straight question, and it's routine, not me deciding you're unsafe. Any thoughts about hurting yourself, or hoping you don't wake up?
[SEG0062] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I'm not that bloke, I'd never do that to her. I just can't be stuffed, that's different.
[SEG0063] person_2 (DOCTOR): Clear, thank you. If that ever changes, you don't sit on it. You tell Jen, and you come here or you go to emergency the same day.
[SEG0064] person_3 (PATIENT): Yep. Won't happen. Heard you.
[SEG0065] person_2 (DOCTOR): Arm out, I'll check the pressure. One thirty-eight over eighty-six. Pulse is seventy-eight... no, ignore that, last patient's still on the screen. Yours is sixty-eight.
[SEG0066] person_3 (PATIENT): See? Normal. Told you both.
[SEG0067] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pressure and pulse are normal, yes. On looking at you, you're kempt, speech is ordinary, no restlessness. Affect's a bit flat. Nothing acute, and I won't put you through a full examination.
[SEG0068] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it depression, then? Just tell us.
[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll think out loud, and I don't want you grabbing one word. Losing a job after twelve years can knock sleep, get-up-and-go and interest, and sometimes that is a drawn-out adjustment, sometimes a depressive episode. I cannot split those two today. I am not stamping a diagnosis on you.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. So I'm fine.
[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): I didn't say fine. No label yet is not the same as fine. Things that mimic this, a low thyroid, anaemia, sleep apnoea if the snoring had suddenly got wild. Has it?
[SEG0072] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He snores a bit. He always has. Not worse. I moved rooms because of the tossing, not the noise.
[SEG0073] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then no bloods today, and no sleep study. I am not concluding any of that. We'll see how a few weeks go before I order anything.
[SEG0074] person_3 (PATIENT): And no tablets. I don't want to start something.
[SEG0075] person_2 (DOCTOR): If we start one later, it'd be sertraline. A lot of GPs go straight to fifty milligrams. Actually I'd start you at twenty-five if we ever do it, not this afternoon. I want to see you again first.
[SEG0076] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So what is he meant to do? Don't say warm milk.
[SEG0077] person_2 (DOCTOR): No milk. Out of bed the same time every day, curtains open, phone not in the bed, and the couch is not for sleeping. If you're still awake after about twenty minutes, get up, do something dull, go back when you're sleepy. That's on you, Dave, not on Jen to police it.
[SEG0078] person_3 (PATIENT): Bit of homework. I'll have a crack. Phone thing, we'll see.
[SEG0079] person_2 (DOCTOR): A crack is enough. Book at reception for three weeks, back here with me. Bring that indapamide box.
[SEG0080] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If he slides before then he will not ring you. What do I do?
[SEG0081] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the mood drops sharply, or either of you is worried, don't wait out the three weeks. Ring us and we'll fit him in. And the harm thoughts, that's same day, no debate. Go on, get the dog out of the ute.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi! Right, lupus review. I think I'm doing okay, but you tell me. I've also got a rash on my cheeks that's come back.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good to see you. Let's start with the rash. When did it come back?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): About two weeks ago. Across my cheeks and nose, a butterfly thing. It's worse in the sun.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any joint pains? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, in my hands, in the mornings. Nothing too bad. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's check what you're taking.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Hydroxychloroquine, 200 mg twice a day. Prednisolone, 5 mg, once a day. And a calcium and vitamin D tablet, once a day, for my bones.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that matches. Any fever, or mouth ulcers, or chest pain when you breathe in?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what do you do for work, are you outdoors?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a postwoman, so yes, outdoors most days.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): That could well be the sun triggering the rash. Let me look. ~
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a pink, slightly raised rash across both cheeks and the bridge of your nose, and the skin elsewhere on the face is clear.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it a flare? ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): With the sun-sensitive rash and a bit of morning hand stiffness, I'd say this is a mild flare of your lupus.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I need more tablets? ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Your current treatment is covering you, and I'd rather get the sun protection right first. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I wear a hat. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): A hat's good, but you need a high-factor sun cream, factor 50, on your face, every day, even when it's cloudy.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Every day? Even in winter? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, because UV gets through cloud. And long sleeves on your arms when you're on your round. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And what about my eyes, the hydroxychloroquine? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): You should have your yearly eye check, so I'll make sure that's booked.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Good, I was going to ask. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the rash spreads, you get a fever, mouth ulcers, swollen ankles, or your urine goes frothy or dark, ring me and come in.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. I'll watch for those. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking everything as you are. ~
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor, it's always good to talk it through. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care, and mind the sun. ~

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Fine. We good?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): We're good. Grab the referral printout at the desk on your way out.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, uh, that's been fine.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Just my tonsils removed, as a teenager.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there someone at home?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No known allergies.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Actually, uh, I remember she had some kind of reaction to erythromycin before. I couldn't swear to it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, maybe, but I don't recall it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll note both of those. Are there any illnesses in your family?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had breast cancer. Let me think, my brother has epilepsy.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you have any chronic illnesses?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, heart failure. Diabetes, for nearly five years. Yes, high blood pressure. My family kept telling me to get it checked. I wasn't sure whether to come in at all, to be honest. I've got gout.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm, okay. Yes, heart failure and gout are known to us, good to have that clear.
[SEG0055] person_4 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 136 over 72, oxygen saturation is 94 percent, temperature 37.4, pulse is 94 beats a minute.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold that for a second.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): There is dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the right base.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again. From what you've told me and what I found, this is probably a pleural effusion needing a cause. We shouldn't forget a tumour. Stop me if I've got anything wrong. You've had breathlessness building over weeks, moderate, and no night sweats or fever.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, that's right.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any scans or blood work done already?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): I did have a CT scan of the chest done last month, but the paper's at home.

[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if the symptoms get worse. That's when to be seen urgently. Let's review you after the scan. Anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, no, I haven't had any of them.

[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Up at last. TSH was one point eight. Normal, not borderline, so that memory doesn't match the result.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Press, left arm, next week. Thank you, I feel a bit better just having a plan.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, hi. I twisted my ankle playing football last night. It's, um, swollen, and I'm not sure if I should have come, my mates said I'm being soft.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I went to tackle someone and my foot got stuck in the turf and sort of rolled outwards. It went, um, on the outside of the left ankle.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was this? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yesterday evening, about eight.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how's it been since?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It swelled up quickly, like an egg, on the outside.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bruising?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): It's gone a bit purple this morning.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hear a crack or a snap?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, no. No crack. Just a sort of pull.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the foot?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No numbness.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain higher up, in the shin or the knee?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, it's only the ankle.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 400 mg, three times a day. Paracetamol, 1 gram, when it's bad. Cetirizine, 10 mg, every morning. And my blue inhaler, salbutamol, when I need it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Um. I think I came out in a rash once from some tablets I got abroad, in Spain. I don't know what they were.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, I'll note it as possible. Any health conditions?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Asthma, and hay fever.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I had my left knee done, the cruciate, in 2019.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in the family I should know about?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): My dad has arthritis.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a student, final year.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you play football?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Twice a week. Saturdays and Wednesdays.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): At weekends, a few pints.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check you. Pulse 72, blood pressure 118 over 74, temperature 36.7, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 14, weight 74 kilos.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that okay? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Let me look at the ankle. Tell me if it hurts.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. There. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's swelling and tenderness over the ligaments on the outside of the left ankle, but no tenderness over the bony bumps.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good? ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's good. And you can take a few steps, I watched you come in. ~
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, limping, but I could. ~
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze or chest tightness today?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. My chest is fine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): So here's what I think. This looks like a sprained ankle, a ligament sprain, probably a moderate one.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it broken? ~
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Unlikely, given you could walk and there's no bony tenderness. But I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the ankle to be sure.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like to arrange an ultrasound of the ankle ligaments, to see how much damage there is.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): How long will I be out? ~
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few weeks. I'd like to arrange physiotherapy to get you back faster.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): That's good. ~
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Rest, ice, compression and elevation for the first few days.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Got it. ~
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't put your weight on it by next week, come back and see me.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Pillay, sit. Sister says two falls. When?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the dizziness been there?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe two weeks? Or longer. I can't put a date on when it started. It just crept in.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not short of breath.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure tablets. Which ones?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, ten milligrams, in the morning. Enalapril, ten milligrams, morning and night. And for sleep I take zopiclone, seven point five, at bedtime. Must I stop all of them? I'm frightened to just stop, hey.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You're leaving out the water tablet. The hydrochlorothiazide. She stopped that one.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, ja, I stopped the hydrochlorothiazide in March, twenty five milligrams. My ankles were like puddings, so I left it. The chemist renewed the bottle but it's still sitting in the cupboard. I haven't touched it since.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diabetes tablets? Aspirin? Anything else?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else. I've had the high blood pressure for years, that's the lot. If you change something, will the pressure shoot straight up? I really don't want a stroke, Doctor.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): One tablet, not the lot. Sister's readings: lying, blood pressure one fifty two over eighty six, pulse sixty eight. Standing, one eighteen over seventy, pulse ninety two. A proper drop.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, that's low when I stand, isn't it? So that's why the room goes? Can I still drive to the shops? It's only past the robot, two minutes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't drive while you're dizzy. This is your pressure falling when you stand. The tablets are doing too much. I'm cutting the amlodipine from ten milligrams to five, starting tomorrow morning.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the amlodipine? Will five be enough for my pressure? I still take the enalapril twice? And the sleeping tablet, is that the thing making me fall? I've got so many questions, sorry.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the enalapril, ten milligrams, morning and night. Keep the zopiclone as it is. Amlodipine five milligrams, once, in the morning, nothing else of it. Stand up slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed first.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it happens at night, when I get up for the loo? Must I phone Naledi? She doesn't stay over, she just checks on me. What if I go down and nobody's there?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sit down the moment it comes. If you black out, or you get chest pain, go to casualty. No brain scan today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No scan, are you sure it's not my head? When I stand I can't catch my breath, just for a minute. I said no to that earlier, but actually, ja, I do get breathless. Is that my heart failing?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same drop, not a new heart diagnosis from this chair. I'm sending bloods, kidney function and sodium.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods? At this clinic or the lab in town? I'm a proper baby with needles. And when must I come back to you?
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring her, Doc. She won't pitch unless I book it. Parking here is a nightmare, hey, I circled the block for ages last Thursday.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Clinic lab, this week. I'll see you in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, okay. So tomorrow I take the five, not the ten. Do I throw the ten milligram bottle away? I'll mix them up in the dark, I know I will. I'm anxious about that.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Put the ten milligram bottle aside. Don't take it. The pharmacy will give you the five milligrams. One tablet, mornings.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): And the hydrochlorothiazide stays stopped? Even though the ankles were the problem in March and they're fine now? I keep thinking they'll swell up again if I don't take something.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay off it. Ankles are not swollen today. Two weeks. We're done.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Thank you, Doctor. Naledi, please don't let me forget that lab. I'm still nervous, but I'll try the slow getting-up.

[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, about the same, five days.

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, over here please and I'll take a look.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): The chest wound has healed, the breastbone is stable, and the vein-harvest wound on the leg is a little swollen.
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): Okay, you know, doctor.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed. And fever, any of that?
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): Nope, no fever.

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your urine normal, no changes?
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): That's normal as far as I know.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): how active are you?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): What does a normal day of food look like?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): um, I've never had an allergy
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Actually, uh, I remember he had some kind of reaction to erythromycin before. I couldn't swear to it.

[SEG0046] person_4 (PATIENT): is it dangerous, doctor?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's reasonable to be concerned, but right now recovering well after bypass surgery is my leading thought, not anything worse.

[SEG0052] person_4 (PATIENT): I think I understand everything. Thanks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye for now.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone in your family had anything serious?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): My cousin has psoriasis.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Erm, I'm on hydrocortisone cream, when needed for the eczema.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): For the anxiety, I believe. My son sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. Alendronate, 70 milligrams, once a week for my bones.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I think the last prescription for the alendronate was 140 milligrams. We changed it at the last visit.
