[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I left it at home. I'm on Seretide inhaler, twice a day.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone ever diagnosed you with something?
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, eczema.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, I have anxiety, for five years. I didn't want to make a fuss, you know. I've had thin bones, yes.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had asthma for five years now.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so eczema and anxiety are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today.
[SEG0053] person_5 (NURSE): Doctor, I've got the readings for you. Weight 68 kilos, SpO2 97 percent on room air. Temp 39.3 degrees, blood pressure 121 over 66, height 174 centimetres, BMI works out to 22.5, pulse is 102 beats a minute.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, noted.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, over here please and I'll take a look.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is a new murmur, small splinter lines under the nails and a tender spot on the finger pad.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check. Putting it all together, it's hard to say. Possible infective endocarditis is one possibility and a viral illness another, and I'd rather not commit yet.
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): Is there something to worry about?
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with possible infective endocarditis do well once it's treated properly.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): We should do blood cultures for possible endocarditis. I'll request blood tests, it'll help with prolonged fever. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed. I think an echocardiogram makes sense here, for new murmur. That will help us see what's going on underneath and decide the next step. You need admission today for blood cultures and a heart scan. I'll also refer you to the cardiology team.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0063] person_1 (PATIENT): Actually, okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): One warning sign to remember: the symptoms get worse. In that case don't wait.
[SEG0065] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, okay, I'll look out for that.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please come and see me straight away. Have I covered everything you wanted?
[SEG0067] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, that's helpful.

[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, his father had a stroke, that is why I pushed him to come. I did not want us to ignore a high reading.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted. Diabetes? Heart problem?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no heart problem. BP was never told high before, except these clinic readings, and even those I do not trust.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Alcohol?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked. Alcohol, only at weddings, maybe twice a year, one small peg, that is all. I am retired from the accounts department at the mill, and I walk to the market most mornings.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Appa, do not start on yesterday's match, the doctor has other patients.

[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Back to the knee. Pain on flat walking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat walking is okay, doctor. Bending is possible, but the last bit on the stairs is where it catches. No fever, no redness, I checked in the mirror this morning, skin looks the same both sides.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): No swelling, no warmth. Bend and straighten are both full. Tender on the inner side of the right knee. That is all.
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): Second reading, after sitting, one hundred and fifty-six over ninety-two.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): See, already coming down. If you check a third time it will be one-thirty only, I know my body. The cuff itself makes me nervous, my heart goes fast, then it settles. Classic white coat.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pulse is eighty-four, regular. I am not calling this established hypertension today.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): It may be white coat. It may be early hypertension. I cannot separate them on two readings.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no tablet today?
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): No tablet today. No point starting a BP medicine on clinic numbers alone.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Get a home reading morning and evening, sitting, for seven days. Write every number and bring the paper.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): One arm only, the right, same each time, after sitting five minutes.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Right arm, five minutes, morning and evening, seven days. And the knee, you are not sending me for any scan?
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): No scan now. If it is not better in three weeks, then an X-ray.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Avoid deep squats, take the stairs slowly. Paracetamol five hundred milligram by mouth, up to three times a day if the pain needs it, with food. Skip it on days you are comfortable.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times only if needed, with food, no squats. If the paper shows high BP, which tablet will you give, because my neighbour got a bad cough from one of them and I do not want that kind of trouble.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): We decide after the seven days. I am not naming a tablet now. Come back with the readings in one week.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will bring him. Should he worry about the stroke thing tonight?
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not tonight. Pulse is steady and there is no chest pain. If he gets chest pain, a severe headache, or weakness on one side, go to emergency. Otherwise just the one-week visit.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Understood, doctor. One week, readings written properly, knee advice followed, and I will not borrow her telmisartan, promise. Sorry for the long match story, I get carried away.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): There is no BP medicine to print. Collect the slip for the knee advice at the desk on your way out.

[SEG0001] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mr Fitzgerald. I'm GrÃ¡inne, I'm the healthcare assistant. I've printed your medication list for the doctor, so we can go through it. ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, thanks a million. Sure, I'll talk the hind legs off a donkey, you'll have to stop me. ~
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Fitzgerald. It's the back, isn't it, and the leg?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): It is, doctor. Lower back, and it runs down the back of my left leg, to the calf, like a hot wire.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. It started after I was lifting sacks of potatoes. I'm a farmer, you see.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it worse sitting, standing, or walking?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Sitting, mostly. And coughing, or sneezing, that sends a jolt down.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or weakness in the foot?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit of tingling in the toes. But the foot's strong. No weakness.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your bladder or bowels, or numbness in your groin? ~
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): None whatsoever. ~
[SEG0013] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor, here's his list. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, GrÃ¡inne. Mr Fitzgerald, let's go through the medicines.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Naproxen, 500 mg twice a day, with food. And paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that helping? ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Takes the edge off. Not the leg. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, and my knees.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped a few years back, ten a day, for forty years.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Would you like me to take his blood pressure, doctor? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today, thanks, GrÃ¡inne. Mr Fitzgerald, I'll check your leg. Lift it straight. ~
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow. That's the one.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's reproduced the pain when I raise the left leg, and your ankle reflex is a bit reduced on that side, but your strength is normal. ~
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that a disc? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): It sounds like sciatica, which is a pinched nerve at the lower back, often from a slipped disc. ~
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need surgery? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people improve without it, over six to twelve weeks. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Could I keep working? ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, gentle activity, but no heavy lifting. Staying in bed is worse.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): How will I lift the sacks? ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ask for help, and bend your knees. ~
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll get my son. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the naproxen with food, and the paracetamol regularly.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): And hot water bottles, doctor? ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heat helps, yes. If you develop numbness between your legs, can't control your bladder or bowels, or your foot becomes weak, go to the emergency department right away.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Otherwise, if it's not better in six weeks, come back and I'll arrange a scan and a physiotherapy referral.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks a million, doctor. ~

[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when did it start?

[SEG0001] person_3 (NURSE): Mr Hartley, I'm Chloe, the nurse. You came in with a wrist injury. Let me get your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, my dear. I'm afraid I've been rather foolish. I fell off a ladder, cleaning the gutters.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): Pulse 88, blood pressure 144 over 86, temperature 36.7.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning, Mr Hartley. I'm Dr Naylor. Tell me what happened. ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was about eight feet up, and the ladder slipped, and I came down on my left hand, with my arm out.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): About two hours ago. And my wrist has swollen up, rather alarmingly.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How bad is the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Severe when I move it. I can hardly turn my hand over.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hit your head, or hurt anywhere else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no head injury. My right knee is a bit sore, but nothing much.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A little tingling in my thumb and index finger.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any medical problems?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure and an underactive thyroid.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And do you do anything which might affect healing, do you smoke?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up thirty years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your wrist. Tell me when it hurts.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow! There. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): The wrist is swollen, with a visible bump, a deformity, on the back of it, it's very tender over the end of the radius, and the fingers are warm with a good pulse.
[SEG0021] person_3 (NURSE): His capillary refill is normal, doctor. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Chloe. Mr Hartley, this looks like a broken wrist, a fracture of the radius, called a Colles' fracture.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, bother. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't be certain without an X-ray, and it could also involve a small bone in the wrist, so I'd like an X-ray of the wrist, and one of the knee.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I have something for the pain? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will give you something strong right away. ~
[SEG0027] person_3 (NURSE): I'll bring it now. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please keep the arm raised on a pillow, and don't eat or drink anything until the X-rays are done, in case you need it set.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need to be put back? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly. If the bone has shifted, we'll set it under local anaesthetic, in the department. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): How very modern. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will take you through to radiology. If your fingers go cold, blue or numb, tell her at once.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I shall. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mr Brennan, you're in room two. I checked you just now, blood pressure 138 over 86, pulse 72, temperature 36.7, and your oxygen is 98 percent. Dr Keane won't be long.

[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Declan, you're very welcome. Come on in and take a seat. What's been troubling you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, thank you, doctor. It is my lower back. It has been sore for a few weeks, or perhaps since we moved house, and I could not say whether that was before Easter or after.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sure, we don't need the exact day. Tell me how it feels, in your own words.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a deep ache in the small of my back, about a six out of ten, travelling a little into the left buttock but no further down the leg. Lifting at the warehouse and sitting too long set it off, and lying flat or a hot water bottle eases it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): I have that. Six out of ten, into the buttock only, worse with lifting and sitting, easier lying flat or with heat.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, that is exactly it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles in the legs?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The move was the difficult part, if I may say. We had boxes in every room, and I was up and down the stairs with the bookcases. My wife said I ought to have hired a van with a lift.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): That does sound heavy going. Coming back to the legs, though, any numbness or tingling at all?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. There is no numbness, and there are no pins and needles.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness, or the leg giving way when you walk?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The legs are strong, and I manage the stairs at work grand.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about the waterworks, any trouble passing urine, any leaking, or not getting there in time?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the waterworks are entirely normal, thank you.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the bowels, any change?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Normal as well. There has been no change.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the move my wife has been doing simpler dinners, as the new kitchen still is not right, and I have been picking at my food. Her sister said I looked thinner in the wedding photographs, though those are years old.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hear you. Have you yourself noticed a real loss of weight, or stood on the scales?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I would not say I have lost weight. The trousers fit just the same.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or turns of feeling hot and shivery?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had a temperature last month and she was quite miserable with it, down in Galway. I brought her a carton of soup on the Sunday.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): That was good of you. And you yourself, any fever with this back pain?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I have had no fever at all.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the pain?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol from the chemist, two of the 500 milligram tablets, three times a day, though I do forget the evening dose some nights. My wife is on metformin for her sugar and she offered me one, but I would not take another person's tablets. My sister swears by biotin for her hair, which is beside the point.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Quite right to leave the metformin and the biotin alone. So the paracetamol is yours, and you miss the odd evening one?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Only the paracetamol is mine, and yes, I miss it now and again.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Roughly how many evenings in a week would you miss it, would you say?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, I could not be sure. Some weeks it is one night, some weeks more. I would not want to give you a wrong figure.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you try anything else?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I was taking ibuprofen too. I thought it was a 400 milligram tablet, but actually it was the 200 milligram ones, two of them, twice a day. I stopped last week.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): What made you stop them?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): They brought on heartburn. That settled once I stopped, I am glad to say.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I know of, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any old trouble with the back, or any operations in the past?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never had an operation. There has been no previous back trouble either. I have been well, apart from this.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me a little about work and home. Do you smoke?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in the warehouse on the industrial estate, lifting stock, and it will be twenty years this autumn. I live with my wife. I have never smoked.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. If you'll stand for me, I'll have a look at the back.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, doctor.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): There's tenderness over the lower lumbar area, a little more on the left. Straight leg raise is clear on both sides, power in the legs is normal, and sensation is intact.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): That spot is precisely where it is sore, yes.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): With a sore back a few things cross my mind, a muscle strain from the lifting, a disc being irritated, even the uncommon serious causes. I'm not going to conclude any of those today, and I certainly won't call this a slipped disc or sciatica.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I will say, as a working impression, is mechanical low back pain. Nothing in the story or the examination is ringing alarm bells.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Would an x-ray be wise, doctor, if you thought it proper?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): I don't see a need for an x-ray today, and I won't be ordering one. If the pain starts down the leg, or you develop weakness, then we might arrange an MRI.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I would be guided by you.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep on with your own paracetamol, two 500 milligram tablets three times a day, and try not to skip the evening one. Given the heartburn, I won't start another anti-inflammatory.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay on the move with short walks, and no lying up for days. The hot water bottle is fine. I'll refer you across to physiotherapy.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Ought I to be careful with the lifting at work?
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ease off the heaviest lifts for a fortnight if your supervisor will allow it, and bend the knees rather than the back. If you get numbness between the legs, trouble with the waterworks, weakness, or a fever, you come straight back the same day.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I will, doctor. You have been very clear, and I am grateful.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it's no better in three weeks, book back in with me.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do that. Thank you for your time.
[SEG0059] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mr Brennan, if that review needs booking I can take it at the desk on your way out. Mind the step there.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Much obliged. Good afternoon to you both.

[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): Mm, I notice it more with pollen.
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): And the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, that's what worries me.
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): I was getting to that! And there's a runny itchy nose as well, about two weeks now.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): I'd say every other day. Moderate, really. I've also had watery eyes, for five days.
[SEG0020] person_5 (UNKNOWN): Yes, that's right, that's how it was.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been any loss of smell?
[SEG0022] person_4 (PATIENT): Definitely no loss of smell.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed facial pain, fever or wheeze?
[SEG0024] person_4 (PATIENT): No, you know, nothing to report there.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your chest okay generally?
[SEG0026] person_4 (PATIENT): No, my breathing's been fine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your urine normal, no changes?
[SEG0028] person_4 (PATIENT): That's normal as far as I know.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0030] person_4 (PATIENT): I have acid reflux, for about ten years. I told my wife I'd come today. I mean, uh, I've had asthma, yes. I took the morning off to come in today. I'd rather not end up on lots of tablets if I can avoid it.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0032] person_4 (PATIENT): I'm on pantoprazole, 40 milligrams, before breakfast. Foracort inhaler, twice a day for my asthma. Loratadine, 10 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, our chart from the last visit lists it as 20 milligrams.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, that's different. Is the latest prescription anywhere near you?
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Not with me. I'll bring it next time.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any inherited conditions that you know of in the family?
[SEG0037] person_4 (PATIENT): Let me think, my sister had breast cancer.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0039] person_4 (PATIENT): I've, I've never had an allergy.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Actually, I'm not sure that's right. I seem to recall a problem with trimethoprim.
[SEG0041] person_4 (PATIENT): Really? I don't think so.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, so that's unclear. I'll record what each of you said.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your routine, work, habits, that sort of thing.
[SEG0044] person_4 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner. I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day. My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now I'm going to do a short physical check.
[SEG0046] person_4 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does that hurt?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): The inside of the nose is pale and boggy with clear mucus.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, you can relax now.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, so my impression is this: I think we're dealing with seasonal allergic rhinitis at this stage.
[SEG0051] person_4 (PATIENT): Oh, um, do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like seasonal allergic rhinitis. I'll start you on fluticasone nasal spray, 50 micrograms, once a day, the season. That's for hay fever.
[SEG0053] person_4 (PATIENT): Is that safe with my other medicines?
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shower after being outdoors and keep windows shut when pollen is high. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0055] person_4 (PATIENT): I'll remember that.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if the symptoms get worse. That's when to be seen urgently.
[SEG0057] person_4 (PATIENT): Oh, yes, I'll bear that in mind.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please come and see me if not better in a month. So, anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0059] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, that's helpful.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye for now.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Have a seat. What's the problem?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a few things, and I want to explain them properly so you don't think I'm just being dramatic. I've been exhausted for months, the sort of tired where I sit in the car outside the flat and can't get myself inside, and I've been blaming the audit at work and the fact that I'm fifty-two.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many months?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six months, I nearly said, but no, it was already there before the June long weekend, so eight months. Weekends too, not only after a long day, so I can't only pin it on the office, even though the office is hectic.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja, about eight months. I thought it was the job as well, shame.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cold?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Very cold. I sleep under an extra blanket when everyone else has the fan on, and my hands are ice on the keyboard. I even bought a small heater for under the desk, and my boss thinks I've lost the plot.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Up, which annoys me because I'm eating less, smaller plate, no second chop at the braai. The bathroom scale said five kilos and I was ready to tell you five, but the chemist scale last Tuesday said eight, so it's eight kilos, and the work trousers don't close.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Constipated the whole time, pretty much. I go every three or four days, hard, and I sit there ages. Prunes, extra water, a walk round the block, none of that has fixed it, and I know that's a lot of detail but it's been miserable.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mood?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Low, flat. I'm not in tears, but I don't want the Saturday braai or people over, and I told myself that's just tiredness and age, not a real mood problem. Work has been grim, so it felt like an explanation.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She cancels plans. She's quieter than she was, hey, and she doesn't laugh at the same things.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I've checked with the thermometer at home a few times because I feel so off, and it's always normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Short of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, no. And not short of breath. I get up the stairs at the office fine, I just don't want to.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hair loss? Dry skin?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry skin, ja, my shins flake even with the cream from the chemist. Hair, no, I'm not losing it. A couple of strands in the shower, same as the last ten years, nothing unusual on the pillow.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Periods regular?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the last year. Some months heavy, some barely there, and I put that with being fifty-two. Not pregnant either, my husband had the snip years ago, so we can leave that.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother, ja. Underactive thyroid, on tablets for years, always cold, always slow, and she died in twenty nineteen from a stroke, not the thyroid. My sister's been on at me to come because she reckons I look like Mum did.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her mum was on Eltroxin forever. Same cold hands. That's why I pushed her to book.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Had a thyroid test yourself?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Once, at the day clinic, and they said borderline, that's the word they used. I nearly told you the TSH was 4.2, but that's wrong, the sister said five-point-something, still borderline, and no tablets. When it was, I can't tell you, ages ago, twenty nineteen or later, I honestly don't know.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she never went back. The paper is in a drawer at home. She hangs onto that word borderline and that's it.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicines now?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The only one I was properly on was ferrous sulphate from my GP, for this tiredness. Two hundred milligrams, I was about to say, no, it was the three hundred and twenty-five milligram tablet, once a day, by mouth. I stopped it in March because it bunged me up even more.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thyroxine ever?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never given it, never took a single tablet. I do take a supermarket multivitamin most mornings, one tablet, nothing fancy, and I couldn't tell you the strength. No cholesterol tablets and no blood pressure tablets.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That vitamin, she misses it more days than she takes it. The bottle hardly moves.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it when I remember, which is not every day, I'll give you that. Some weeks it's three times and then I lose track, so don't write it down as religious.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is sixty-two... no, fifty-six. Thyroid isn't enlarged. Hands are cool. Skin on the shins is dry.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Is fifty-six a problem? I used to run half marathons and it sat low then, but I haven't trained in ages, just a walk to the robot and back, and even that feels like a mission now.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not an emergency. This could be an underactive thyroid, or it could be the workload and getting older. I'm not deciding that today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): If it's thyroid like my mum I want it found, and if it's just the audit and my age I don't want tablets for nothing. I've been reading online, which is silly, and half the sites say thyroid and half say burnout, so I've been going in circles for weeks.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bloods will sort the thyroid question. TSH, free T4, and a full blood count, tomorrow morning, not fasting.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Does the blood count cover iron? I stopped the ferrous sulphate, and nobody actually checked a level before they handed me the script, which still irritates me. If I'm anaemic that explains some of this, though not the cold, I don't think.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, the full blood count covers anaemia. No thyroid tablets today, and don't restart the iron.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not even every second day?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Leave it off. It was making the constipation worse.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, I don't want it back. On the mood, I'm not asking for an antidepressant, my cousin had a horrible time on one and I forget the name, but if the flatness needs something separate I should say so now instead of pretending I'm fine.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing for mood today. If the thyroid bloods are normal and you still feel flat, we'll discuss it at the review.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I come back only if it's abnormal? I don't want to take a morning off the audit for a normal result, although the cold and the eight kilos will still be there even if the TSH is lovely.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back next week either way. We go through the results here.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Next week I can do Thursday, I think, not Wednesday, the auditors are in. Should I bring that old clinic printout if I find it? I might have the number wrong, five-point-something is what stuck, and they said borderline, but I wouldn't swear to the figure.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring it if you find it. Tomorrow's test stands either way.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll dig in the drawer tonight. She'll never look.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sleep all right?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep is fine once I'm warm. I drop off and I don't lie awake. I wake a bit early some mornings from the cold, but it's not insomnia, so please don't write that down as a sleep problem.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nausea, vomiting, tummy pain?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No nausea, no vomiting, no tummy pain. Appetite is down, that's true, food just doesn't appeal, which is why the smaller portions. The weight still went up, which is the confusing bit, and I've turned that over in my head a hundred times.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waterworks?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. No burning, and I'm not up all night. I drink lots of water for the bowels, and rooibos, so I go a bit more in the day, but that's the fluids, not a problem.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The rooibos is all day at her desk. And she stays till seven when the audit is on. It's not a quiet job.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, long hours, and I sit most of the day, which doesn't help the bowels, I know that. I used to walk at lunch and I stopped that months ago. That's the whole picture, I hope I haven't gone on too long.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Enough to go on. Bloods tomorrow morning at the lab, not fasting. Back here next week for the results, whatever they show.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me take your readings now.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bear with me while this finishes...

[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hm, okay. Rate it for me, mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Moderate, I'd say. Oh, uh, and not sleeping for days. As for not sleeping for days, severe, really.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had thoughts of ending your life before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, something like this happened last year, and it went away on its own.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: having taken tablets, recent loss, drinking or hearing voices?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I, I haven't had having taken tablets, recent loss, drinking or hearing voices, no.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your skin been okay?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No rashes.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your joints, any aches elsewhere?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else aches.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, um, I've never reacted to anything.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's run through your medicines.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): I take something called sert... sertraline, 50 milligrams, maybe, once a day for my mood.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, have you got the box or the prescription on you?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Not with me. I'll bring it next time.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's talk a little about your daily life and habits.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop. I grab fast food at lunch most days. I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My son has asthma.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have any procedures done?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had my appendix taken out, when I was in my twenties.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any long-term conditions?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Depression, for nearly five years.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, depression is known to us, good to have that clear.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, may I examine you now?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me feel here.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You are calm but very flat, and you have thought through how you would do it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Taking everything into account, it points towards a high risk of suicide needing urgent assessment. I'd like to arrange an urgent mental health assessment for suicidal thoughts.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): We have a slot Monday at 10 am, if that works.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want you to stay with me while we arrange help, and your family will be called. I think the crisis team should see you too.

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, will do.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back straight away.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does all of that make sense?
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the pressure desperate?

[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mornings, the water tablet. I was about to say forty milligrams, but no, the box says twenty. Furosemide twenty.

[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You do, mostly. Then there's the little white one. Amlodipine, five milligrams.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): And the blood pressure tablet. The other little white one. You always forget that.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mam, there isn't another one. The little white one is the amlodipine. I hope to God I haven't been dropping two into the box.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll count a single amlodipine five milligrams once a day. Not two. You've been on blood pressure treatment for years, is that right, and the amlodipine is for that?
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Years, yes. Since before I moved back in.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. I'm sick of hearing about it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else in there?
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): A small pale yellow tablet with the breakfast. Label's destroyed, got wet on the sink, and I cannot tell you the name of it. It's not the water one and it's not the white one.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then it stays unnamed. I'd rather a blank than a wrong guess. What did the other doctor stop?
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril, five milligrams. The hospital doctor stopped it because of a dry cough.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That was two months back. No, wait, about six weeks, the same time Siobhan says the ankles started.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ramipril five, stopped about six weeks ago, cough settled since. Allergies, anything that doesn't agree with her?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. How many times do I have to say it.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Penicillin, Mam. You came out in a rash with it when I was small, and you've steered clear of it ever since.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I did not. That's a yarn.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record that you recall none, and Siobhan remembers a penicillin rash from years back. We won't be using penicillin today either way. Any painkillers from the chemist?
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Paracetamol, the odd time, for the legs. Not every day, and I wouldn't put a dose on it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The odd one. I don't want a pile of new tablets.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. The ankle swelling could be the amlodipine, that one is well able to cause swelling, or it could be fluid retention. I am not calling this heart failure. I won't conclude that today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you've no idea, in other words.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I've two things it might be, and one thing I'm not saying. What I will change is the water tablet, for the swelling: furosemide up from twenty milligrams to forty milligrams, by mouth, every morning.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Forty instead of the twenty. Same tablet.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same tablet, new strength. If you go dizzy, or the swelling takes off, ring the surgery. And when you redo the box, one amlodipine only, don't double it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): More of the water tablet. Grand. Lovely.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll also have bloods this week, kidney function and the salts, seeing as we're increasing the diuretic.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her to the nurse for that.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): The drive over was a pure nuisance. Stuck at the bridge, rain belting down.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I was telling her about Aoife's camogie, the under-tens. Soaked to the skin and they still got the win.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Two points she scored, then nothing would do her but chips. A terror.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair play, camogie in that rain. My nephew's the same with the hurling, comes in plastered in muck and delighted with himself.
[SEG0056] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She wants a pink helmet now. We spent Saturday in the sports shop trying on every single one.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): The price of a pink helmet. Don't start me.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the helmets. I want to see you back here in two weeks, swelling and the blood results.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, if the car park doesn't finish me.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing worsens before then, or you can't get your air lying down, don't sit on it. Come back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0061] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye, and I'll sort the box tonight once the chemist has the new strength.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prescription will be at reception. [SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the lot. I'm wore out. Are we done?
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): We're done. Mind the step.

[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Got it. He'll be in shortly. If the screen in here freezes, just ignore it, it's been doing that all day.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, sorry, one second, this thing wants my password again. Okay. Mr. Ellison, what's going on?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have had a cough for six weeks. It came on just after I had the flu.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I clicked into the wrong note.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. The cough has lasted six weeks, and it is distinctly worse at night.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Helen, his sister. I'm staying in the guest room, and honestly the coughing after he lies down is hard to sleep through.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Worse at night. Any fever with it, or are you bringing anything up?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. In the morning I do bring up a little clear mucus. Nothing bloody, I am glad to say.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): And weight loss? Night sweats?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not lost weight. No night sweats either.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the whole order panel just blanked. You said no weight loss, is that right?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I ought to correct that. My pants have become quite loose at the waist. I had not regarded it as weight loss until you asked again.
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've seen it. He had to pull the belt in two holes.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Any recent travel, or contact with somebody who has tuberculosis?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not traveled. And I have not had contact with anyone who has tuberculosis.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Um, that's not totally fair. Our cousin Denise had tuberculosis last fall. They had her on rifampin and isoniazid. He took soup over to her place.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I set the container on the porch, Helen. I would not call that contact. Those medicines were entirely hers.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to name a cause today. Let me listen. Big breath for me.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, no wheeze. Heart sounds regular. Sorry, the cursor jumped. How long did the flu itself last?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): About a week, in early March, I believe. The cough has simply continued since then.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I take amlodipine, five milligrams, once daily, for my blood pressure. I did use Delsym, the dextromethorphan syrup, for three nights, and then I stopped it. It made me unpleasantly drowsy.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just so the chart doesn't get messy, my metformin is for my diabetes, not his. And I take biotin for my hair. Neither of those is Arthur's.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine five milligrams daily, and the Delsym is stopped. Any allergies?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no drug allergies that I am aware of.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I do walk most evenings, perhaps twenty minutes, if that is useful.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering a chest X-ray. I'd rather not guess what's behind the cough until we see the film.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand completely. Might that be done today?
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, radiology today. If the film is fine and the cough is still there in two weeks, come back and we'll decide on next steps.
[SEG0035] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk you down once the order actually shows up. This computer, I swear.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should he stay on the amlodipine in the meantime?
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep taking the amlodipine the way you have been. If you cough up blood, or you get short of breath, don't wait for that visit.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I will do exactly that.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Hi there.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where shall we begin?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, uh, I've been having shortness of breath.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you tell me when it first started?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been about three months now. A neighbour of mine said I should see someone about it. I wasn't sure whether to come in at all, um, to be honest.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more about it: how bad it gets, how often, and whether anything makes it better or worse. These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's worse with lying flat. Mostly mild.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other symptoms with it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A racing heart goes along with it, most of the time. The racing heart? That's been for two days.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed fever, leg swelling or cough?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any of them.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any muscle or joint problems besides this?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, joints are fine.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few questions about your lifestyle now.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I quit smoking around ten years ago. Yes, I work in a bakery, early starts. My husband and I live above the shop. I swim twice a week.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there any regular medication you use?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I'm not on anything.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you have any medical conditions I should know about?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I've always been fairly healthy.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have any procedures done?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I had my septum straightened, in my thirties.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, before we go further, any allergies?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I have any, no.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's start with the basic checks.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sit still for a moment...
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: blood pressure 97 over 63, pulse 110, temperature 36.5.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm just checking this side.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your neck veins are swollen, the heart sounds are muffled and your blood pressure is low.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, you can relax now.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, here's what I'm thinking. My working impression is possible cardiac tamponade. The reason I say that is that your story and my examination fit together.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Is this permanent?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with possible cardiac tamponade do well once it's treated properly. I'm sending you for an urgent echocardiogram because of possible tamponade. You need an urgent heart scan and possibly a drain. Cut down on salt and fried food for now, it really does make a difference. Do get help quickly if the symptoms get worse. Let's plan a check straight away. That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I think I understand everything. Thanks.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): so, how long has it been like this? I'm asking so that we don't miss anything

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): a few quick ones: urinary symptoms, weight loss or blood in the stool?

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?

[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): okay so the vitals from earlier. Temperature is 38.6 degrees BP is 119 over 79 pulse 100.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is tender in the lower left with no guarding or rigidity.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): All finished thank you.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): from what you've told me and and what I found, this looks most like acute diverticulitis
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll request blood tests, it'll help with abdominal pain. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed. I'd like to arrange a CT scan for left iliac fossa pain. I'm going to put you on co-amoxiclav, 625 milligrams, three times a day, five days. That should help with diverticulitis

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Hale, in you come. I took your blood pressure in the corridor because you looked flushed, and it was up, so Dr Okonkwo should see the figures as well as your form.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Flushed, yes, well the corridor's boiling and I'd legged it from the car park, Pauline had the meter running, and the card machine rejected me twice, so I was all wound up, which is a silly way to arrive when all I actually need is this occupational health form for work.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Hale, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Sit yourself down. What's brought you in today, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): So I work in the council housing office, a desk job, and I mentioned to my manager that my right knee aches, which I now think was a mistake, because they've stopped me doing the stair inspections until a doctor signs this form to say I'm alright for the desk work, even though I sit down nearly all day.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Pauline, I drive him Tuesdays and Fridays. The form's in the blue folder, and he will talk the hind leg off a donkey if you let him.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's quite alright, Pauline, the detail helps. Nurse, what did you get for the blood pressure?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): First reading, once he was sat, was one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): I left it a couple of minutes and did it again. The second was one hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two, and his pulse was seventy-six and regular.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): That is the white coat business, I'm sure of it. It does this every single time I come in, and then I go home and I'm fine, and I feel completely well. If you feel well you assume the machine in the clinic is just being dramatic.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): White coat is ever so common, so I won't jump. How has the knee been for you?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's an ache, right knee, across the front, not a stabbing pain. Stairs in the multi-storey make it worse, sitting eases it, and I wouldn't say it's severe, more a nuisance that clicks into my head when I'm walking back from the photocopier.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And how long has the ache been there?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it, I'm afraid. Sometime after the clocks went back, or it might have been before, last autumn or the winter, and I genuinely could not tell you which.
[SEG0014] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He was limping a bit at Christmas, when I took him for the turkey. I only see him two days a week, so I miss bits.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Christmas rings a bell, though I was also hauling boxes of files that week, so the limp might have been that. Either way I still can't tell you when it actually started.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the knee lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't lock, and it has never given way. I'm steady on my feet. Pauline's very strict about that.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He is steady. I wouldn't have him driving if he wasn't.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. With those blood pressure numbers, any headache, chest pain, or breathlessness?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, no chest pain, and I'm not breathless. I feel well in myself, which is exactly why I think this is white coat and not some silent disaster, though I do know people say high blood pressure doesn't announce itself.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad had a stroke, incidentally, years back, in his seventies. I only say it because it popped into my head, not because I'm building a case. He lived on a good while after.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's useful to know, even in passing. What do you make of these clinic readings yourself?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I make them out to be nerves. They did a cholesterol at a health check once, and the nurse then said it was borderline, but she never gave me a figure I can remember, and nobody started me on a tablet.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you remember when that cholesterol check was?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. A good few years ago, could be five, could be more, and I haven't a clue about the month.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He still buys the full-fat cheese, whatever he says about easing off. Sorry, Graham.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try to ease off, Pauline, for about a fortnight, and then Christmas happened. Anyway, that's not why we're here.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Given the clinic readings, and your dad's stroke sitting in the background, I think I'd like to start a small dose of amlodipine today, five milligrams.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. A tablet, today. I wasn't expecting that, if I'm honest, because I feel fine and the form is the thing I came for, and a new tablet might make me woozy at the office, which would be a whole other form.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Before you write it, doctor, he's got a monitor at home. He doesn't use it like he should, mind.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on, what sort of figures does he get at home?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I used it on Sunday. I thought it said one hundred and thirty over eighty, but no, hang on, I've got the scrap in my wallet, it was one hundred and twenty-two over seventy-eight.
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he was gabbling and sweaty in your waiting room, same as always. The second clinic one had already come down a bit, hadn't it, nurse?
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): It had. One hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two from one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight. Still high, but it was falling while he sat.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I also had a large coffee in the car, which I shouldn't have, and I'd rushed, as I said, so I don't think today is a fair day to judge my blood pressure for the rest of my life and stick me on a tablet forever.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's new information, and it does change things. I suspect white coat hypertension, though I can't be sure from today, so you've talked me out of starting amlodipine.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't start any blood pressure tablets today. I'd rather you check it at home, morning and evening, seated, for a week, and bring the readings in.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do that. The monitor's the Omron one from Boots, Pauline set the date on it because I got the year wrong, which is typical, and I'll write them in the notebook if I remember. I might forget the evening one if Match of the Day is on.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll remind him on Tuesdays and Fridays. The other evenings he's on his own, so I can't promise those.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's plenty. Use the same arm, sitting quietly for a few minutes first, and don't bother if you've just dashed up the stairs.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Right arm, I assume, that's the one they always use. And what about the knee form, because my manager will be on at me, and Friday is when they wanted it, though Monday would do if the post is slow, which it is round our way.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the knee before I sign anything. Hop on the couch, or just swing round in the chair, whichever is easier.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Chair is easier. The couch is a bit high and I'd make a meal of getting down, and then we'd be here all afternoon, and Pauline's got another client at half twelve.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): No swelling that I can see, and it's not hot. You bend it fully, and it's a bit tender over the front if I press. Nothing worrying there.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Tender, yes, that's the spot, just under the kneecap. It's only the right, the left has always been fine, touch wood, even after that fun run I did and regretted.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): So this is a straightforward ache at the front of the right knee. I don't think you need a scan for it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, because I hate those machines. My brother had an MRI for his back and he said it was like being posted through a letterbox, and I've got broad shoulders.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll sign the occupational health form to say you're fit for your desk job. I'd lay off lots of stairs for a couple of weeks while it settles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol helps the knee a bit. I take two of the five-hundred milligram ones, so a gram, not every day, just when I've been on the stairs.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's a sensible dose. Carry on with that as you need it. No anti-inflammatory if you can help it, with the blood pressure question still open.
[SEG0051] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He had ibuprofen in the cupboard from his brother. I told him not to take his brother's tablets.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take them. I just looked at the box. His name's on it, Derek, which is not me.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Stick to your own paracetamol. Now, for the pressure, a week of home readings, then I want to see you back here with the notebook.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): In a week exactly, or roughly a week? Only I've got a half day Thursday week, and parking is easier then, and if the readings are all normal I don't want to be started on a tablet at that visit either.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book about a week from today, Thursday is fine if that's when you can park. If the home readings are truly normal we still won't start tablets. We'll decide when we see them.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that at the desk on your way out, Mr Hale. And I'll print a little home blood pressure sheet if you want lines to write on.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes please, lines are better, my handwriting goes walkabout. And can you put morning and evening on it so Pauline can tell me off properly.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse Bennett will sort the sheet and the appointment. Anything else worrying you, even if it feels minor?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Not medically. The meter in the car park ate my change once last month, but that's the council, and I work for them, so I shouldn't complain, except I will, at the water cooler, at length.
[SEG0060] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll be off, then. I'll make sure the notebook actually comes back with him.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lovely. No new tablets today, home readings for a week, and the form will be signed before you leave. Take care, both of you.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me on short notice. My blood pressure is still up, even on my usual treatment, and my carer here thought I should come.

[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Lina, that's very helpful. Mr Hartley, have you noticed any symptoms from it? ~
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Headaches, mostly in the mornings, at the back of my head.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about when you stand up?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit dizzy, yes. I hold the bench for a second.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blurred vision?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes are fine.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the ankles?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No swelling.

[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the same as at home. ~
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is. Which is why I believe the home machine. Let me listen to your heart.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Go ahead. ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, with no murmurs.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing at all.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): What I'm seeing is blood pressure above target, which is consistent with your home readings.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): What does that mean? ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): It means the treatment isn't doing enough. Before I change anything, I'd like to arrange a blood test for your kidney function and salts.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): When can he do that? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Today, if he's willing. I'd like to check it's safe to adjust things. ~
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Of course. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lina, can you keep recording the morning readings, and bring the diary back? ~
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And try to cut the salt in his meals.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll do that. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks with the diary.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Thank you very much. ~
